```{r mlr_regularized_coefficients, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# OLS vs LASSO vs RIDGE — COEFFICIENT COMPARISON
# All three models are fit once on the full initial training
# window, the same window used for the OLS and ARIMAX coefficient
# tables earlier in the document, rather than inside the
# walk-forward loop. This keeps the comparison focused on what
# each method does to the same fixed set of coefficients, without
# the added complexity of 40+ re-estimations per model.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# REUSABLE EXTRACTION FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   df_levels      : levels dataset (complete cases only)
#   var_dep        : name of the dependent variable column
#   n_train        : size of the initial training window
#   couleur_header : hex colour for the table header row
#   caption_text   : caption string passed to kable()
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_coefs_regularized <- function(df_levels, var_dep, n_train,
                                        couleur_header, caption_text) {

  # STEP 1 — Isolate the training window and build the matrix/vector
  # inputs glmnet requires. x_train column order follows vars_exo,
  # which is the same order coef() returns coefficients in below.
  fenetre_train <- df_levels[1:n_train, c(var_dep, vars_exo)]
  x_train       <- as.matrix(fenetre_train[, vars_exo])
  y_train       <- fenetre_train[[var_dep]]

  # STEP 2 — Fit OLS on the same window, for the baseline column.
  # This mirrors extraire_coefs_mlr() above; the intercept is
  # dropped since it carries no economic interpretation in a
  # levels regression with trending variables.
  modele_lm <- lm(as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ .")), data = fenetre_train)
  coef_ols  <- coef(modele_lm)[vars_exo]   # drop intercept, fix order

  # STEP 3 — Fit LASSO (alpha = 1) via 5-fold cross-validation to
  # select the penalty strength, then extract coefficients at the
  # lambda that minimised cross-validated error. coef() on a
  # cv.glmnet object returns a sparse matrix with the intercept as
  # the first row; [-1] drops it, and as.numeric() converts the
  # sparse column to a plain vector.
  set.seed(42)
  cv_lasso    <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 1, nfolds = 5)
  coef_lasso  <- as.numeric(coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.min"))[-1]
  names(coef_lasso) <- vars_exo

  # STEP 4 — Same procedure for Ridge (alpha = 0).
  set.seed(42)
  cv_ridge    <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 0, nfolds = 5)
  coef_ridge  <- as.numeric(coef(cv_ridge, s = "lambda.min"))[-1]
  names(coef_ridge) <- vars_exo

  # STEP 5 — Assemble the comparison table. dropped_lasso flags
  # variables LASSO shrunk exactly to zero, i.e. effectively
  # removed from the specification.
  df_coef <- data.frame(
    Variable      = labels_mlr[vars_exo],
    OLS           = round(coef_ols,   4),
    LASSO         = round(coef_lasso, 4),
    Ridge         = round(coef_ridge, 4),
    dropped_lasso = coef_lasso == 0,
    row.names     = NULL
  )

  # STEP 6 — Render with the LASSO column greyed out and italicised
  # wherever the coefficient was shrunk to zero, so dropped
  # variables are visually distinct from retained ones at a glance.
  kable(df_coef %>% select(-dropped_lasso),
        caption   = caption_text,
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Variable", "OLS", "LASSO", "Ridge")) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                  font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
    column_spec(3,
                color  = ifelse(df_coef$dropped_lasso, "grey60", "black"),
                italic = df_coef$dropped_lasso) %>%
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE,
             background = couleur_header, color = "white")
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA COEFFICIENT COMPARISON
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_coefs_regularized(
  df_levels      = df_arabica_levels,
  var_dep        = "arabica_price",
  n_train        = n_train_ara_lev,
  couleur_header = "#8B4513",
  caption_text   = "OLS, LASSO and Ridge coefficients — Arabica (full training set)"
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ROBUSTA COEFFICIENT COMPARISON
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_coefs_regularized(
  df_levels      = df_robusta_levels,
  var_dep        = "robusta_price",
  n_train        = n_train_rob_lev,
  couleur_header = "#2E8B57",
  caption_text   = "OLS, LASSO and Ridge coefficients — Robusta (full training set)"
)
```

The coefficient tables reveal something the performance comparison alone could not: LASSO barely performs variable selection here at all. Across 28 coefficients (14 predictors × 2 varieties), only two are shrunk exactly to zero, CPI for Arabica and Temperature for Robusta. Every other predictor is retained by LASSO at a magnitude close to its OLS counterpart, meaning the performance gains and losses documented above come almost entirely from shrinkage, not from dropping variables.

The two variables LASSO does eliminate are not arbitrary. CPI carries the highest VIF among all Arabica predictors (above 27, as shown in the earlier VIF table) and was already flagged as a source of unreliable OLS estimates. Temperature is Robusta's most unstable coefficient of all: its OLS estimate is positive (0.516), consistent with no clear physical story, while Ridge pushes it to a large negative value (−12.706), and LASSO drops it entirely rather than trying to resolve the disagreement. A coefficient whose sign depends on which estimator is used is not one that should be read as evidence of a genuine physical relationship between temperature and Robusta prices; it is a symptom of the same collinearity documented throughout this section, and LASSO's response, to remove it, is arguably the most honest of the three.

Ridge tells a more nuanced story than "shrinkage" alone would suggest. Most coefficients do shrink toward zero relative to OLS, as expected: the Fed Funds Rate falls from 46.01 to 26.37 for Robusta, DXY from 15.39 to 8.53, CPI from −20.75 to −5.57. But a few move in the opposite direction. Arabica's ONI coefficient grows from −0.007 under OLS to −0.024 under Ridge, more than tripling in magnitude despite the overall regularisation. This is a known property of Ridge in the presence of severe collinearity: OLS can artificially suppress a coefficient when its effect is entangled with correlated predictors, and Ridge, by redistributing weight more evenly across the correlated group, can partially "free" that coefficient rather than shrink it. Far from contradicting the regularisation story, this reinforces it: the OLS coefficients reported earlier in this section were never a reliable guide to individual effect sizes to begin with.

Read together with the performance results, this offers a partial answer to why variable importance differs between the two varieties. Robusta's predictors are more severely entangled, evidenced by the Temperature sign reversal and the larger absolute shrinkage Ridge applies across the board, and it is precisely this variety where regularisation delivers the larger performance gain. Arabica's coefficients are comparatively better-behaved to begin with, which is consistent with regularisation having less to fix and, in this case, making things marginally worse rather than better.

## ARIMAX

ARIMAX combines a standard linear regression on the 14 exogenous predictors with an ARMA structure applied to what that regression leaves unexplained. The idea is simple: prices don't just react to WTI, CPI, and the rest of the predictor set, they also carry their own momentum, so treating the residual as pure noise (the way MLR does) throws away information a time series model can actually use.

*This chunk estimates the ARIMAX model for both coffee series using a walk-forward expanding window. At each step, `auto.arima()` selects the optimal $(p,d,q)$ order by minimising AIC over the current training window, then generates a one-step-ahead forecast using the next row of exogenous regressors. The model is therefore re-specified at every forecast origin, allowing the autoregressive structure to adapt as new observations are added to the training window. As with the MLR function above, the code is written as a sequence of explicit, separate steps.*

```{r arimax, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(forecast)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARIMAX ESTIMATION FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#             ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train : size of the initial training window (number of
#             rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
#   model     : the ARIMAX model fitted once on the initial
#               training set only (used later for reporting
#               the selected order, coefficients, and residuals)
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_arimax <- function(df, var_dep, n_train) {

  # STEP 1 — Separate the dependent variable from the
  # exogenous regressors. auto.arima() requires the regressors
  # as a plain numeric matrix, not a data frame.
  serie_dependante    <- df[[var_dep]]
  matrice_regresseurs <- as.matrix(df[, vars_exo])

  # Safety check: drop any regressor column that is entirely
  # NA (this should not normally happen, since rows with any
  # NA were already removed upstream by preparer_niveaux()).
  colonnes_valides    <- apply(matrice_regresseurs, 2,
                               function(col) !all(is.na(col)))
  matrice_regresseurs <- matrice_regresseurs[, colonnes_valides, drop = FALSE]

  # STEP 2 — Split into the initial training set and the test
  # set, using the row count computed in the preprocessing chunk.
  n_total <- length(serie_dependante)

  y_train    <- serie_dependante[1:n_train]
  y_test     <- serie_dependante[(n_train + 1):n_total]

  xreg_train <- matrice_regresseurs[1:n_train, ]
  xreg_test  <- matrice_regresseurs[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]

  n_test <- length(y_test)

  # STEP 3 — Walk-forward loop.
  # At forecasting step i, auto.arima() is re-estimated on ALL
  # observations available up to that point: the initial
  # training set, plus every test-period observation already
  # passed (rows 1 to i-1 of y_test / xreg_test). The order
  # (p, d, q) is re-selected by AIC at every step — it is not
  # fixed in advance. The freshly estimated model then produces
  # a single one-step-ahead forecast for observation i, using
  # row i of xreg_test as the future regressor values.
  #
  # Search constraints passed to auto.arima():
  #   max.p = 3, max.q = 3 : keeps the search computationally
  #     feasible across the ~43 re-estimations of the loop
  #   max.d = 1            : consistent with the integration
  #     order established in the stationarity tests
  #   stepwise = TRUE, approximation = TRUE : faster greedy
  #     search instead of an exhaustive grid, needed because
  #     the model is re-estimated at every single step
  #
  # tryCatch() catches any estimation failure (which can happen
  # at the very first steps, when the window is still small)
  # and records NA for that step instead of stopping the loop.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_observations_vues <- i - 1   # 0 at step 1, 1 at step 2, ...

    # Observations of the test period already "seen" before step i
    indices_vus <- seq_len(nb_observations_vues)
    y_vu        <- y_test[indices_vus]
    xreg_vu     <- xreg_test[indices_vus, , drop = FALSE]

    # The expanding training window for this step
    y_fenetre    <- c(y_train, y_vu)
    xreg_fenetre <- rbind(xreg_train, xreg_vu)

    modele_arima <- tryCatch(
      auto.arima(y_fenetre, xreg = xreg_fenetre,
                 stepwise      = TRUE,
                 approximation = TRUE,
                 max.p = 3, max.q = 3, max.d = 1),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(modele_arima)) {
      predictions[i] <- NA
      next
    }

    # One-step-ahead forecast using row i of the test regressors
    ligne_regresseurs_futurs <- matrix(xreg_test[i, ], nrow = 1)
    prevision <- forecast(modele_arima, h = 1,
                          xreg = ligne_regresseurs_futurs)
    predictions[i] <- prevision$mean[1]
  }

  # STEP 4 — Fit one additional model on the initial training
  # set only (not the walk-forward loop). This single model is
  # kept purely for reporting purposes later in the document:
  # the selected ARIMA order, the regression coefficients, and
  # the residual diagnostics all refer to this training-set-only
  # model rather than to any of the ~43 models re-estimated
  # during the walk-forward loop above.
  modele_sur_entrainement <- auto.arima(y_train, xreg = xreg_train,
                                        stepwise      = TRUE,
                                        approximation = TRUE)

  list(actual    = y_test,
       predicted = predictions,
       model     = modele_sur_entrainement)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ESTIMATION — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# Both series use their respective levels datasets and
# pre-computed training set sizes from the preprocessing chunk.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_arimax_ara <- fit_arimax(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev)
res_arimax_rob <- fit_arimax(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS
# calculer_metriques() is applied to the walk-forward
# predictions accumulated over the full test period. Results
# are stored in the same standardised format as the other five
# models for direct combination in the comparative performance
# chunk later in this document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_arimax <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_ara$actual, res_arimax_ara$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_rob$actual, res_arimax_rob$predicted))
)
```

ARIMAX turns out to be one of the strongest models tested in this study. It reaches an $R^2$ of 0.821 for Arabica and 0.929 for Robusta, meaning the model captures the vast majority of price movement over both test periods. Beyond the walk-forward loop that produces these out-of-sample forecasts, a separate ARIMAX model is estimated once on the initial training window only, and never updated thereafter. This second model plays no role in the reported performance metrics; it exists solely to provide a single, stable reference point, an order, a set of coefficients, and a set of residuals, that the sections below all refer back to, rather than trying to summarise 43 potentially different models estimated over the course of the walk-forward procedure.

### Model Order and Estimation

```{r arimax_order}
# Report the ARIMA order selected on the full training set
# for each series, for methodological transparency.
cat("Arabica - ARIMA order selected by auto.arima():\n")
print(res_arimax_ara$model)
cat("\nRobusta - ARIMA order selected by auto.arima():\n")
print(res_arimax_rob$model)
```

On the full training set, `auto.arima()` settles on a Regression with ARIMA(1,0,0) errors for Arabica and a Regression with ARIMA(3,0,1) errors for Robusta. Neither model differences the residuals $(d=0)$, which makes sense once you consider what the regression component is already doing: prices and the exogenous predictors trend together over the sample, so the regression absorbs that shared drift on its own, leaving behind a residual that doesn't need further differencing to behave. The AR(1) coefficient of 0.967 for Arabica is a striking number in its own right. It says the residual carries over from one month to the next almost entirely, which lines up with the strong persistence already visible in the descriptive statistics. Robusta's richer ARMA(3,1) structure suggests there is more short-run dynamics to capture in this series, consistent with it being the more volatile of the two.

### Regression Coefficients

The tables below report the coefficients of the exogenous regressors from the ARIMAX model estimated on the full training set for each variety. Two things are worth keeping in mind while reading them. First, these coefficients come from the single reference model, not the walk-forward loop, so they describe an average relationship over the training period rather than a set of stable structural parameters. Second, the same multicollinearity already documented in the correlation and PCA sections applies here too: a regressor showing up as statistically insignificant doesn't mean it contributes nothing to the forecasts, just that OLS-style estimation can't isolate its individual effect cleanly when it moves in lockstep with several other predictors.

*This chunk computes the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for each of the 14 exogenous regressors included in the ARIMAX model, separately for Arabica and Robusta. VIF is computed on an equivalent OLS model estimated on the initial training window, which is the standard approach since the `vif()` function from the `car` package operates on `lm()` objects. The ARMA error structure of ARIMAX does not affect the collinearity structure of the regressors, so the VIF values are directly interpretable in the ARIMAX context.*

```{r arimax_coefficients, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARIMAX COEFFICIENT TABLES — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# coef() and vcov() extract the regression coefficients and
# their variance-covariance matrix from the final ARIMAX model
# fitted on the full training set. t-statistics and p-values
# are computed manually since forecast objects do not have a
# native tidy() method that separates ARMA from xreg terms.
# Only the exogenous regressor coefficients are displayed —
# the ARMA error structure terms (ar1, ma1, etc.) are excluded
# to focus on the interpretable predictors.
# Header colour and significance colour-coding now match the
# convention used elsewhere in the document (extraire_coefs_mlr,
# calculer_vif): couleur_header sets the brown/green header per
# variety, and the significance column is colour-coded so the
# reader can spot significant predictors at a glance rather than
# scanning p-values row by row.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# REUSABLE COEFFICIENT EXTRACTION AND FORMATTING FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   model          : the ARIMAX model object (res_arimax_ara$model
#                    or res_arimax_rob$model), fitted once on the
#                    full initial training window elsewhere in the
#                    document — never re-fitted here
#   couleur_header : hex colour for the table header row, brown
#                    for Arabica ("#8B4513") or green for Robusta
#                    ("#2E8B57"), matching every other table in
#                    this document
#   caption_text   : caption string passed to kable()
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_coefs_arimax <- function(model, couleur_header, caption_text) {

  # STEP 1 — Extract raw coefficients and their standard errors.
  # coef() returns ALL estimated parameters, including the ARMA
  # error-structure terms (ar1, ar2, ma1, etc.) alongside the 14
  # exogenous regressor coefficients — these are filtered out in
  # STEP 3 below. vcov() returns the full variance-covariance
  # matrix; diag() extracts just the variances (the diagonal),
  # and sqrt() converts each variance to a standard error.
  co <- coef(model)
  se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(model)))

  # STEP 2 — Compute t-statistics and p-values by hand.
  # forecast::Arima objects have no built-in tidy() method that
  # separates ARMA terms from exogenous regressors the way
  # broom::tidy() does for lm() objects, so this is done manually:
  #   t-statistic = coefficient estimate divided by its std. error
  #   p-value     = two-sided test against a standard normal
  #                 distribution (pnorm), since these are
  #                 maximum-likelihood estimates rather than
  #                 OLS estimates with a t-distribution
  tstat <- co / se
  pval  <- 2 * pnorm(abs(tstat), lower.tail = FALSE)

  # STEP 3 — Assemble the display data frame and keep only the
  # exogenous regressors. grepl() with a regex matches any
  # variable name starting with "ar", "ma", "intercept" or
  # containing "drift" (case-insensitive), and filter(!...)
  # removes those rows, leaving only the 14 predictor coefficients.
  # The Sig column applies the conventional significance stars
  # used throughout this document (***, **, *, ., or blank).
  df_coef <- data.frame(
    Variable  = names(co),
    Estimate  = round(co,    4),
    Std_Error = round(se,    4),
    t_stat    = round(tstat, 3),
    P_value   = round(pval,  4),
    Sig       = case_when(
      pval < 0.001 ~ "***",
      pval < 0.01  ~ "**",
      pval < 0.05  ~ "*",
      pval < 0.1   ~ ".",
      TRUE         ~ ""
    ),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("^ar|^ma|^intercept|drift", Variable,
                ignore.case = TRUE))

  # STEP 4 — Build a colour vector for the significance column.
  # Computed once here, outside kable(), so it can be reused for
  # both the text colour of the Sig column (STEP 5) and the row
  # background shading, keeping the two visual cues consistent
  # with each other: green for conventional significance
  # (p < 0.05), orange for the weaker 0.05-0.1 band, grey for
  # everything else.
  sig_colors <- case_when(
    df_coef$P_value < 0.05 ~ "#27ae60",
    df_coef$P_value < 0.1  ~ "#d35400",
    TRUE                   ~ "grey50"
  )

  # STEP 5 — Render the table with kableExtra.
  # column_spec(6, ...) colours and bolds the Sig column using the
  # sig_colors vector built in STEP 4. row_spec() with which()
  # lightly shades every row where P_value < 0.05, so significant
  # predictors are visible at a glance without reading each
  # p-value individually. row_spec(0, ...) colours the header row
  # using couleur_header, the brown/green convention passed in as
  # an argument so this single function serves both varieties.
  kable(df_coef,
        caption   = caption_text,
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Variable", "Estimate", "Std. Error",
                      "t-stat", "p-value", "Sig.")) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                  font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
    column_spec(6, bold = TRUE, color = sig_colors) %>%
    row_spec(which(df_coef$P_value < 0.05), background = "#f7fbf8") %>%
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = couleur_header, color = "white")
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA ARIMAX COEFFICIENTS
# Calls the function above with the Arabica reference model
# and the brown header colour used throughout the document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_coefs_arimax(
  res_arimax_ara$model,
  couleur_header = "#8B4513",
  caption_text   = "ARIMAX regression coefficients — Arabica (full training set)"
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ROBUSTA ARIMAX COEFFICIENTS
# Calls the function above with the Robusta reference model
# and the green header colour used throughout the document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

extraire_coefs_arimax(
  res_arimax_rob$model,
  couleur_header = "#2E8B57",
  caption_text   = "ARIMAX regression coefficients — Robusta (full training set)"
)
```

For Arabica, only two regressors clear conventional significance thresholds: Sugar No.11 $(p<0.001)$ and WTI $(p<0.01)$. The Sugar coefficient of 1.022 means a one-unit rise in the Sugar No.11 price comes with roughly a USD 1.02/lb increase in Arabica futures, and the positive WTI coefficient fits the energy cost story already discussed elsewhere in this document. Everything else, including the USDA fundamentals, the climate indices and the COT position, is individually insignificant here even though several of these variables contribute meaningfully to the machine learning models' forecasts. That apparent contradiction is exactly what severe multicollinearity produces: a group of correlated predictors can carry real, usable information collectively while none of them stands out individually in a linear regression.

Robusta tells a similar story with a different cast of significant variables. CPI $(p<0.01)$ and WTI $(p<0.05)$ come through as significant, underlining how much macroeconomic conditions matter for this series. COT net Managed Money is highly significant too $(p<0.001)$, with a coefficient of 0.003, small on a per-contract basis but economically meaningful once you scale it up to the tens of thousands of contracts these funds typically hold. As with Arabica, the USDA fundamentals stay insignificant, for the same collinearity reasons.

### Multicollinearity Diagnostics

Before taking those coefficients at face value, it's worth asking how much the model can actually tell individual predictors apart given how correlated they are with each other.

*This chunk computes the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for each of the 14 exogenous regressors included in the ARIMAX model, separately for Arabica and Robusta.*

```{r arimax_vif, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# VARIANCE INFLATION FACTORS — ARIMAX REGRESSORS
# The coefficient tables above show that few regressors reach
# conventional significance thresholds in either ARIMAX model.
# One plausible explanation is severe multicollinearity among
# the 14 predictors, already suggested by the correlation
# matrix and PCA analyses. The Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
# quantifies this formally: for each regressor, it measures
# how much its variance is inflated relative to what it would
# be if it were orthogonal to all other predictors.
#
# VIF interpretation thresholds:
#   VIF < 5      : acceptable
#   5 ≤ VIF < 10 : moderate multicollinearity
#   VIF ≥ 10     : severe — coefficient estimates and standard
#                  errors are unreliable
#
# VIF is computed on an equivalent OLS model estimated on the
# initial training window. This is the standard approach since
# vif() from the car package operates on lm() objects. The
# ARMA error structure of ARIMAX does not affect the regressor
# collinearity structure, so the VIF values are directly
# interpretable in the ARIMAX context.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(car)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# DISPLAY LABELS
# Internal variable names are replaced with the same readable
# English labels used in the correlation matrix and PCA plots,
# ensuring visual consistency across all figures in the document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

labels_vif <- c(
  "sugar_price"    = "Sugar",
  "cocoa_price"    = "Cocoa",
  "cpi"            = "CPI",
  "wti"            = "WTI",
  "fed_funds_rate" = "Fed Funds Rate",
  "dxy"            = "DXY",
  "production"     = "Production",
  "consumption"    = "Consumption",
  "exports"        = "Exports",
  "ending_stocks"  = "Ending stocks",
  "indice_precip"  = "Precipitation",
  "indice_temp"    = "Temperature",
  "oni"            = "ONI",
  "cot_net_mm"     = "COT net MM"
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# REUSABLE VIF FUNCTION
# Encapsulates the lm() estimation, vif() computation and
# kableExtra rendering in a single call. Avoids duplicating
# the same block for Arabica and Robusta.
#
# Arguments:
#   df_levels      : levels dataset (complete cases only)
#   var_dep        : name of the dependent variable column
#   n_train        : size of the initial training window
#   couleur_header : hex colour for the table header row
#   caption_text   : caption string passed to kable()
# ----------------------------------------------------------

calculer_vif <- function(df_levels, var_dep, n_train,
                         couleur_header, caption_text) {

  # Fit the equivalent OLS model on the training window.
  # as.formula() constructs the formula dynamically so the
  # function works with any dependent variable name.
  modele_lm <- lm(
    as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ .")),
    data = df_levels[1:n_train, c(var_dep, vars_exo)]
  )

  vif_scores <- vif(modele_lm)

  # Replace internal names with display labels
  names(vif_scores) <- labels_vif[names(vif_scores)]

  # Build the display data frame with a diagnostic column
  # so the severity interpretation is explicit in the table
  # rather than conveyed only through row colour.
  df_vif <- data.frame(
    Variable   = names(vif_scores),
    VIF        = round(vif_scores, 2),
    Diagnostic = case_when(
      vif_scores >= 10 ~ "Severe",
      vif_scores >=  5 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE             ~ "Acceptable"
    ),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  # Colour vectors for text and background of Diagnostic cell,
  # applied row by row via column_spec() below.
  text_colors <- case_when(
    vif_scores >= 10 ~ "#c0392b",
    vif_scores >=  5 ~ "#d35400",
    TRUE             ~ "#27ae60"
  )

  bg_colors <- case_when(
    vif_scores >= 10 ~ "#fdf2f2",
    vif_scores >=  5 ~ "#fef6ec",
    TRUE             ~ "#f2faf5"
  )

  kable(df_vif,
        caption   = caption_text,
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Variable", "VIF", "Diagnostic")) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                  font_size = 11, full_width = FALSE) %>%
    # Colour the VIF value in red/orange for severe/moderate cases
    column_spec(2,
                bold  = vif_scores >= 5,
                color = ifelse(vif_scores >= 10, "#c0392b",
                        ifelse(vif_scores >=  5, "#d35400",
                               "black"))) %>%
    # Colour the Diagnostic cell background and text
    column_spec(3,
                bold       = vif_scores >= 5,
                color      = text_colors,
                background = bg_colors) %>%
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE,
             background = couleur_header, color = "white")
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA VIF
# Training window: n_train_ara_lev rows (2006-06 to end of
# training period), the same window used by fit_arimax().
# ----------------------------------------------------------

calculer_vif(
  df_levels      = df_arabica_levels,
  var_dep        = "arabica_price",
  n_train        = n_train_ara_lev,
  couleur_header = "#8B4513",
  caption_text   = "Variance Inflation Factors — Arabica ARIMAX regressors (training set)"
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ROBUSTA VIF
# Training window: n_train_rob_lev rows (2008-01 to end of
# training period). The shorter sample may amplify
# multicollinearity relative to Arabica, since macroeconomic
# variables trend more uniformly over this restricted window.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

calculer_vif(
  df_levels      = df_robusta_levels,
  var_dep        = "robusta_price",
  n_train        = n_train_rob_lev,
  couleur_header = "#2E8B57",
  caption_text   = "Variance Inflation Factors — Robusta ARIMAX regressors (training set)"
)
```

The VIF table puts a number on something the correlation matrix and PCA had already hinted at. Exports, Production and Consumption are the worst offenders, with VIF values between 21 and 49 depending on the variety, which isn't surprising since all three trend upward together as global coffee demand grows over the period. CPI is in the same boat, with a VIF above 27 in both cases, because it shares that same broad upward trend with nearly every other nominal variable in the dataset. DXY crosses the severity threshold too, likely from its extended co-movement with CPI through the post-2008 monetary policy cycle.

The variables on the safer end of the table tell a more encouraging story. COT net MM, the climate indices, Ending stocks and the Fed Funds Rate all sit comfortably below 5, and these happen to be exactly the variables whose ARIMAX coefficients came out with economically sensible signs and, where significant, results that can actually be trusted. The bigger picture here is that low t-statistics for Production, Consumption and Exports don't mean supply fundamentals don't matter to coffee prices. They mean OLS can't tell apart three series that move almost identically over time, no matter how much data you throw at it. The information is real, it just can't be attributed to one variable over another within a linear framework.

### Residual Diagnostics

Under a correctly specified ARIMAX model, the residuals remaining after accounting for both the regression and the ARMA structure should approximate white noise, exhibiting no systematic pattern left uncaptured.

*This chunk provides a formal visual diagnostic of the ARIMAX residuals for both series via ACF and PACF plots. Under correct model specification, the residuals should exhibit no systematic autocorrelation at any lag, that is, all spikes in both plots should fall within the blue dashed confidence bands ($\pm 1.96 / \sqrt{T}$).*

```{r arimax_residuals_diagnostics, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ACF AND PACF OF ARIMAX RESIDUALS — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# If the ARIMAX model is correctly specified, the residuals
# should behave as white noise: no significant autocorrelation
# at any lag. The ACF and PACF plots provide a visual check
# of this assumption. Spikes exceeding the blue dashed
# confidence bands (±1.96/√T) indicate residual autocorrelation
# that the model has failed to capture.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

acf(residuals(res_arimax_ara$model),
    main = "ACF — Arabica residuals",
    lag.max = 24, col = "#8B4513")

pacf(residuals(res_arimax_ara$model),
     main = "PACF — Arabica residuals",
     lag.max = 24, col = "#8B4513")

acf(residuals(res_arimax_rob$model),
    main = "ACF — Robusta residuals",
    lag.max = 24, col = "#2E8B57")

pacf(residuals(res_arimax_rob$model),
     main = "PACF — Robusta residuals",
     lag.max = 24, col = "#2E8B57")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The two series don't behave the same way here. Robusta is close to clean, with only minor exceedances at lags 1 and 15 in the ACF and a single spike at lag 15 in the PACF, nothing that points to a systematic pattern the ARIMA(3,0,1) structure missed.

Arabica is a different story. The ACF shows significant spikes at lags 1, 2, 5, 6, 16 and 24, and the PACF at lags 1, 5, 8 and 10, which means the ARIMA(1,0,0) structure isn't fully capturing this series' autocorrelation. A higher-order specification, adding AR terms around lags 5 or 6, would probably reduce this residual dependence, but the walk-forward loop's computational budget capped the search at $p=3$. This is acknowledged as a direction for future refinement rather than something that undermines the out-of-sample result: Arabica still reaches an $R^2$ of 0.821 under walk-forward validation despite this imperfection.

*This chunk formally tests the stationarity of the ARIMAX residuals using the same ADF/KPSS procedure applied to the raw series in the Stationarity Tests section, reusing `tester_serie()` directly. This complements the ACF/PACF diagnostics above: autocorrelation and stationarity are related but distinct properties, and confirming both gives a fuller picture of whether the $d=0$ specification is well supported.*

```{r arimax_residuals_stationarity, warning = FALSE}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STATIONARITY OF ARIMAX RESIDUALS — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# The d=0 specification selected by auto.arima() for both series
# implies that the regression component absorbs the trending
# co-movement between prices and the exogenous regressors, leaving
# residuals that do not require differencing. This chunk tests that
# claim directly, applying the same ADF/KPSS procedure used on the
# raw series earlier in the document to the residuals of the
# reference ARIMAX model instead.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# STEP 1 — Extract residuals from the two reference ARIMAX models
# (fitted once on the full initial training window elsewhere in
# the document, never re-fitted here).
residus_ara <- residuals(res_arimax_ara$model)
residus_rob <- residuals(res_arimax_rob$model)

# STEP 2 — Run the same ADF/KPSS testing function already defined
# in the main Stationarity Tests chunk, applied here to the
# residuals rather than the raw price series.
resultats_residus <- rbind(
  cbind(Variable = "ARIMAX residuals (Arabica)", tester_serie(residus_ara)),
  cbind(Variable = "ARIMAX residuals (Robusta)", tester_serie(residus_rob))
)

# STEP 3 — Render the table. Since both varieties sit in the same
# table (one row each) rather than two separate tables, row_spec()
# is used to apply a light variety-specific background tint per
# row instead of pack_rows(), which is designed for grouping
# multiple rows rather than colouring a single one. The ADF and
# KPSS result columns keep their existing green/red text colour
# coding, now bolded for better legibility against the tinted rows.
kable(resultats_residus,
      caption   = "ADF and KPSS stationarity tests — ARIMAX residuals (reference model)",
      booktabs  = TRUE,
      row.names = FALSE,
      col.names = c("Variable", "ADF stat", "ADF p-val", "ADF result",
                    "KPSS stat", "KPSS p-val", "KPSS result")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 10, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  # Bold the Variable column so each row's variety is easy to spot
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE) %>%
  # Bold and colour-code the ADF and KPSS result columns
  column_spec(4, bold = TRUE,
              color = ifelse(resultats_residus$ADF_result == "Stationary",
                             "darkgreen", "#c0392b")) %>%
  column_spec(7, bold = TRUE,
              color = ifelse(resultats_residus$KPSS_result == "Stationary",
                             "darkgreen", "#c0392b")) %>%
  # Light variety-specific row tinting, consistent with the
  # brown/green convention used throughout the document
  row_spec(1, background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  row_spec(2, background = "#e8f5ec") %>%
  # Bold, dark header row (neutral colour since the table spans
  # both varieties rather than being variety-specific)
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = "#4a4a4a", color = "white")
```

The results mostly back up the $d=0$ specification, though not with the same confidence for both varieties. Robusta is unambiguous: the ADF rejects the unit root ($p = 0.010$) and the KPSS doesn't reject stationarity, confirming the ARIMA(3,0,1) structure is operating on a genuinely stationary residual, which fits the clean ACF/PACF result above.

Arabica sits closer to the edge. The KPSS doesn't reject stationarity, but the ADF result lands right at the conventional 5% threshold ($p = 0.054$), and `R`'s own warning flags that the true p-value is smaller than what's printed, so this is a genuinely borderline case rather than a clean pass or fail. It's the same kind of ambiguity already seen for several raw series in the main stationarity analysis. Put together with the residual autocorrelation already noted above, the picture for Arabica is consistent: the $d=0$ specification is reasonable and the residuals are close to stationary, but the model isn't perfectly specified for this series, a limitation already on the table rather than a new concern.

## Random Forest

*This chunk estimates the Random Forest model for both series. The implementation follows the same walk-forward structure as MLR and ARIMAX above, with two differences specific to this model family: all variables, including the dependent variable, are Min-Max scaled to $[0, 1]$ before estimation, and the forest is grown with 500 trees at each step with importance recording enabled. The variable importance scores from the final iteration of the loop are retained and used in the importance plot chunk later in the document.*

```{r random_forest, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(randomForest)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# RANDOM FOREST ESTIMATION FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#             ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train : size of the initial training window (number of
#             rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual     : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted  : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
#                (still on the [0, 1] scaled range — the
#                back-transformation to USD happens later,
#                in the trajectory plot chunk)
#   importance : permutation-based variable importance scores
#                from the LAST walk-forward step only, i.e. the
#                forest grown on the largest training window
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_rf <- function(df, var_dep, n_train) {

  # STEP 1 — Keep only the columns this model needs, the same
  # safety check as in the MLR function. No complete.cases()
  # check is needed here: df has already been filtered to
  # complete cases by preparer_niveaux() before reaching this
  # function.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column (including the
  # dependent variable) to the [0, 1] range. sapply() applies
  # minmax_scale() to each column in turn and returns a matrix,
  # which is then converted back to a data frame.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Split into the initial training set and the test set.
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 4 — Walk-forward loop.
  # At each step, a brand new forest of 500 trees is grown on
  # the expanding training window (initial training set plus
  # all test rows already passed), exactly as in the MLR loop.
  # This is more computationally expensive than for MLR, since
  # growing 500 trees is slower than fitting one linear model,
  # but it is necessary to prevent any future observation from
  # influencing the ensemble.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    foret <- randomForest(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                          ntree = 500, importance = TRUE)

    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, ]
    predictions[i]  <- predict(foret, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  # STEP 5 — Variable importance scores from the forest grown
  # at the LAST loop iteration (the one with the most training
  # data) are kept for the importance plot later in the document.
  scores_importance <- importance(foret)

  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual     = valeurs_observees,
       predicted  = predictions,
       importance = scores_importance)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ESTIMATION — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_rf_ara <- fit_rf(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev)
res_rf_rob <- fit_rf(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_rf <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_ara$actual, res_rf_ara$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_rob$actual, res_rf_rob$predicted))
)
```

The Random Forest model achieves an $R^2$ of 0.811 for Arabica and 0.695 for Robusta. The model's ensemble structure, averaging predictions across 500 decision trees, provides robustness to outliers and non-linear relationships that the linear benchmarks cannot capture. The walk-forward re-estimation at each step ensures that the model is never trained on future observations, mitigating overfitting concerns that would arise under standard cross-validation. Performance on Robusta is somewhat lower than on Arabica, consistent with the shorter and more volatile training sample available for this variety.

### Random Forest: Tree Count and Complexity Tuning

The Random Forest specification estimated above uses 500 trees with no explicit control on tree complexity beyond randomForest's defaults. This section tests whether varying the number of trees, or constraining individual tree complexity, changes out-of-sample performance. Three levers are tested separately, each isolated by holding the other two at their default value: the number of trees (`ntree`), the minimum size of a terminal node (`nodesize`, R's closest equivalent to the pruning-style complexity control requested during supervision, since `randomForest` has no `cp` parameter, that being specific to a single `rpart` tree), and the maximum number of terminal nodes allowed per tree (`maxnodes`).

*This chunk defines a generic Random Forest estimation function that accepts `ntree`, `nodesize` and `maxnodes` as arguments, alongside the three configuration lists to be tested. The function mirrors the walk-forward structure of `fit_rf()` above, with the three complexity parameters exposed rather than hard-coded, so the same function serves all three comparisons in this section.*

```{r rf_tuning_setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# RANDOM FOREST — TREE COUNT AND COMPLEXITY TUNING
# randomForest has no cp (complexity parameter) argument, since cp
# is specific to a single rpart tree and its cost-complexity pruning
# procedure; a Random Forest never prunes individual trees that way.
# The closest available levers for controlling the complexity of the
# trees grown within a Random Forest are nodesize (minimum size of a
# terminal node — larger values force shallower, simpler trees) and
# maxnodes (a hard cap on the number of terminal nodes per tree).
# Both are tested here alongside ntree (the number of trees), each
# varied separately while the other two are held at randomForest's
# defaults (ntree = 500, nodesize = 5 for regression, maxnodes = NULL
# i.e. unconstrained), so that each comparison isolates one lever.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# Configurations to test, one list per lever. Values are stored as
# named lists so the name (used as a row label in the results table)
# and the actual argument value are kept together.
configs_ntree <- list(
  "ntree = 100"  = 100,
  "ntree = 300"  = 300,
  "ntree = 1000" = 1000
)

configs_nodesize <- list(
  "nodesize = 1"  = 1,
  "nodesize = 10" = 10,
  "nodesize = 20" = 20
)

configs_maxnodes <- list(
  "maxnodes = 10"  = 10,
  "maxnodes = 50"  = 50,
  "maxnodes = 100" = 100
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# WALK-FORWARD ESTIMATION FUNCTION — RANDOM FOREST, TUNABLE
#
# Arguments:
#   df       : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep  : name of the dependent variable column
#              ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train  : size of the initial training window (number of rows),
#              computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#   ntree    : number of trees to grow, default 500 to match the
#              baseline Random Forest specification above
#   nodesize : minimum size of a terminal node, default 5, the
#              randomForest default for regression
#   maxnodes : maximum number of terminal nodes per tree, default
#              NULL (no limit), the randomForest default
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_rf_tuned <- function(df, var_dep, n_train,
                          ntree = 500, nodesize = 5, maxnodes = NULL) {

  # STEP 1 — Restrict the dataset to the columns this model needs,
  # identical to fit_rf() above.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column, including the dependent
  # variable, to the [0, 1] range, identical to every other ML
  # model in this document.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Split into the initial training set and the test set.
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 4 — Walk-forward loop. Identical expanding-window logic to
  # fit_rf() above: at each step, a brand new forest is grown on the
  # initial training set plus every test row already passed, using
  # the ntree/nodesize/maxnodes values passed in as arguments rather
  # than hard-coded, so the same loop serves all three comparisons
  # in this section.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    foret <- randomForest(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                          ntree    = ntree,
                          nodesize = nodesize,
                          maxnodes = maxnodes)

    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, ]
    predictions[i]  <- predict(foret, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  # STEP 5 — Return the observed and predicted test values.
  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}
```

*This chunk runs all three sets of configurations, for both coffee varieties, holding the other two parameters at their `randomForest` default in each case.*

```{r rf_tuning_run, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# RUN ALL THREE PARAMETER SWEEPS, BOTH SERIES
# Each of the three outer loops iterates over one configuration list
# (configs_ntree, configs_nodesize, configs_maxnodes), calling
# fit_rf_tuned() with only that one parameter changed from its
# default, so each comparison isolates a single lever. Results are
# stored in six named lists (one per lever, per variety).
# ----------------------------------------------------------

resultats_ntree_ara    <- list()
resultats_ntree_rob    <- list()
resultats_nodesize_ara <- list()
resultats_nodesize_rob <- list()
resultats_maxnodes_ara <- list()
resultats_maxnodes_rob <- list()

for (nom_config in names(configs_ntree)) {
  cat("Running", nom_config, "- Arabica...\n")
  resultats_ntree_ara[[nom_config]] <- fit_rf_tuned(
    df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev,
    ntree = configs_ntree[[nom_config]])

  cat("Running", nom_config, "- Robusta...\n")
  resultats_ntree_rob[[nom_config]] <- fit_rf_tuned(
    df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev,
    ntree = configs_ntree[[nom_config]])
}

for (nom_config in names(configs_nodesize)) {
  cat("Running", nom_config, "- Arabica...\n")
  resultats_nodesize_ara[[nom_config]] <- fit_rf_tuned(
    df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev,
    nodesize = configs_nodesize[[nom_config]])

  cat("Running", nom_config, "- Robusta...\n")
  resultats_nodesize_rob[[nom_config]] <- fit_rf_tuned(
    df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev,
    nodesize = configs_nodesize[[nom_config]])
}

for (nom_config in names(configs_maxnodes)) {
  cat("Running", nom_config, "- Arabica...\n")
  resultats_maxnodes_ara[[nom_config]] <- fit_rf_tuned(
    df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev,
    maxnodes = configs_maxnodes[[nom_config]])

  cat("Running", nom_config, "- Robusta...\n")
  resultats_maxnodes_rob[[nom_config]] <- fit_rf_tuned(
    df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev,
    maxnodes = configs_maxnodes[[nom_config]])
}
```

*This chunk compiles all three comparisons, together with the baseline Random Forest already estimated earlier in this section (`res_rf_ara`, `res_rf_rob`), into a single table grouped by variety with `pack_rows()`, consistent with the ANN depth and MLR regularisation tables elsewhere in the document.*

```{r rf_tuning_table, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# COMPILE COMPARISON TABLE — BASELINE VS ntree / nodesize / maxnodes
# Each variety block now carries a Group column (Baseline, Number of
# Trees, Node Size, Max Nodes) in addition to Parameter, so that a
# second, nested level of pack_rows() can visually separate the three
# parameter families within each variety, on top of the existing
# outer grouping by variety.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

construire_bloc_rf <- function(nom_serie, res_baseline,
                                res_ntree, res_nodesize, res_maxnodes) {
  rbind(
    data.frame(Group = "Baseline",
               Parameter = "ntree = 500, nodesize = 5, maxnodes = none",
               calculer_metriques(res_baseline$actual, res_baseline$predicted)),
    do.call(rbind, lapply(names(res_ntree), function(nom) {
      data.frame(Group = "Number of Trees (ntree)", Parameter = nom,
                 calculer_metriques(res_ntree[[nom]]$actual,
                                    res_ntree[[nom]]$predicted))
    })),
    do.call(rbind, lapply(names(res_nodesize), function(nom) {
      data.frame(Group = "Node Size (nodesize)", Parameter = nom,
                 calculer_metriques(res_nodesize[[nom]]$actual,
                                    res_nodesize[[nom]]$predicted))
    })),
    do.call(rbind, lapply(names(res_maxnodes), function(nom) {
      data.frame(Group = "Max Nodes (maxnodes)", Parameter = nom,
                 calculer_metriques(res_maxnodes[[nom]]$actual,
                                    res_maxnodes[[nom]]$predicted))
    }))
  ) %>% mutate(Series = nom_serie, .after = Group)
}

df_rf_tuning <- rbind(
  construire_bloc_rf("Arabica", res_rf_ara,
                     resultats_ntree_ara, resultats_nodesize_ara,
                     resultats_maxnodes_ara),
  construire_bloc_rf("Robusta", res_rf_rob,
                     resultats_ntree_rob, resultats_nodesize_rob,
                     resultats_maxnodes_rob)
)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# RENDER WITH TWO NESTED GROUPING LEVELS
# The outer pack_rows() calls (Arabica / Robusta) use the same bold,
# coloured style as every other variety-grouped table in this
# document. The inner pack_rows() calls, added afterwards, use a
# lighter grey italic style with no background fill, so the four
# parameter families read as sub-headers nested inside each variety
# block rather than competing visually with the main grouping.
# Row indices for both levels refer to the row numbers of the
# original 20-row table (10 per variety), consistent with how
# pack_rows() is used elsewhere for single-level grouping.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_rf_tuning %>%
  select(Parameter, R2, MSE, MAE) %>%
  kable(caption   = "Random Forest — tree count and complexity tuning",
        booktabs  = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Parameter", "R²", "MSE", "MAE")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  row_spec(10, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  # Outer grouping: variety blocks
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 10,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 11, 20,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec") %>%
  # Inner grouping: parameter families within each variety
  pack_rows("Number of Trees (ntree)", 2, 4,
            bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE, color = "grey40") %>%
  pack_rows("Node Size (nodesize)", 5, 7,
            bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE, color = "grey40") %>%
  pack_rows("Max Nodes (maxnodes)", 8, 10,
            bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE, color = "grey40") %>%
  pack_rows("Number of Trees (ntree)", 12, 14,
            bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE, color = "grey40") %>%
  pack_rows("Node Size (nodesize)", 15, 17,
            bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE, color = "grey40") %>%
  pack_rows("Max Nodes (maxnodes)", 18, 20,
            bold = FALSE, italic = TRUE, color = "grey40")
```

Across all three levers, the results tell a consistent story: the number of trees barely matters, while the two complexity controls, `nodesize` and `maxnodes`, matter a great deal, and in the same direction. Allowing individual trees to grow more complex, that is, more freely, improves performance up to a point, but constraining them too aggressively hurts substantially.

**Number of trees (`ntree`)**. Varying `ntree` between 100 and 1000 changes almost nothing. Arabica moves within a narrow band of $R^2$ = 0.810 to 0.814, and Robusta within 0.683 to 0.698, with no clear monotonic direction in either case. This is the expected behaviour for a Random Forest: each tree is grown independently on a bootstrap sample, and averaging over more trees mainly reduces the variance of the ensemble's prediction rather than changing what it has learned. Once enough trees are grown to average out the noise from individual bootstrap samples, roughly 100 in this case, adding more brings diminishing and eventually negligible returns. The baseline choice of 500 trees is comfortably within this plateau for both varieties.

**Minimum terminal node size (`nodesize`)**. This is where the two varieties start to diverge, though the direction is the same for both. Smaller values, which allow trees to split further and grow deeper, improve performance: `nodesize = 1` reaches $R^2$ = 0.826 for Arabica and 0.717 for Robusta, both above their respective baselines (0.811 and 0.695). Larger values degrade performance steadily: at `nodesize = 20`, Arabica falls to 0.725 and Robusta falls further still, to 0.595, a full 10 points below its baseline. Robusta is consistently more sensitive to this constraint than Arabica across every value tested, which fits the pattern already established elsewhere in this study: Robusta's shorter, more volatile training sample benefits less from an artificially simplified tree structure, since restricting node size caps the model's ability to capture the finer-grained relationships this variety's price dynamics 

**Maximum number of terminal nodes (`maxnodes`)**. The same qualitative pattern appears, and here it is far more dramatic at the aggressive end. Capping trees at only 10 terminal nodes is clearly too restrictive: $R^2$ falls to 0.695 for Arabica and to 0.577 for Robusta, the single worst result in the entire comparison and nearly 12 points below the Robusta baseline. Relaxing the cap to 50 or 100 nodes brings both varieties back to within a hair of the baseline (0.807-0.809 for Arabica, 0.69-0.695 for Robusta), suggesting that the unconstrained baseline was already close to the complexity these trees actually need, and that only a severe artificial ceiling meaningfully hurts performance.

**Taken together**, these three sweeps point to the same conclusion from three different angles: the Random Forest's baseline configuration, 500 trees with no explicit complexity constraint, was already close to optimal, or at least safely on the right side of the complexity/performance trade-off. The only genuine improvements found, `nodesize = 1` for both varieties, are modest (roughly +0.015 for Arabica, +0.022 for Robusta) and come at the cost of growing near-maximal trees, which increases the risk of overfitting individual bootstrap samples even if the walk-forward test performance does not yet show it. The clearest and most robust finding across the whole table is the negative one: constraining tree complexity too aggressively, whether through a small `maxnodes` or a large `nodesize`, is reliably harmful, and more so for Robusta than for Arabica.

### Random Forest: Single-Tree Pruning with CART

The tuning above covered `ntree`, `nodesize` and `maxnodes`, but not `cp`, and there is a good reason for that: `cp` is not actually a Random Forest parameter. It belongs to CART, the algorithm behind a single decision tree, which grows the tree deliberately too large and then prunes it back afterwards. That is a fundamentally different idea from a forest of hundreds of trees, each grown independently and left unpruned, where the averaging across trees does the work that pruning would otherwise do for a single tree. Rather than leave this as an abstract distinction, this section fits an actual CART tree with proper pruning, so the difference between the two approaches shows up in real numbers rather than just in the explanation. The cross-validation used to select the pruning level is entirely internal to each walk-forward training window: it never touches the observations held out for testing, so the out-of-sample comparison against the Random Forest below remains on equal footing. As with the cross-validation used to select the LASSO and Ridge penalties earlier in this analysis, `rpart`'s internal folds are built by random sampling rather than chronological order, so the pruning decision at each walk-forward step is informed by a mix of earlier and later observations within that window, not a strict past-to-future split. This stays contained within each training window and does not affect the integrity of the walk-forward test results themselves.

*This chunk builds a single CART tree at each walk-forward step. The tree is first grown deliberately oversized, then pruned back using the cost-complexity table `rpart` produces internally, choosing the pruning level with the one-standard-error rule: the smallest tree whose cross-validated error stays within one standard error of the best one found.*

```{r cart_pruning_setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# CART WITH COST-COMPLEXITY PRUNING — rpart
# randomForest has no cp argument. cp governs the pruning of a
# single tree grown by CART, which has no real equivalent for an
# ensemble of independently bootstrapped, unpruned trees. This
# chunk fits a single CART tree via rpart, using its built-in
# cost-complexity pruning, to show directly what cp does and how
# it differs from the nodesize/maxnodes controls tested above.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(rpart)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# WALK-FORWARD ESTIMATION FUNCTION — PRUNED CART
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#             ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train : size of the initial training window (number of rows),
#             computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
#   final_fit : the full unpruned tree and its cptable from the
#               LAST walk-forward step (largest training window),
#               kept so the cost-complexity table can be shown
#               afterwards
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_cart_pruned <- function(df, var_dep, n_train) {

  # STEP 1 — Restrict the dataset to the columns this model needs,
  # identical to fit_rf() above.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column to [0, 1], matching the
  # Random Forest baseline so MSE/MAE stay on a comparable scale.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Split into the initial training set and the test set.
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 4 — Walk-forward loop. At each step, a tree is grown with
  # a permissive cp floor (0.0001) so it is deliberately oversized,
  # using rpart's default 10-fold internal cross-validation (xval)
  # to build the cost-complexity table. The one-standard-error rule
  # is then applied by hand: find the smallest tree whose
  # cross-validated error is within one standard error of the
  # lowest error found in the table.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  arbre_final <- NULL   # kept from the last iteration for reporting

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    # Grow a deliberately oversized tree. minsplit = 10 keeps the
    # tree from splitting nodes with fewer than 10 observations,
    # a permissive floor consistent with rpart's own default.
    arbre_complet <- rpart(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                           method  = "anova",
                           control = rpart.control(cp = 0.0001,
                                                   minsplit = 10,
                                                   xval = 10))

    # One-standard-error rule: find the row of the smallest tree
    # whose cross-validated error (xerror) is within the minimum
    # xerror plus its standard error (xstd). rpart's cptable is
    # ordered from smallest tree (row 1) to largest (last row), so
    # the smallest eligible row index is the simplest qualifying
    # tree.
    table_cp    <- arbre_complet$cptable
    ligne_min   <- which.min(table_cp[, "xerror"])
    seuil_1se   <- table_cp[ligne_min, "xerror"] + table_cp[ligne_min, "xstd"]
    lignes_ok   <- which(table_cp[, "xerror"] <= seuil_1se)
    ligne_1se   <- min(lignes_ok)
    cp_optimal  <- table_cp[ligne_1se, "CP"]

    # Prune the oversized tree down to the cp selected above.
    arbre_elague <- prune(arbre_complet, cp = cp_optimal)
    arbre_final  <- list(complet = arbre_complet, elague = arbre_elague,
                        cp_optimal = cp_optimal)

    # Predict the single next observation.
    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, ]
    predictions[i]  <- predict(arbre_elague, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  # STEP 5 — Return observed and predicted test values, plus the
  # final iteration's full tree and cptable for the cost-complexity
  # illustration below.
  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions,
       final_fit = arbre_final)
}
```

*This chunk runs the pruned CART tree for both coffee varieties.*

```{r cart_pruning_run, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# RUN PRUNED CART, BOTH SERIES
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_cart_ara <- fit_cart_pruned(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev)
res_cart_rob <- fit_cart_pruned(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev)
```

*This chunk puts the pruned single tree side by side with the Random Forest baseline from earlier in this section, grouped by variety the same way as every other comparison table in this analysis.*

```{r cart_pruning_table, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# COMPILE COMPARISON TABLE — SINGLE PRUNED TREE VS RANDOM FOREST
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_cart_comparison <- rbind(
  rbind(
    data.frame(Specification = "Random Forest (baseline)",
               calculer_metriques(res_rf_ara$actual, res_rf_ara$predicted)),
    data.frame(Specification = "Single pruned tree (CART, cp via 1-SE rule)",
               calculer_metriques(res_cart_ara$actual, res_cart_ara$predicted))
  ) %>% mutate(Series = "Arabica", .after = Specification),

  rbind(
    data.frame(Specification = "Random Forest (baseline)",
               calculer_metriques(res_rf_rob$actual, res_rf_rob$predicted)),
    data.frame(Specification = "Single pruned tree (CART, cp via 1-SE rule)",
               calculer_metriques(res_cart_rob$actual, res_cart_rob$predicted))
  ) %>% mutate(Series = "Robusta", .after = Specification)
)

df_cart_comparison %>%
  select(Specification, R2, MSE, MAE) %>%
  kable(caption   = "Random Forest vs a single pruned CART tree",
        booktabs  = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Specification", "R²", "MSE", "MAE")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  row_spec(2, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 2,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 3, 4,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec")
```

*This chunk shows the actual cost-complexity table behind the pruning decision, for the last walk-forward step of each variety (the model trained on the largest window). Each row is a candidate tree size, with its cross-validated error and standard error; the row picked by the one-standard-error rule is highlighted, so the pruning choice is visible rather than just a number reported in the text.*

```{r cart_pruning_complexity, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# COST-COMPLEXITY TABLE — FINAL ITERATION, BOTH VARIETIES
# Shows the cptable produced by rpart on the largest training window
# for each series, with the row selected by the 1-SE rule flagged
# explicitly, so the pruning decision is visible rather than just a
# number reported in the text. This is a single representative
# iteration (the last walk-forward step, on the largest training
# window), not a summary across all ~40 walk-forward steps — the
# same convention already used for the ARIMAX order and coefficient
# tables earlier in the document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

afficher_cptable <- function(res_cart, couleur_header, caption_text) {

  # STEP 1 — Pull the raw cptable from the tree fitted at the final
  # walk-forward step (stored in final_fit by fit_cart_pruned()),
  # along with the cp value the 1-SE rule selected for that step.
  table_cp   <- as.data.frame(res_cart$final_fit$complet$cptable)
  cp_choisi  <- res_cart$final_fit$cp_optimal

  # STEP 2 — Flag the row matching the selected cp. A small numeric
  # tolerance (1e-10) is used instead of exact equality, since
  # floating-point values rarely match to the last decimal.
  table_cp$Selected <- ifelse(abs(table_cp$CP - cp_choisi) < 1e-10,
                              "<- 1-SE rule", "")

  # STEP 3 — Render with descriptive column names rather than
  # rpart's internal abbreviations (CP, xerror, xstd), consistent
  # with how variable names are relabelled for display elsewhere in
  # this document (labels_mlr, labels_corr, etc.).
  kable(table_cp,
        caption   = caption_text,
        booktabs  = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
        digits    = 5,
        col.names = c("Complexity Parameter (cp)", "Number of Splits",
                      "Training Error (rel. to root)",
                      "Cross-Validated Error", "Cross-Validated Std. Error",
                      "")) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                  font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
    # Highlight the row selected by the 1-SE rule so the pruning
    # decision is visually distinct from the rest of the table.
    row_spec(which(table_cp$Selected != ""), bold = TRUE,
             background = "#fff9e6") %>%
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, background = couleur_header, color = "white")
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA COST-COMPLEXITY TABLE
# ----------------------------------------------------------

afficher_cptable(res_cart_ara, "#8B4513",
                 "Cost-complexity table — Arabica (final walk-forward iteration)")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ROBUSTA COST-COMPLEXITY TABLE
# ----------------------------------------------------------

afficher_cptable(res_cart_rob, "#2E8B57",
                 "Cost-complexity table — Robusta (final walk-forward iteration)")
```

The comparison leaves little room for ambiguity. A single pruned CART tree falls well short of the Random Forest for both varieties: $R^2$ drops from 0.811 to 0.672 for Arabica, a loss of 0.139, and from 0.695 to 0.395 for Robusta, a loss of exactly 0.300. Robusta is hit noticeably harder, consistent with the pattern already seen throughout this study, where its shorter and more volatile sample tends to punish any simplification of the model more severely than Arabica does.

This gap is exactly what the difference between CART and Random Forest predicts. A single tree, however carefully pruned, has to commit to one specific sequence of splits chosen from one training sample. The Random Forest instead averages over hundreds of trees, each grown on its own bootstrap sample and each considering only a random subset of predictors at every split. Individually, many of these trees are cruder or noisier than a single well-pruned CART tree would be, but averaging across them cancels out a good part of that noise, in a way that no amount of pruning can replicate within a single tree. The one-standard-error rule applied here is, if anything, a fairly disciplined pruning choice, and it still cannot close this gap.

The cost-complexity tables make the pruning decision itself visible rather than just asserted. For Arabica, the cross-validated error drops sharply over the first few splits, from 1.010 with no splits at all to 0.307 at 5 splits, then keeps improving more slowly before the one-standard-error rule settles on 13 splits (cp = 0.00604, cross-validated error 0.201), rather than the lower-error, larger trees available further down the table. For Robusta, the same logic applies with a smaller tree: the rule selects 9 splits (cp = 0.01817, cross-validated error 0.333), even though slightly larger trees a few rows down achieve marginally lower cross-validated error. In both cases, the rule is doing exactly what it is designed to do: trading a small, statistically insignificant amount of cross-validated accuracy for a simpler, more conservative tree, rather than chasing the single lowest error value in the table.

Taken together, this section answers the `cp` question directly rather than leaving it as an unused parameter. `cp` governs a real and useful mechanism, but one that belongs to a single tree deliberately grown large and pruned back through cross-validation. A Random Forest does not need it, and this comparison shows why: even a properly pruned single tree, chosen through the same disciplined one-standard-error logic used throughout classical CART, still forecasts noticeably worse than an ensemble of unpruned trees for both coffee varieties.

## XGBoost

The baseline XGBoost model used fixed hyperparameters that were chosen manually, which is a reasonable starting point but not the most rigorous approach. This section does things more carefully by testing a large number of hyperparameter combinations and picking the one that works best. The twist compared to a standard grid search is that each combination is evaluated on three different portions of the training data rather than just one. This way, the winning combination has to perform consistently across the full training period, not just get lucky on one particular window. The grid used for Arabica is finer and centred around values that performed well in preliminary experiments, while the grid for Robusta is broader since no strong prior exists on the optimal range for that series.

*This chunk tests a large number of combinations of four XGBoost hyperparameters: the number of boosting rounds, the maximum tree depth, the learning rate and the row sampling ratio. For each combination, the model is trained and evaluated three times on different chronological slices of the training window, using 60%, 70% and 80% of the data as training sets respectively, with the following 20% as validation in each case. The average validation MSE across the three evaluations is used to select the best combination, which is then passed directly to the estimation chunk below. Arabica and Robusta use separate grids calibrated to the structure of each series.*

```{r xgboost_tuning, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
```
