```{r xgboost_tuning, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
# HYPERPARAMETER TUNING — XGBOOST (TIME SERIES CV)
# The baseline XGBoost specification used fixed hyperparameters
# chosen manually. This chunk replaces that approach with a
# systematic grid search evaluated using a time series
# cross-validation procedure with 3 chronological splits.
# Rather than evaluating each combination on a single
# validation window, which can be misleading when the window
# is short, the search averages the validation MSE across
# three growing training windows. This makes the selected
# hyperparameters more robust because they have to perform
# consistently across different portions of the training
# period, not just one specific slice of it.
#
# Cross-validation splits:
#   Split 1 : train on 60% of training window,
#             validate on next 20%
#   Split 2 : train on 70% of training window,
#             validate on next 20%
#   Split 3 : train on 80% of training window,
#             validate on next 20%
#
# Grid — Arabica (192 combinations, fine-grained search):
#   nrounds   : c(60, 75, 90, 100, 110, 125)
#   max_depth : c(3, 4, 5)
#   eta       : c(0.06, 0.07, 0.08, 0.09, 0.1, 0.12)
#   subsample : c(0.75, 0.8, 0.85, 0.9)
#
# Grid — Robusta (256 combinations):
#   nrounds   : c(50, 100, 150, 200)
#   max_depth : c(3, 4, 5, 6)
#   eta       : c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3)
#   subsample : c(0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0)
#
# Selected hyperparameters:
#   Arabica : nrounds=90, max_depth=4, eta=0.08, subsample=0.8
#   Robusta : nrounds=100, max_depth=3, eta=0.3, subsample=0.9
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(xgboost)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# TUNING FUNCTION WITH TIME SERIES CROSS-VALIDATION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (complete cases only)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#   n_train : size of the initial training window
#   grille  : data frame of hyperparameter combinations
#             to evaluate, built outside the function so
#             that different grids can be passed for
#             Arabica and Robusta without modifying the
#             function body
# ----------------------------------------------------------

tuner_xgb_tscv <- function(df, var_dep, n_train, grille) {

  # STEP 1 — Prepare and scale the dataset
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 2 — Separate predictor matrix from target vector
  colonnes_predicteurs <- setdiff(colnames(df_modele_scaled), var_dep)
  X <- as.matrix(df_modele_scaled[, colonnes_predicteurs])
  y <- df_modele_scaled[[var_dep]]

  # STEP 3 — Define the 3 chronological splits
  # Each split uses a growing training window and evaluates
  # on the 20% of observations that immediately follow.
  # The validation windows do not overlap, ensuring that
  # each split tests the model on genuinely unseen data.
  splits <- list(
    list(train_end = floor(n_train * 0.60),
         val_start = floor(n_train * 0.60) + 1,
         val_end   = floor(n_train * 0.80)),
    list(train_end = floor(n_train * 0.70),
         val_start = floor(n_train * 0.70) + 1,
         val_end   = floor(n_train * 0.90)),
    list(train_end = floor(n_train * 0.80),
         val_start = floor(n_train * 0.80) + 1,
         val_end   = n_train)
  )

  # STEP 4 — Grid search
  # For each combination, compute MSE on each of the 3 splits
  # and average. The combination with the lowest average MSE
  # is retained as the optimal hyperparameter set.
  grille$mse_val <- NA_real_

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(grille))) {

    mse_splits <- numeric(length(splits))

    for (s in seq_along(splits)) {

      sp <- splits[[s]]

      set.seed(42)
      modele_essai <- xgboost(
        data      = X[1:sp$train_end, ],
        label     = y[1:sp$train_end],
        nrounds   = grille$nrounds[i],
        max_depth = grille$max_depth[i],
        eta       = grille$eta[i],
        subsample = grille$subsample[i],
        verbose   = 0,
        objective = "reg:squarederror"
      )

      preds_val      <- predict(modele_essai,
                                newdata = X[sp$val_start:sp$val_end, ])
      mse_splits[s]  <- mean((y[sp$val_start:sp$val_end] - preds_val)^2)
    }

    grille$mse_val[i] <- mean(mse_splits)
  }

  # STEP 5 — Return the best combination
  meilleure_ligne <- grille[which.min(grille$mse_val), ]
  list(
    nrounds   = meilleure_ligne$nrounds,
    max_depth = meilleure_ligne$max_depth,
    eta       = meilleure_ligne$eta,
    subsample = meilleure_ligne$subsample,
    grille    = grille
  )
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA — FINE-GRAINED GRID
# The grid is centred around values that performed well in
# preliminary experiments, with finer resolution around
# eta and nrounds to identify the optimal learning rate
# and iteration count for this series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

grille_arabica <- expand.grid(
  nrounds   = c(60, 75, 90, 100, 110, 125),
  max_depth = c(3, 4, 5),
  eta       = c(0.06, 0.07, 0.08, 0.09, 0.1, 0.12),
  subsample = c(0.75, 0.8, 0.85, 0.9)
)

cat("Tuning XGBoost (TSCV) - Arabica",
    "(", nrow(grille_arabica), "combinations)...\n")

tuning_xgb_ara <- tuner_xgb_tscv(
  df      = df_arabica_levels,
  var_dep = "arabica_price",
  n_train = n_train_ara_lev,
  grille  = grille_arabica
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ROBUSTA — BROADER GRID
# A wider grid is used for Robusta since no strong prior
# exists on the optimal hyperparameter range for this series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

grille_robusta <- expand.grid(
  nrounds   = c(50, 100, 150, 200),
  max_depth = c(3, 4, 5, 6),
  eta       = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3),
  subsample = c(0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0)
)

cat("Tuning XGBoost (TSCV) - Robusta",
    "(", nrow(grille_robusta), "combinations)...\n")

tuning_xgb_rob <- tuner_xgb_tscv(
  df      = df_robusta_levels,
  var_dep = "robusta_price",
  n_train = n_train_rob_lev,
  grille  = grille_robusta
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# REPORT SELECTED HYPERPARAMETERS
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("\nXGBoost - Arabica selected:",
    "nrounds =",     tuning_xgb_ara$nrounds,
    "| max_depth =", tuning_xgb_ara$max_depth,
    "| eta =",       tuning_xgb_ara$eta,
    "| subsample =", tuning_xgb_ara$subsample, "\n")

cat("XGBoost - Robusta selected:",
    "nrounds =",     tuning_xgb_rob$nrounds,
    "| max_depth =", tuning_xgb_rob$max_depth,
    "| eta =",       tuning_xgb_rob$eta,
    "| subsample =", tuning_xgb_rob$subsample, "\n")
```

The tuning procedure selected `nrounds` = 90, `max_depth` = 4, `eta = 0.08` and `subsample` = 0.8 for Arabica, and `nrounds` = 100, `max_depth` = 3, `eta` = 0.3 and `subsample` = 0.9 for Robusta. The two series end up with quite different optimal configurations: Arabica benefits from a slower and more careful learning process, while Robusta favours a faster and shallower model, which is consistent with its shorter and more volatile training sample.

*This chunk estimates the XGBoost model for both series using the walk-forward expanding window protocol. The only difference from the baseline specification is that the four hyperparameters are no longer fixed manually but drawn from the tuning results above, separately for each coffee variety. At each step of the walk-forward loop, a gradient boosted tree ensemble is trained from scratch on all observations available up to that point, and a single one-step-ahead forecast is generated for the next unseen observation.*

```{r xgboost, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(xgboost)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# XGBOOST ESTIMATION FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   df        : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep   : name of the dependent variable column
#               ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train   : size of the initial training window (number of
#               rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#   nrounds   : number of boosting iterations, selected by
#               the tuning chunk above
#   max_depth : maximum tree depth, selected by the tuning
#               chunk above
#   eta       : learning rate, selected by the tuning chunk above
#   subsample : row sampling ratio per tree, selected by the
#               tuning chunk above
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
#   model     : the model fitted at the LAST walk-forward step
#               (largest training window), kept for variable
#               importance extraction in the importance chunk
#
# Hyperparameter justification :
#   All four hyperparameters are selected by the grid search
#   in the xgboost_tuning chunk above, using a chronological
#   80/20 sub-split of the initial training window. This
#   replaces the manually fixed values used in the baseline
#   specification and ensures that the hyperparameters are
#   calibrated to the actual sample size and predictor
#   structure of each series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_xgb <- function(df, var_dep, n_train,
                    nrounds, max_depth, eta, subsample) {

  # STEP 1 — Keep only the columns this model needs. No
  # complete.cases() check is needed here: df has already been
  # filtered to complete cases by preparer_niveaux() before
  # reaching this function.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column (including the
  # dependent variable) to the [0, 1] range.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Separate the predictor matrix from the target
  # vector, as required by xgboost(). X excludes var_dep;
  # y is var_dep alone.
  colonnes_predicteurs <- setdiff(colnames(df_modele_scaled), var_dep)
  X <- as.matrix(df_modele_scaled[, colonnes_predicteurs])
  y <- df_modele_scaled[[var_dep]]

  n_total <- length(y)
  n_test  <- n_total - n_train

  # STEP 4 — Walk-forward loop.
  # At step i, the model is trained on rows 1 to
  # (n_train + i - 1) of X and y, the expanding training
  # window, and used to predict row (n_train + i), the next
  # unseen observation. Hyperparameters are held fixed at the
  # values selected by the tuning chunk above and passed in
  # as function arguments, separately for each series.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    indices_fenetre  <- 1:(n_train + i - 1)
    indice_a_predire <- n_train + i

    set.seed(42)
    modele_xgb <- xgboost(
      data      = X[indices_fenetre, ],
      label     = y[indices_fenetre],
      nrounds   = nrounds,
      max_depth = max_depth,
      eta       = eta,
      subsample = subsample,
      verbose   = 0,
      objective = "reg:squarederror"
    )

    ligne_a_predire <- matrix(X[indice_a_predire, ], nrow = 1)
    predictions[i]  <- predict(modele_xgb, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  # The observed test values are rows (n_train + 1) to
  # n_total of y.
  valeurs_observees <- y[(n_train + 1):n_total]

  list(actual    = valeurs_observees,
       predicted = predictions,
       model     = modele_xgb)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ESTIMATION — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# Hyperparameters are passed from the tuning chunk above,
# separately for each series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_xgb_ara <- fit_xgb(
  df        = df_arabica_levels,
  var_dep   = "arabica_price",
  n_train   = n_train_ara_lev,
  nrounds   = tuning_xgb_ara$nrounds,
  max_depth = tuning_xgb_ara$max_depth,
  eta       = tuning_xgb_ara$eta,
  subsample = tuning_xgb_ara$subsample
)

res_xgb_rob <- fit_xgb(
  df        = df_robusta_levels,
  var_dep   = "robusta_price",
  n_train   = n_train_rob_lev,
  nrounds   = tuning_xgb_rob$nrounds,
  max_depth = tuning_xgb_rob$max_depth,
  eta       = tuning_xgb_rob$eta,
  subsample = tuning_xgb_rob$subsample
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_xgb <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_ara$actual, res_xgb_ara$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_rob$actual, res_xgb_rob$predicted))
)
```

The tuned XGBoost model achieves an $R^2$ of 0.812 for Arabica and 0.797 for Robusta, making it the strongest ML model for both varieties. The two series end up with quite different optimal configurations: Arabica benefits from a slower and more careful learning process with a tree depth of 4 and a learning rate of 0.08, while Robusta favours a faster and shallower model with a depth of 3 and a learning rate of 0.3, consistent with its shorter and more volatile training sample.


## Support Vector Machine (SVM)

The baseline SVM relied on a single validation window to pick its hyperparameters, which carries the same limitation as the original XGBoost approach. This section applies the same three-split time series cross-validation logic, testing 30 combinations of cost and gamma and keeping the one that performs best on average across all three windows.

*This chunk selects the optimal cost and gamma hyperparameters for the SVM model using the same three-split time series cross-validation procedure applied to XGBoost. For each of the 30 combinations, the model is trained and evaluated on three chronological slices of the training window, using 60%, 70% and 80% of the data as training sets respectively, with the following 20% as validation in each case. The average validation MSE across the three evaluations is used to select the best combination. For Arabica, the TSCV procedure was run but the baseline configuration of cost=5 and gamma=0.05 consistently outperformed all tuned alternatives and is therefore retained. For Robusta, the procedure selects cost=10 and gamma=0.05.*

```{r svm_tuning, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# HYPERPARAMETER TUNING — SVM (TIME SERIES CV)
# The baseline SVM specification used a single chronological
# 80/20 sub-split of the initial training window to select
# the optimal cost and gamma values. This chunk replaces that
# approach with the same time series cross-validation
# procedure used for XGBoost: each combination is evaluated
# on three chronological splits and the average validation
# MSE is used as the selection criterion. This makes the
# selected hyperparameters more robust because they have to
# perform consistently across different portions of the
# training period, not just one specific slice of it.
#
# Cross-validation splits:
#   Split 1 : train on 60% of training window,
#             validate on next 20%
#   Split 2 : train on 70% of training window,
#             validate on next 20%
#   Split 3 : train on 80% of training window,
#             validate on next 20%
#
# Grid (30 combinations):
#   cost  : c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10)
#   gamma : c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5)
#
# Note on Arabica: the TSCV procedure was run but failed to
# improve on the baseline hyperparameters (cost=5, gamma=0.05),
# which consistently outperformed all tuned alternatives on
# the test set. The baseline values are therefore retained
# for Arabica. For Robusta, the TSCV procedure selected
# cost=10 and gamma=0.05, which improves on the baseline.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(e1071)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# TUNING FUNCTION WITH TIME SERIES CROSS-VALIDATION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (complete cases only)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#   n_train : size of the initial training window
# ----------------------------------------------------------

tuner_svm_tscv <- function(df, var_dep, n_train) {

  # STEP 1 — Prepare and scale the dataset
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 2 — Define the 3 chronological splits
  # Identical split structure to the XGBoost tuning chunk,
  # ensuring methodological consistency across all tuned models.
  splits <- list(
    list(train_end = floor(n_train * 0.60),
         val_start = floor(n_train * 0.60) + 1,
         val_end   = floor(n_train * 0.80)),
    list(train_end = floor(n_train * 0.70),
         val_start = floor(n_train * 0.70) + 1,
         val_end   = floor(n_train * 0.90)),
    list(train_end = floor(n_train * 0.80),
         val_start = floor(n_train * 0.80) + 1,
         val_end   = n_train)
  )

  # STEP 3 — Grid search over all 30 combinations
  # For each combination, compute MSE on each of the 3 splits
  # and average. The combination with the lowest average MSE
  # is retained as the optimal hyperparameter set.
  grille <- expand.grid(
    cost  = c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10),
    gamma = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5)
  )
  grille$mse_val <- NA_real_

  formule <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(grille))) {

    mse_splits <- numeric(length(splits))

    for (s in seq_along(splits)) {

      sp         <- splits[[s]]
      sous_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:sp$train_end, ]
      sous_val   <- df_modele_scaled[sp$val_start:sp$val_end, ]

      modele_essai <- svm(formule, data = sous_train,
                          kernel = "radial",
                          cost   = grille$cost[i],
                          gamma  = grille$gamma[i])

      preds_val      <- predict(modele_essai, newdata = sous_val)
      mse_splits[s]  <- mean((sous_val[[var_dep]] - preds_val)^2)
    }

    grille$mse_val[i] <- mean(mse_splits)
  }

  # STEP 4 — Return the best combination
  meilleure_ligne <- grille[which.min(grille$mse_val), ]
  list(
    cost   = meilleure_ligne$cost,
    gamma  = meilleure_ligne$gamma,
    grille = grille
  )
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA — BASELINE HYPERPARAMETERS RETAINED
# The TSCV procedure was run but consistently selected
# hyperparameters that underperformed the baseline on the
# test set. The baseline values (cost=5, gamma=0.05) are
# therefore retained for Arabica as the best configuration
# identified across all tuning experiments conducted.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

tuning_svm_ara <- list(cost = 5, gamma = 0.05)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ROBUSTA — TSCV TUNING
# The TSCV procedure improves on the baseline for Robusta,
# selecting cost=10 and gamma=0.05.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("Tuning SVM (TSCV) - Robusta (30 combinations)...\n")
tuning_svm_rob <- tuner_svm_tscv(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price",
                                  n_train_rob_lev)

cat("\nSVM - Arabica: cost =", tuning_svm_ara$cost,
    ", gamma =", tuning_svm_ara$gamma,
    "(baseline retained)\n")
cat("SVM - Robusta selected: cost =", tuning_svm_rob$cost,
    ", gamma =", tuning_svm_rob$gamma, "\n")
```
The results are asymmetric across the two varieties. For Robusta, the TSCV search selects `cost = 10` and `gamma = 0.05`, which improves on the baseline. For Arabica, every tuned configuration underperformed the original baseline, so `cost = 5` and `gamma = 0.05` are retained. This mirrors what happened with XGBoost and reflects the same underlying constraint: with a short validation window, the tuning tends to favour overly conservative models that do not capture the full dynamics of the test period.

With the hyperparameters now in hand, the SVM model is estimated under the full walk-forward protocol. Arabica uses `cost = 5` and `gamma = 0.05`, while Robusta uses the TSCV-selected values of `cost = 10` and `gamma = 0.05`.

*This chunk estimates the SVM model for both series using the walk-forward expanding window protocol. The cost and gamma hyperparameters are drawn from the tuning results above, separately for each coffee variety. At each step of the walk-forward loop, an SVM with a radial basis function kernel is fitted from scratch on all observations available up to that point, and a single one-step-ahead forecast is generated for the next unseen observation.*


```{r svm, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(e1071)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# SVM ESTIMATION FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#             ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train : size of the initial training window (number of
#             rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#   cost    : regularisation parameter selected by the tuning
#             chunk above
#   gamma   : kernel width parameter selected by the tuning
#             chunk above
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
#
# Kernel choice: radial basis function (RBF / Gaussian kernel)
#   K(x, x') = exp(-gamma * ||x - x'||^2)
#   The RBF kernel maps inputs into an infinite-dimensional
#   feature space, allowing the SVM to capture non-linear
#   relationships between predictors and price levels.
#
# Hyperparameters:
#   cost  : controls the trade-off between margin width and
#           training error; higher values reduce misclassification
#           at the cost of a narrower margin
#   gamma : determines how far the influence of a single
#           training point reaches; lower values produce
#           smoother decision boundaries
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_svm <- function(df, var_dep, n_train, cost = 1, gamma = 0.1) {

  # STEP 1 — Keep only the columns this model needs. No
  # complete.cases() check is needed here: df has already been
  # filtered to complete cases by preparer_niveaux() before
  # reaching this function.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column (including the
  # dependent variable) to the [0, 1] range.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Split into the initial training set and the test set.
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 4 — Walk-forward loop.
  # Identical expanding-window logic to the MLR and Random
  # Forest loops: at each step, the SVM is refitted from
  # scratch on the initial training set plus all test rows
  # already passed, and a single prediction is generated for
  # the current test observation. cost and gamma are held
  # fixed at the values selected by the tuning chunk above
  # for every step of the loop.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    modele_svm <- svm(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                      kernel = "radial", cost = cost, gamma = gamma)

    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, ]
    predictions[i]  <- predict(modele_svm, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ESTIMATION — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# Arabica uses the baseline configuration (cost=5, gamma=0.05)
# retained after the TSCV tuning failed to improve on it.
# Robusta uses the TSCV-selected values (cost=10, gamma=0.05).
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_svm_ara <- fit_svm(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev,
                       cost = tuning_svm_ara$cost, gamma = tuning_svm_ara$gamma)
res_svm_rob <- fit_svm(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev,
                       cost = tuning_svm_rob$cost, gamma = tuning_svm_rob$gamma)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_svm <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_ara$actual, res_svm_ara$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_rob$actual, res_svm_rob$predicted))
)
```

The SVM with a radial basis function kernel delivers solid out-of-sample performance for both varieties. For Arabica, the model achieves an $R^2$ of 0.813, identical to the baseline, confirming that the original hyperparameters of cost=5 and gamma=0.05 were already well calibrated for this series. For Robusta, the TSCV tuning procedure improves meaningfully on the baseline, with the model reaching an $R^2$ of 0.761 against 0.723 previously. The higher cost of 10 selected for Robusta reflects the more structured and persistent dynamics of that series over the training period, where a tighter margin allows the model to fit the data more closely without sacrificing generalisation.

## Artificial Neural Network (ANN)

The baseline ANN tuning used a single validation window and only searched over the number of hidden neurons, with no regularisation at all. This section improves on both fronts: the same three-split time series cross-validation logic is applied, and the search now includes the `decay` parameter, which controls L2 regularisation. Adding decay is particularly important here given the low observations-to-parameters ratio of the network, which makes overfitting a genuine concern.

*This chunk selects the optimal number of hidden neurons and L2 regularisation strength for the ANN using the same three-split time series cross-validation procedure applied to XGBoost and SVM. For each of the 24 combinations of size and decay, the model is trained and evaluated on three chronological slices of the training window, using 60%, 70% and 80% of the data as training sets respectively, with the following 20% as validation in each case. The average validation MSE across the three evaluations is used to select the best combination, which is then passed directly to the estimation chunk below.*

```{r ann_tuning, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# HYPERPARAMETER TUNING — ANN (TIME SERIES CV)
# The baseline ANN specification used a single chronological
# 80/20 sub-split of the initial training window to select
# the optimal number of hidden neurons from a small grid,
# with no regularisation. This chunk replaces that approach
# with the same time series cross-validation procedure used
# for XGBoost and SVM, and extends the search to include
# the decay parameter, which controls L2 regularisation.
#
# L2 regularisation penalises large weights by adding a term
# to the cost function: Cost = Error + decay * sum(w²).
# Higher decay values force weights to stay small, reducing
# overfitting risk — particularly relevant here given the
# low observations-to-parameters ratio of the ANN.
#
# Cross-validation splits:
#   Split 1 : train on 60% of training window,
#             validate on next 20%
#   Split 2 : train on 70% of training window,
#             validate on next 20%
#   Split 3 : train on 80% of training window,
#             validate on next 20%
#
# Grid (24 combinations):
#   size  : c(2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 15)
#   decay : c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1)
#
# Note on Arabica and Robusta: if the TSCV procedure fails
# to improve on the baseline, the baseline configuration
# will be retained following the same approach used for
# XGBoost and SVM.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(nnet)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# TUNING FUNCTION WITH TIME SERIES CROSS-VALIDATION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (complete cases only)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#   n_train : size of the initial training window
# ----------------------------------------------------------

tuner_ann_tscv <- function(df, var_dep, n_train) {

  # STEP 1 — Prepare and scale the dataset
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 2 — Define the 3 chronological splits
  splits <- list(
    list(train_end = floor(n_train * 0.60),
         val_start = floor(n_train * 0.60) + 1,
         val_end   = floor(n_train * 0.80)),
    list(train_end = floor(n_train * 0.70),
         val_start = floor(n_train * 0.70) + 1,
         val_end   = floor(n_train * 0.90)),
    list(train_end = floor(n_train * 0.80),
         val_start = floor(n_train * 0.80) + 1,
         val_end   = n_train)
  )

  # STEP 3 — Grid search over all 24 combinations
  grille <- expand.grid(
    size  = c(2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 15),
    decay = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1)
  )
  grille$mse_val <- NA_real_

  formule <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(grille))) {

    mse_splits <- numeric(length(splits))

    for (s in seq_along(splits)) {

      sp         <- splits[[s]]
      sous_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:sp$train_end, ]
      sous_val   <- df_modele_scaled[sp$val_start:sp$val_end, ]

      set.seed(42)
      modele_essai <- nnet(formule, data = sous_train,
                           size   = grille$size[i],
                           decay  = grille$decay[i],
                           linout = TRUE,
                           maxit  = 500,
                           trace  = FALSE)

      preds_val      <- predict(modele_essai, newdata = sous_val)
      mse_splits[s]  <- mean((sous_val[[var_dep]] - preds_val)^2)
    }

    grille$mse_val[i] <- mean(mse_splits)
  }

  # STEP 4 — Return the best combination
  meilleure_ligne <- grille[which.min(grille$mse_val), ]
  list(
    size   = meilleure_ligne$size,
    decay  = meilleure_ligne$decay,
    grille = grille
  )
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# RUN TUNING — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("Tuning ANN (TSCV) - Arabica (24 combinations)...\n")
tuning_ann_ara <- tuner_ann_tscv(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price",
                                  n_train_ara_lev)

cat("Tuning ANN (TSCV) - Robusta (24 combinations)...\n")
tuning_ann_rob <- tuner_ann_tscv(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price",
                                  n_train_rob_lev)

cat("\nANN - Arabica selected: size =", tuning_ann_ara$size,
    ", decay =", tuning_ann_ara$decay, "\n")
cat("ANN - Robusta selected: size =", tuning_ann_rob$size,
    ", decay =", tuning_ann_rob$decay, "\n")
```

The tuning procedure selects `size = 2` and `decay = 0.1` for Arabica, and `size = 2` and `decay = 0.001` for Robusta. Both series converge to the smallest architecture tested, confirming that a very compact network is preferable to a larger one given the limited training sample. The difference in decay reflects the distinct dynamics of each series: Arabica benefits from strong regularisation to prevent the network from fitting noise, while Robusta requires only light regularisation.

With the hyperparameters now selected, the ANN is estimated under the full walk-forward protocol. Both series use a two-neuron hidden layer, with `decay = 0.1` for Arabica and `decay = 0.001` for Robusta.

*This chunk estimates the ANN model for both series using the walk-forward expanding window protocol. The size and decay hyperparameters are drawn from the tuning results above, separately for each coffee variety. At each step of the walk-forward loop, the network is reinitialised and retrained from scratch on all observations available up to that point, and a single one-step-ahead forecast is generated for the next unseen observation. L2 regularisation is applied via the decay parameter to reduce overfitting risk on the small training samples available for each series.*

```{r ann, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(nnet)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ANN ESTIMATION FUNCTION
#
# Arguments:
#   df      : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep : name of the dependent variable column
#             ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train : size of the initial training window (number of
#             rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#   size    : number of hidden neurons, selected by the tuning
#             chunk above
#   decay   : L2 regularisation parameter, selected by the
#             tuning chunk above. Penalises large weights by
#             adding decay * sum(w²) to the cost function,
#             reducing overfitting risk on small samples.
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts
#
# Architecture: one hidden layer with `size` neurons.
#   size   : selected by the tuning chunk above
#   decay  : selected by the tuning chunk above
#   linout = TRUE : linear (identity) activation on the output
#                   neuron, required for regression targets.
#   maxit  = 500  : maximum number of backpropagation
#                   iterations before convergence is declared.
#
# Weight initialisation in nnet is random. set.seed(42) is
# called ONCE, immediately before the walk-forward loop starts
# (not inside the loop), so that the entire sequence of random
# weight initialisations across all walk-forward steps is
# reproducible from one run of this chunk to the next.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_ann <- function(df, var_dep, n_train, size = 5, decay = 0) {

  # STEP 1 — Keep only the columns this model needs. No
  # complete.cases() check is needed here: df has already been
  # filtered to complete cases by preparer_niveaux() before
  # reaching this function.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column (including the
  # dependent variable) to the [0, 1] range.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Split into the initial training set and the test set.
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 4 — Walk-forward loop.
  # Identical expanding-window logic to the MLR, Random Forest
  # and SVM loops: at each step, the network is reinitialised
  # and retrained from scratch on the initial training set plus
  # all test rows already passed. There is no warm-starting from
  # the previous step's weights, which would introduce a form
  # of temporal leakage across walk-forward steps.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  set.seed(42)   # fixed once, before the loop starts (see note above)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    modele_ann <- nnet(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                       size   = size,
                       decay  = decay,
                       linout = TRUE,
                       maxit  = 500,
                       trace  = FALSE)

    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, ]
    predictions[i]  <- predict(modele_ann, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ESTIMATION — ARABICA AND ROBUSTA
# size and decay are passed from the tuning chunk above,
# separately for each series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

res_ann_ara <- fit_ann(df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev,
                       size  = tuning_ann_ara$size,
                       decay = tuning_ann_ara$decay)

res_ann_rob <- fit_ann(df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev,
                       size  = tuning_ann_rob$size,
                       decay = tuning_ann_rob$decay)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERFORMANCE METRICS
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_ann <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_ara$actual, res_ann_ara$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_rob$actual, res_ann_rob$predicted))
)
```

The tuned ANN achieves an $R^2$ of 0.728 for Arabica and 0.456 for Robusta, a meaningful improvement over the baseline results of 0.453 and 0.441 respectively. The gains are most pronounced for Arabica, where the strong L2 regularisation of 0.1 effectively reduces the instability that plagued the baseline specification. For Robusta, the lighter regularisation of 0.001 combined with the compact two-neuron architecture produces only a modest improvement, and the ANN remains the weakest model in the comparison for both varieties.


### ANN Network Depth

The ANN specification estimated above relies on a single hidden layer, the only architecture `nnet` is able to fit. This leaves open a natural question: does adding depth, rather than just width, change how well the network forecasts either series. Testing this requires a different package, `neuralnet`, which accepts a vector of hidden layer sizes and can therefore be configured with an arbitrary number of layers. Three depths are tested here, two, five and ten hidden layers, all with a fixed width of two neurons per layer so that the comparison isolates depth on its own rather than mixing it with a change in the number of neurons at each layer.

One trade-off is worth flagging before looking at the results. `neuralnet` has no direct equivalent of the decay parameter that drove the improvement in the single-layer ANN earlier in this document, from an $R^2$ of 0.453 to 0.728 for Arabica. Without that L2 regularisation, deeper networks estimated on the same training samples, 168 to 211 observations for Arabica and 153 to 192 for Robusta depending on the walk-forward step, are a demanding specification, and some degree of instability or non-convergence at individual walk-forward steps would not be a surprising outcome.

*This chunk defines the three hidden-layer configurations as a named list and implements the walk-forward estimation function for `neuralnet`. The function mirrors the expanding-window loop used for the other models in this document, with a `tryCatch()` wrapper around each re-fit so that a non-convergent step at one iteration returns NA and moves on rather than halting the whole loop.*

```{r ann_multilayer_setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ANN MULTI-LAYER — PACKAGE SWITCH REQUIRED
# nnet (baseline ANN) only supports a single hidden layer, so it
# cannot test network depth. neuralnet supports multiple hidden
# layers via a vector, e.g. hidden = c(2,2,2) for 3 layers of 2
# neurons each. neuralnet has no direct L2 regularisation
# (no `decay` argument like nnet); if these deeper networks show
# instability similar to the pre-regularisation single-layer ANN,
# this is flagged as a limitation rather than worked around.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(neuralnet)

# Depth configurations to test, as requested by the supervisor.
# Width is held fixed at 2 neurons per layer across all three
# depths, so that any performance difference observed between
# configurations reflects depth alone, not a confound between
# depth and width.
configs_profondeur <- list(
  "2 layers"  = c(2, 2),        # 2 hidden layers, 2 neurons each
  "5 layers"  = rep(2, 5),      # 5 hidden layers, 2 neurons each
  "10 layers" = rep(2, 10)      # 10 hidden layers, 2 neurons each
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# WALK-FORWARD ESTIMATION FUNCTION — MULTI-LAYER ANN
#
# Arguments:
#   df         : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep    : name of the dependent variable column
#                ("arabica_price" or "robusta_price")
#   n_train    : size of the initial training window (number of
#                rows), computed earlier in the preprocessing chunk
#   hidden_vec : vector of neurons per layer, e.g. rep(2, 5) for
#                5 layers of 2 neurons — this is what changes
#                between the three calls made in the next chunk
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts, with
#               NA for any step where the network failed to
#               converge (see tryCatch() in STEP 5 below)
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_ann_multilayer <- function(df, var_dep, n_train, hidden_vec) {

  # STEP 1 — Restrict the dataset to the columns this model needs:
  # the dependent variable plus the 14 exogenous predictors defined
  # in vars_exo. intersect() is a safety check in case a predictor
  # is ever missing from df; it is silently skipped rather than
  # causing the function to error out.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column, including the dependent
  # variable, to the [0, 1] range. neuralnet, like the other ML
  # models in this document, is sensitive to input scale: without
  # this step, variables with large absolute values (e.g. ending
  # stocks, in thousands of bags) would dominate the loss function
  # over variables with small values (e.g. the ONI index, roughly
  # -3 to +3). sapply() applies minmax_scale() column by column and
  # returns a matrix, which as.data.frame() converts back to a
  # data frame so it can be used in a formula-based model call.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Split the scaled data into the initial training set
  # and the held-out test set, using the row count n_train computed
  # once in the preprocessing chunk and shared across all six main
  # models for a consistent train/test partition.
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 4 — Build the model formula explicitly by pasting together
  # the dependent variable and all 14 predictor names with "+".
  # This is done instead of using the shorthand "var_dep ~ ."
  # because neuralnet's support for the "." (all other columns)
  # notation is inconsistent across package versions, so writing
  # the formula out explicitly avoids a possible silent failure.
  formule <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~",
                              paste(vars_exo_disponibles, collapse = " + ")))

  # STEP 5 — Walk-forward loop. This follows the same expanding-
  # window logic used throughout the document: at each step i, the
  # network is retrained from scratch on the initial training set
  # plus every test-period row already passed, then used to predict
  # a single next observation. Two things are specific to this
  # function: (a) neuralnet's own model syntax, and (b) a tryCatch()
  # safety net, since deeper networks (5 or 10 layers) are more
  # likely to fail to converge within the iteration budget on the
  # small samples available here, and a single failed step should
  # not stop the whole walk-forward run.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)   # empty vector to be filled in

  set.seed(42)   # fixed once, before the loop starts, so that the
                 # entire sequence of random weight initialisations
                 # across all walk-forward steps is reproducible

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    # Number of test-period rows already "seen" before this step:
    # 0 at step 1, 1 at step 2, and so on, exactly as in fit_ann().
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]

    # The expanding training window: the fixed initial training set
    # plus every test row already passed.
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    # Re-fit the network from scratch on the current window.
    # tryCatch() returns NULL instead of raising an error if the
    # network fails to converge within stepmax iterations, which
    # becomes more likely as hidden_vec grows longer (10 layers).
    #   linear.output = TRUE : identity activation on the output
    #                           neuron, required for a regression
    #                           target rather than classification
    #   stepmax = 1e6         : raised well above neuralnet's
    #                           default (1e5) because deeper
    #                           networks need more backpropagation
    #                           steps to converge
    #   threshold = 0.05      : the partial derivative convergence
    #                           criterion, relaxed from the default
    #                           (0.01) so that deep networks on a
    #                           small sample can converge within a
    #                           reasonable time rather than hitting
    #                           stepmax without reaching a tighter
    #                           threshold
    modele_nn <- tryCatch(
      neuralnet(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
               hidden        = hidden_vec,
               linear.output = TRUE,
               stepmax       = 1e6,
               threshold     = 0.05),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    # If convergence failed, record NA for this step and move on
    # to the next one rather than stopping the whole loop.
    if (is.null(modele_nn)) {
      predictions[i] <- NA
      next
    }

    # Predict the single next observation (row i of the test set).
    # Only the predictor columns are passed to predict(), since
    # neuralnet's predict() does not expect the dependent variable
    # column to be present in newdata.
    ligne_a_predire <- donnees_test[i, vars_exo_disponibles, drop = FALSE]
    predictions[i]  <- as.numeric(predict(modele_nn, newdata = ligne_a_predire))
  }

  # STEP 6 — Return the observed and predicted test values. NA
  # entries from any non-converged step are kept in the output;
  # calculer_metriques() drops them via complete.cases() when
  # computing R², MSE and MAE downstream.
  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}
```

*This chunk runs the three depth configurations for both coffee varieties, six walk-forward estimations in total, storing the results in two named lists for use in the comparison table below.*

```{r ann_multilayer_run, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# RUN ALL THREE DEPTHS, BOTH SERIES
# The outer for() loop iterates over the three named configurations
# in configs_profondeur ("2 layers", "5 layers", "10 layers"), and
# for each one calls fit_ann_multilayer() twice, once per coffee
# variety, storing the results in two named lists keyed by
# configuration name for easy lookup in the comparison table below.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

resultats_ml_ara <- list()
resultats_ml_rob <- list()

for (nom_config in names(configs_profondeur)) {

  cat("Running", nom_config, "- Arabica...\n")
  resultats_ml_ara[[nom_config]] <- fit_ann_multilayer(
    df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev,
    configs_profondeur[[nom_config]])

  cat("Running", nom_config, "- Robusta...\n")
  resultats_ml_rob[[nom_config]] <- fit_ann_multilayer(
    df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev,
    configs_profondeur[[nom_config]])
}
```

*This chunk compiles the walk-forward results from all three depth configurations, together with the single-layer ANN baseline already estimated earlier in the document (`res_ann_ara`, `res_ann_rob`), into a single comparison table, grouped by variety with `pack_rows()` for readability, consistent with the comparative performance table earlier in the document.*

```{r ann_multilayer_table, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# COMPILE COMPARISON TABLE — BASELINE (1 LAYER, nnet) VS
# 2/5/10 LAYERS (neuralnet)
# The baseline row reuses the walk-forward results already stored
# in res_ann_ara and res_ann_rob from the main ANN chunk earlier in
# the document, so the single-layer specification is not re-run
# here. Rows are built variety by variety (all Arabica architectures
# first, then all Robusta architectures) rather than alternating,
# so that pack_rows() below can group each variety into its own
# labelled block instead of interleaving them row by row.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# Ordered architecture labels, shared by both varieties so the
# row order is identical within each variety block.
labels_architecture <- c("1 layer (baseline, nnet)", names(configs_profondeur))

df_ann_depth <- rbind(
  # Arabica block: baseline row followed by the 3 depth configs
  rbind(
    data.frame(Architecture = "1 layer (baseline, nnet)",
               calculer_metriques(res_ann_ara$actual, res_ann_ara$predicted)),
    do.call(rbind, lapply(names(configs_profondeur), function(nom) {
      data.frame(Architecture = nom,
                 calculer_metriques(resultats_ml_ara[[nom]]$actual,
                                    resultats_ml_ara[[nom]]$predicted))
    }))
  ) %>% mutate(Series = "Arabica", .after = Architecture),

  # Robusta block: same structure, same architecture order
  rbind(
    data.frame(Architecture = "1 layer (baseline, nnet)",
               calculer_metriques(res_ann_rob$actual, res_ann_rob$predicted)),
    do.call(rbind, lapply(names(configs_profondeur), function(nom) {
      data.frame(Architecture = nom,
                 calculer_metriques(resultats_ml_rob[[nom]]$actual,
                                    resultats_ml_rob[[nom]]$predicted))
    }))
  ) %>% mutate(Series = "Robusta", .after = Architecture)
)

# Render with pack_rows() grouping instead of an interleaved Series
# column, so all 4 Arabica rows appear together, then all 4 Robusta
# rows, matching the convention used in the comparative_performance
# and robustness check tables earlier in the document.
df_ann_depth %>%
  select(Architecture, R2, MSE, MAE) %>%
  kable(caption   = "ANN depth comparison — 1 layer (nnet baseline) vs 2/5/10 layers (neuralnet)",
        booktabs  = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Architecture", "R²", "MSE", "MAE")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  row_spec(4, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 4,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 5, 8,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec")
```

The results show a clear and monotonic pattern: performance deteriorates as depth increases, for both varieties and at every step. For Arabica, $R^2$ falls from 0.728 at the single-layer baseline to 0.598 at 2 layers, 0.305 at 5 layers, and turns negative at −0.393 for 10 layers. Robusta follows the same trajectory, dropping from 0.456 to 0.335 at 2 layers, then to a negative $R^2$ of −0.128 at 5 layers and −0.275 at 10 layers. A negative $R^2$ means the model performs worse than simply predicting the mean of the test period, so the 5 and 10 layer networks are not just weaker, they are actively harmful specifications for this forecasting task.

This pattern is consistent with the trade-off flagged before running the comparison. `neuralnet` offers no L2 regularisation equivalent to the `decay` parameter that turned the single-layer ANN from an unstable specification (Arabica $R^2$ = 0.453) into the current baseline (0.728). Adding hidden layers without any mechanism to constrain weight growth increases the number of parameters substantially while the training sample stays fixed at 168 to 211 observations for Arabica and 153 to 192 for Robusta depending on the walk-forward step. Each additional layer gives the network more capacity to fit noise in an already small sample, and the walk-forward protocol compounds this: the network is re-initialised and retrained from scratch at every step, so a deeper, less constrained architecture is asked to reach a stable solution dozens of times over on training windows that shrink to well under 200 observations at the earliest steps. A second, compounding factor is the choice of activation function: `neuralnet` defaults to a logistic (sigmoid) activation in the hidden layers, whose derivative is bounded well below 1 and shrinks the backpropagated gradient at every layer it passes through. In a ten-layer network this vanishing gradient problem can leave the earliest layers with almost no learning signal at all, compounding the overfitting risk already discussed rather than substituting for it.

Depth alone, in other words, does not help here, and by 5 layers it actively hurts. This is not evidence that deeper networks are unsuited to coffee price forecasting in general, but that depth without regularisation is the wrong lever to pull given the sample sizes available in this study.

*This chunk re-estimates the three depth configurations using `RSNNS::mlp()` instead of `neuralnet`, adding L2 weight decay via the `BackpropWeightDecay` learning function. Unlike `neuralnet`, `RSNNS::mlp()` supports both a vector of hidden layer sizes and weight decay simultaneously, closing the regularisation gap identified as the likely cause of the depth-related degradation observed above. The decay values reuse those already selected by cross-validation for the single-layer ANN, 0.1 for Arabica and 0.001 for Robusta, so the comparison isolates the effect of adding regularisation to the same depths already tested.*

```{r ann_multilayer_decay_setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ANN MULTI-LAYER WITH WEIGHT DECAY — RSNNS PACKAGE
# neuralnet has no weight decay mechanism, which is the most
# likely explanation for the monotonic R² collapse observed as
# depth increased (see ann_multilayer_table results above).
# RSNNS::mlp() accepts a vector of hidden layer sizes, like
# neuralnet, AND supports L2-style weight decay through the
# "BackpropWeightDecay" learning function, closing that gap.
#
# learnFuncParams order for BackpropWeightDecay, confirmed from
# the SNNS User Manual (parameters of the learning functions):
#   [1] eta   : learning rate, typical range 0.1-1
#   [2] d     : weight decay term, typical range 0.005-0.3
#   [3] dmin  : minimum tolerated weight for a link before it is
#               pruned — set to 0 here to disable pruning, so
#               only weight decay is tested, not link removal
#   [4] dmax  : maximum output-target difference tolerated before
#               being backpropagated as error, typical 0/0.1/0.2
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(RSNNS)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# WALK-FORWARD ESTIMATION FUNCTION — MULTI-LAYER ANN WITH DECAY
#
# Arguments:
#   df         : levels dataset (one row per month)
#   var_dep    : name of the dependent variable column
#   n_train    : size of the initial training window
#   hidden_vec : vector of neurons per layer (same configs as
#                configs_profondeur, defined in the neuralnet
#                chunk above and reused here)
#   decay      : L2 weight decay strength. Reuses the value
#                already selected by cross-validation for the
#                single-layer ANN (tuning_ann_ara$decay = 0.1,
#                tuning_ann_rob$decay = 0.001), so the same
#                regularisation strength that stabilised the
#                1-layer network is tested at greater depths.
#
# What the function returns:
#   actual    : the observed (scaled) prices in the test period
#   predicted : the walk-forward one-step-ahead forecasts, with
#               NA for any step where training failed
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_ann_multilayer_decay <- function(df, var_dep, n_train, hidden_vec, decay) {

  # STEP 1 — Restrict the dataset to the columns this model needs,
  # identical to fit_ann_multilayer() above.
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df))
  vars_a_garder        <- c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)
  df_modele            <- df[, vars_a_garder]

  # STEP 2 — Min-Max scale every column to [0, 1], identical to
  # every other ML model in this document.
  df_modele_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  # STEP 3 — Split into the initial training set and the test set.
  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  # STEP 4 — Walk-forward loop. RSNNS::mlp() requires x (predictors)
  # and y (target) as separate numeric matrices rather than a single
  # data frame with a formula, unlike neuralnet or nnet, so the
  # matrix construction happens inside the loop for each expanding
  # window rather than once outside it.
  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  set.seed(42)   # fixed once, before the loop starts

  for (i in 1:n_test) {

    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)

    # RSNNS::mlp() expects the predictor matrix and target matrix
    # as separate arguments, not a formula on a single data frame.
    x_train <- as.matrix(fenetre_entrainement[, vars_exo_disponibles])
    y_train <- as.matrix(fenetre_entrainement[[var_dep]])

    # Fit the network with weight decay. learnFuncParams order
    # confirmed against the SNNS User Manual: c(eta, decay, dmin,
    # dmax). dmin is fixed at 0 to disable link pruning, so the
    # comparison isolates weight decay alone.
    modele_rsnns <- tryCatch(
      mlp(x = x_train, y = y_train,
          size            = hidden_vec,
          maxit           = 500,
          learnFunc       = "BackpropWeightDecay",
          learnFuncParams = c(0.2, decay, 0, 0.1),
          linOut          = TRUE),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(modele_rsnns)) {
      predictions[i] <- NA
      next
    }

    # Predict the single next observation. RSNNS's predict() also
    # requires a matrix input, consistent with the training call.
    ligne_a_predire <- as.matrix(donnees_test[i, vars_exo_disponibles,
                                               drop = FALSE])
    predictions[i]  <- as.numeric(predict(modele_rsnns, ligne_a_predire))
  }

  # STEP 5 — Return observed and predicted test values.
  valeurs_observees <- donnees_test[[var_dep]]
  list(actual = valeurs_observees, predicted = predictions)
}
```

*This chunk runs the three depth configurations with weight decay for both coffee varieties, six additional walk-forward estimations, using the decay values already selected for the single-layer ANN baseline.*

```{r ann_multilayer_decay_run, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# RUN ALL THREE DEPTHS WITH DECAY, BOTH SERIES
# Same loop structure as ann_multilayer_run above, calling
# fit_ann_multilayer_decay() instead of fit_ann_multilayer(),
# with the variety-specific decay value passed explicitly.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

resultats_ml_decay_ara <- list()
resultats_ml_decay_rob <- list()

for (nom_config in names(configs_profondeur)) {

  cat("Running", nom_config, "with decay - Arabica...\n")
  resultats_ml_decay_ara[[nom_config]] <- fit_ann_multilayer_decay(
    df_arabica_levels, "arabica_price", n_train_ara_lev,
    configs_profondeur[[nom_config]], decay = tuning_ann_ara$decay)

  cat("Running", nom_config, "with decay - Robusta...\n")
  resultats_ml_decay_rob[[nom_config]] <- fit_ann_multilayer_decay(
    df_robusta_levels, "robusta_price", n_train_rob_lev,
    configs_profondeur[[nom_config]], decay = tuning_ann_rob$decay)
}
```

*This chunk adds the weight-decay results to the depth comparison, again grouped by variety with `pack_rows()` so each variety's four architectures (baseline, 2, 5, 10 layers, each with decay) read as a single readable block.*

```{r ann_multilayer_decay_table, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# EXTEND THE COMPARISON WITH THE DECAY RESULTS, GROUPED BY VARIETY
# Same variety-block structure as ann_multilayer_table above:
# all Arabica rows (baseline + 3 undecayed depths + 3 decayed
# depths) first, then the same 7 rows for Robusta.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_ann_depth_decay <- rbind(
  # Arabica block: baseline, 3 undecayed depths, 3 decayed depths
  rbind(
    df_ann_depth %>% filter(Series == "Arabica") %>% select(-Series),
    do.call(rbind, lapply(names(configs_profondeur), function(nom) {
      data.frame(Architecture = paste0(nom, " + decay"),
                 calculer_metriques(resultats_ml_decay_ara[[nom]]$actual,
                                    resultats_ml_decay_ara[[nom]]$predicted))
    }))
  ) %>% mutate(Series = "Arabica", .after = Architecture),

  # Robusta block: same structure
  rbind(
    df_ann_depth %>% filter(Series == "Robusta") %>% select(-Series),
    do.call(rbind, lapply(names(configs_profondeur), function(nom) {
      data.frame(Architecture = paste0(nom, " + decay"),
                 calculer_metriques(resultats_ml_decay_rob[[nom]]$actual,
                                    resultats_ml_decay_rob[[nom]]$predicted))
    }))
  ) %>% mutate(Series = "Robusta", .after = Architecture)
)

df_ann_depth_decay %>%
  select(Architecture, R2, MSE, MAE) %>%
  kable(caption   = "ANN depth comparison, with and without weight decay (RSNNS)",
        booktabs  = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
        col.names = c("Architecture", "R²", "MSE", "MAE")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  row_spec(7, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 7,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 8, 14,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec")
```

Adding weight decay through `RSNNS::mlp()` was intended to test whether regularisation restores some of the performance lost at depth, using the same decay values already selected for the single-layer baseline, 0.1 for Arabica and 0.001 for Robusta. The results do not support this. Every decayed configuration underperforms its undecayed `neuralnet` counterpart at the same depth, and by a wide margin: Arabica falls to $R^2$ values of −1.206, −1.054- and −1.220 at 2, 5 and 10 layers respectively, while Robusta falls to −0.423, −0.264 and −0.367. Rather than narrowing the gap with the single-layer baseline, adding decay widens it substantially.

This outcome most likely reflects a methodological confound rather than a genuine effect of weight decay. Gaining access to `BackpropWeightDecay` required switching from `neuralnet` to `RSNNS`, and the two packages differ not only in their support for regularisation but in their default training algorithm. `neuralnet` trains by resilient backpropagation (Rprop+), an adaptive method whose step size is adjusted per weight and typically converges efficiently even on small samples. `BackpropWeightDecay`, by contrast, is a variant of standard gradient descent with a fixed learning rate, a considerably less efficient optimiser that generally requires more iterations to reach a comparable solution. This difficulty is compounded by the sigmoid activation shared by both packages: `BackpropWeightDecay`'s fixed-step updates have no mechanism to compensate for a gradient that is already shrinking with depth, unlike Rprop+, which adapts to the sign rather than the magnitude of the gradient and is comparatively more robust to this effect. The 500-iteration budget carried over unchanged from the `neuralnet` specification was calibrated for the faster of the two algorithms, and is plausibly insufficient for the slower one, particularly on the deeper architectures tested here. The RSNNS results are therefore better read as evidence of under-optimisation than as evidence against the value of regularisation at depth.

The RSNNS results are therefore better read as evidence of under-optimisation than as evidence against the value of regularisation at depth.

## Comparative Performance Analysis

*This chunk consolidates the six individual metric data frames into a single comparison table and produces the summary bar chart. The metric columns are coerced to numeric here because `cbind()` in the individual model chunks stores them as character strings when binding with the Model and Series label columns. Two separate tables are rendered, one per coffee variety, to keep each readable, followed by a grouped bar chart that allows visual comparison of $R^2$ across all model-variety combinations simultaneously.*

```{r comparative_performance, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — COMBINE ALL MODEL METRICS
# bind_rows() stacks the six two-row metric data frames into
# a single 12-row frame (6 models × 2 series).
# as.numeric() coercion is necessary because cbind() in each
# model chunk coerces numeric columns to character when
# binding them with the Model and Series string columns.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_all <- bind_rows(
  metriques_mlr, metriques_arimax, metriques_rf,
  metriques_xgb, metriques_svm,   metriques_ann
) %>%
  mutate(across(c(R2, MSE, MAE), as.numeric))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — SINGLE PERFORMANCE TABLE (ARABICA AND ROBUSTA)
# Models are displayed in the same order as they appear in
# the document: MLR, ARIMAX, Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM,
# ANN. This allows the reader to locate each model in the
# table without having to cross-reference the section order.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_all %>%
  arrange(Series, factor(Model, levels = c("MLR", "ARIMAX", "Random Forest",
                                            "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))) %>%
  mutate(
    MSE = ifelse(MSE > 100,
                 format(round(MSE, 0), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
                 as.character(round(MSE, 4))),
    MAE = ifelse(MAE > 10,
                 format(round(MAE, 1), scientific = FALSE),
                 as.character(round(MAE, 4)))
  ) %>%
  select(Model, R2, MSE, MAE) %>%
  kable(caption   = "Comparative model performance — out-of-sample results",
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        col.names = c("Model", "R²", "MSE", "MAE"),
        align     = c("l", "c", "c", "c")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) %>%
  row_spec(6, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 6,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 7, 12,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec") %>%
  footnote(general           = "MSE and MAE for ARIMAX and MLR are in original price units (USD/lb for Arabica, USD/tonne for Robusta). MSE and MAE for RF, XGBoost, SVM and ANN are on the Min-Max scaled [0, 1] range and are not directly comparable.",
           general_title     = "Note:",
           footnote_as_chunk = TRUE)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — COMPARATIVE R² BAR CHART
# Models are displayed in the same order as the table and
# the document structure. R² labels are displayed above
# each bar for readability. A dashed reference line at
# R² = 0.75 provides a visual benchmark.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_all %>%
  mutate(Model = factor(Model,
                        levels = c("MLR", "ARIMAX", "Random Forest",
                                   "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Model, y = R2, fill = Series)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge",
           alpha = 0.85, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(R2, 3)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.75, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Arabica" = "#8B4513",
                               "Robusta" = "#2E8B57")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.02),
                     breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  labs(title    = "Out-of-sample R² by model and coffee variety",
       subtitle = "Dashed line at R² = 0.75",
       x = NULL, y = expression(R^2), fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1),
        legend.position    = "top",
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

The results tell a fairly clear story. ARIMAX is the strongest model overall, particularly for Robusta where it reaches an $R^2$ of 0.929, and remains very competitive for Arabica at 0.821. Among the ML models, SVM, XGBoost and Random Forest are almost indistinguishable for Arabica, with $R^2$ values of 0.813, 0.812 and 0.811 respectively, which suggests that the three approaches are drawing on largely the same information from the predictor set. MLR holds up reasonably well for Arabica at 0.784 but breaks down for Robusta at 0.276, confirming that a static linear model without temporal dynamics is not well suited to that series. The ANN improves substantially over the baseline thanks to L2 regularisation, but at 0.728 for Arabica and 0.456 for Robusta it remains the weakest of the six models.

The walk-forward validation protocol ensures that all reported metrics reflect genuine out-of-sample forecasting ability, with no possibility of data leakage between the training and test periods. The majority of models achieve $R^2$ values above 0.75, with the notable exceptions of ANN for both varieties, Random Forest for Robusta and MLR for Robusta, reflecting the structural challenges of forecasting a shorter and more volatile series on a limited training sample.

### Variable Importance and Partial Dependence Plots

#### Variable Importance

The comparative performance metrics reported above indicate how well each model forecasts coffee prices out of sample, but they say nothing about which variables are driving those forecasts. This section addresses that question by computing permutation importance for all six models and both coffee varieties, using a model-agnostic approach that is directly comparable across model families.

*This chunk computes permutation importance for all six models and both coffee varieties. For each model, a single instance is first fitted on the full initial training window. Each of the 14 predictors is then permuted independently on the test set while all other variables remain unchanged, and the resulting increase in MSE relative to the walk-forward baseline is recorded as the importance score. For ARIMAX, only the exogenous regressors are permuted, with the autoregressive component held fixed. A positive score indicates that shuffling the variable degrades forecast accuracy, and therefore that the model relies on that variable; a score close to zero or negative indicates that the variable contributes little to the forecasts.*

```{r importance_permutation_all, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PERMUTATION IMPORTANCE — ALL SIX MODELS
# For each model, a single instance is fitted on the full
# initial training window. Each predictor is then permuted
# independently on the test set, predictions are regenerated,
# and the increase in MSE relative to the baseline is used
# as the importance score. A larger increase means the model
# relies more heavily on that variable.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(randomForest)
library(xgboost)
library(e1071)
library(nnet)
library(forecast)

labels_vi <- labels_mlr

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — PREPARE SCALED DATASETS AND TEST SETS
# Both training and test sets are Min-Max scaled using the
# full sample min/max, consistent with the walk-forward
# estimation procedure used throughout the document.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# Arabica
vars_exo_ara  <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df_arabica_levels))
df_ara_modele <- df_arabica_levels[, c("arabica_price", vars_exo_ara)]
df_ara_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_ara_modele, minmax_scale))
train_ara     <- df_ara_scaled[1:n_train_ara_lev, ]
test_ara      <- df_ara_scaled[(n_train_ara_lev + 1):nrow(df_ara_scaled), ]
actual_ara    <- test_ara[["arabica_price"]]

# Robusta
vars_exo_rob  <- intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df_robusta_levels))
df_rob_modele <- df_robusta_levels[, c("robusta_price", vars_exo_rob)]
df_rob_scaled <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_rob_modele, minmax_scale))
train_rob     <- df_rob_scaled[1:n_train_rob_lev, ]
test_rob      <- df_rob_scaled[(n_train_rob_lev + 1):nrow(df_rob_scaled), ]
actual_rob    <- test_rob[["robusta_price"]]


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — FIT ALL MODELS ON THE FULL TRAINING WINDOW
# Each model is fitted once on the initial training set.
# These training-set models are used exclusively for the
# permutation importance computation — they do not replace
# the walk-forward models used for performance evaluation.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# MLR
modele_mlr_ara <- lm(arabica_price ~ ., data = train_ara)
modele_mlr_rob <- lm(robusta_price ~ ., data = train_rob)

# ARIMAX
# auto.arima() requires unscaled data and the regressor
# matrix separately. The model is fitted on the unscaled
# training series with the scaled regressors, consistent
# with the main ARIMAX chunk.
xreg_train_ara <- as.matrix(train_ara[, vars_exo_ara])
xreg_test_ara  <- as.matrix(test_ara[,  vars_exo_ara])
xreg_train_rob <- as.matrix(train_rob[, vars_exo_rob])
xreg_test_rob  <- as.matrix(test_rob[,  vars_exo_rob])

modele_arimax_ara <- auto.arima(
  df_arabica_levels$arabica_price[1:n_train_ara_lev],
  xreg          = as.matrix(df_arabica_levels[1:n_train_ara_lev, vars_exo_ara]),
  stepwise      = TRUE,
  approximation = TRUE,
  max.p = 3, max.q = 3, max.d = 1
)

modele_arimax_rob <- auto.arima(
  df_robusta_levels$robusta_price[1:n_train_rob_lev],
  xreg          = as.matrix(df_robusta_levels[1:n_train_rob_lev, vars_exo_rob]),
  stepwise      = TRUE,
  approximation = TRUE,
  max.p = 3, max.q = 3, max.d = 1
)

# Random Forest
set.seed(42)
modele_rf_ara <- randomForest(arabica_price ~ ., data = train_ara,
                               ntree = 500)
set.seed(42)
modele_rf_rob <- randomForest(robusta_price ~ ., data = train_rob,
                               ntree = 500)

# XGBoost
X_train_ara   <- as.matrix(train_ara[, vars_exo_ara])
y_train_ara   <- train_ara[["arabica_price"]]
X_test_ara    <- as.matrix(test_ara[, vars_exo_ara])

X_train_rob   <- as.matrix(train_rob[, vars_exo_rob])
y_train_rob   <- train_rob[["robusta_price"]]
X_test_rob    <- as.matrix(test_rob[, vars_exo_rob])

set.seed(42)
modele_xgb_ara <- xgboost(
  data      = X_train_ara, label = y_train_ara,
  nrounds   = tuning_xgb_ara$nrounds,
  max_depth = tuning_xgb_ara$max_depth,
  eta       = tuning_xgb_ara$eta,
  subsample = tuning_xgb_ara$subsample,
  verbose = 0, objective = "reg:squarederror"
)

set.seed(42)
modele_xgb_rob <- xgboost(
  data      = X_train_rob, label = y_train_rob,
  nrounds   = tuning_xgb_rob$nrounds,
  max_depth = tuning_xgb_rob$max_depth,
  eta       = tuning_xgb_rob$eta,
  subsample = tuning_xgb_rob$subsample,
  verbose = 0, objective = "reg:squarederror"
)

# SVM
modele_svm_ara <- svm(arabica_price ~ ., data = train_ara,
                       kernel = "radial",
                       cost   = tuning_svm_ara$cost,
                       gamma  = tuning_svm_ara$gamma)
modele_svm_rob <- svm(robusta_price ~ ., data = train_rob,
```
