```{r importance_permutation_all, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
                       kernel = "radial",
                       cost   = tuning_svm_rob$cost,
                       gamma  = tuning_svm_rob$gamma)

# ANN
set.seed(42)
modele_ann_ara <- nnet(arabica_price ~ ., data = train_ara,
                        size   = tuning_ann_ara$size,
                        decay  = tuning_ann_ara$decay,
                        linout = TRUE, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE)
set.seed(42)
modele_ann_rob <- nnet(robusta_price ~ ., data = train_rob,
                        size   = tuning_ann_rob$size,
                        decay  = tuning_ann_rob$decay,
                        linout = TRUE, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — BASELINE MSE FOR EACH MODEL
# The baseline MSE is computed from the walk-forward
# predictions already stored in the result objects, not
# from the training-set models fitted above. This ensures
# that the importance scores reflect the actual forecasting
# performance reported in the comparative table.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

mse_base <- list(
  mlr_ara   = mean((actual_ara - as.numeric(res_mlr_ara$predicted))^2),
  mlr_rob   = mean((actual_rob - as.numeric(res_mlr_rob$predicted))^2),
  arimax_ara = mean((res_arimax_ara$actual - res_arimax_ara$predicted)^2,
                    na.rm = TRUE),
  arimax_rob = mean((res_arimax_rob$actual - res_arimax_rob$predicted)^2,
                    na.rm = TRUE),
  rf_ara    = mean((actual_ara - as.numeric(res_rf_ara$predicted))^2),
  rf_rob    = mean((actual_rob - as.numeric(res_rf_rob$predicted))^2),
  xgb_ara   = mean((actual_ara - as.numeric(res_xgb_ara$predicted))^2),
  xgb_rob   = mean((actual_rob - as.numeric(res_xgb_rob$predicted))^2),
  svm_ara   = mean((actual_ara - as.numeric(res_svm_ara$predicted))^2),
  svm_rob   = mean((actual_rob - as.numeric(res_svm_rob$predicted))^2),
  ann_ara   = mean((actual_ara - as.numeric(res_ann_ara$predicted))^2),
  ann_rob   = mean((actual_rob - as.numeric(res_ann_rob$predicted))^2)
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — PERMUTATION IMPORTANCE FUNCTION
# For each predictor, the column is shuffled in the test
# set, predictions are regenerated using the training-set
# model, and the increase in MSE relative to baseline is
# recorded. The procedure is wrapped in a function that
# accepts any predict-compatible model object.
#
# Arguments:
#   test_set    : scaled test set data frame
#   var_dep     : name of the dependent variable column
#   vars_exo_v  : vector of predictor names
#   predict_fun : function(model, newdata) -> numeric vector
#   modele      : fitted model object
#   mse_base    : baseline MSE from walk-forward predictions
# ----------------------------------------------------------

permutation_importance <- function(test_set, var_dep, vars_exo_v,
                                    predict_fun, modele, mse_base_val) {
  set.seed(42)
  resultats <- lapply(vars_exo_v, function(var) {
    test_perm        <- test_set
    test_perm[[var]] <- sample(test_perm[[var]])
    preds            <- predict_fun(modele, test_perm)
    actual           <- test_set[[var_dep]]
    mse_perm         <- mean((actual - preds)^2)
    data.frame(
      Variable   = labels_vi[var],
      Importance = mse_perm - mse_base_val
    )
  })
  do.call(rbind, resultats) %>%
    filter(!is.na(Variable)) %>%
    arrange(desc(Importance))
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 5 — COMPUTE PERMUTATION IMPORTANCE FOR ALL MODELS
# Each model uses its own predict function wrapper to
# ensure consistent output format across model families.
# ARIMAX uses forecast() with the permuted xreg matrix;
# XGBoost requires a matrix input rather than a data frame.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# MLR
imp_perm_mlr_ara <- permutation_importance(
  test_ara, "arabica_price", vars_exo_ara,
  function(m, d) predict(m, newdata = d),
  modele_mlr_ara, mse_base$mlr_ara)

imp_perm_mlr_rob <- permutation_importance(
  test_rob, "robusta_price", vars_exo_rob,
  function(m, d) predict(m, newdata = d),
  modele_mlr_rob, mse_base$mlr_rob)

# ARIMAX — permutation applied to xreg only
# The AR component is kept fixed; only the contribution of
# each exogenous regressor is evaluated.
imp_perm_arimax_ara <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars_exo_ara, function(var) {
  set.seed(42)
  xreg_perm        <- xreg_test_ara
  xreg_perm[, var] <- sample(xreg_perm[, var])
  fc <- forecast(modele_arimax_ara,
                 h    = nrow(xreg_perm),
                 xreg = xreg_perm)
  preds    <- as.numeric(fc$mean)
  mse_perm <- mean((res_arimax_ara$actual - preds)^2, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(Variable   = labels_vi[var],
             Importance = mse_perm - mse_base$arimax_ara)
})) %>% filter(!is.na(Variable)) %>% arrange(desc(Importance))

imp_perm_arimax_rob <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars_exo_rob, function(var) {
  set.seed(42)
  xreg_perm        <- xreg_test_rob
  xreg_perm[, var] <- sample(xreg_perm[, var])
  fc <- forecast(modele_arimax_rob,
                 h    = nrow(xreg_perm),
                 xreg = xreg_perm)
  preds    <- as.numeric(fc$mean)
  mse_perm <- mean((res_arimax_rob$actual - preds)^2, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(Variable   = labels_vi[var],
             Importance = mse_perm - mse_base$arimax_rob)
})) %>% filter(!is.na(Variable)) %>% arrange(desc(Importance))

# Random Forest
imp_perm_rf_ara <- permutation_importance(
  test_ara, "arabica_price", vars_exo_ara,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_rf_ara, mse_base$rf_ara)

imp_perm_rf_rob <- permutation_importance(
  test_rob, "robusta_price", vars_exo_rob,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_rf_rob, mse_base$rf_rob)

# XGBoost — requires matrix input
imp_perm_xgb_ara <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars_exo_ara, function(var) {
  set.seed(42)
  X_perm        <- X_test_ara
  X_perm[, var] <- sample(X_perm[, var])
  preds         <- predict(modele_xgb_ara, newdata = X_perm)
  mse_perm      <- mean((actual_ara - preds)^2)
  data.frame(Variable   = labels_vi[var],
             Importance = mse_perm - mse_base$xgb_ara)
})) %>% filter(!is.na(Variable)) %>% arrange(desc(Importance))

imp_perm_xgb_rob <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars_exo_rob, function(var) {
  set.seed(42)
  X_perm        <- X_test_rob
  X_perm[, var] <- sample(X_perm[, var])
  preds         <- predict(modele_xgb_rob, newdata = X_perm)
  mse_perm      <- mean((actual_rob - preds)^2)
  data.frame(Variable   = labels_vi[var],
             Importance = mse_perm - mse_base$xgb_rob)
})) %>% filter(!is.na(Variable)) %>% arrange(desc(Importance))

# SVM
imp_perm_svm_ara <- permutation_importance(
  test_ara, "arabica_price", vars_exo_ara,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_svm_ara, mse_base$svm_ara)

imp_perm_svm_rob <- permutation_importance(
  test_rob, "robusta_price", vars_exo_rob,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_svm_rob, mse_base$svm_rob)

# ANN
imp_perm_ann_ara <- permutation_importance(
  test_ara, "arabica_price", vars_exo_ara,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_ann_ara, mse_base$ann_ara)

imp_perm_ann_rob <- permutation_importance(
  test_rob, "robusta_price", vars_exo_rob,
  function(m, d) as.numeric(predict(m, newdata = d)),
  modele_ann_rob, mse_base$ann_rob)

cat("Permutation importance computed for all 6 models.\n")
```

The permutation importance scores are now available for all six models and both varieties. The plots below summarise the top three variables per model for each coffee variety across the four ML models, allowing direct comparison of predictor hierarchies. MLR and ARIMAX are excluded from this comparison for reasons discussed in the code. The full rankings for all 14 variables are reported in the Appendices.

*This chunk produces the top-3 comparative importance plots for the main text. For each ML model and each variety, the three variables with the highest permutation importance scores are extracted and displayed side by side using `facet_wrap()`. MLR is excluded because severe multicollinearity causes all its permutation scores to be negative. ARIMAX is excluded because it predicts in original price units rather than the Min-Max scaled range, making its importance scores not directly comparable to those of the ML models. The y-axis scale varies freely across panels to accommodate differences in the magnitude of importance scores between models.*

```{r importance_comparative_plots, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# COMPARATIVE IMPORTANCE PLOTS (MAIN TEXT)
# Only the four ML models are included in the comparative
# chart, as they share the same Min-Max scaled prediction
# space and produce directly comparable importance scores.
# MLR is excluded because severe multicollinearity causes
# all permutation scores to be negative, making the chart
# uninformative. ARIMAX is excluded because it predicts in
# original price units rather than the [0,1] scaled range,
# making its importance scores several orders of magnitude
# larger than those of the ML models and not directly
# comparable.
# Negative importance scores are set to zero and excluded
# from the ranking before the top 3 are selected.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

construire_top3 <- function(imp_list, noms_modeles) {
  do.call(rbind, mapply(function(imp_df, nom) {
    imp_df %>%
      filter(Importance > 0) %>%
      slice_max(Importance, n = 3) %>%
      mutate(Model = nom)
  }, imp_list, noms_modeles, SIMPLIFY = FALSE)) %>%
    mutate(
      Model          = factor(Model,
                              levels = c("Random Forest", "XGBoost",
                                         "SVM", "ANN")),
      Variable_Model = paste(Variable, Model, sep = "__"),
      Variable_Model = reorder(Variable_Model, Importance)
    )
}

top3_ara <- construire_top3(
  list(imp_perm_rf_ara, imp_perm_xgb_ara,
       imp_perm_svm_ara, imp_perm_ann_ara),
  c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")
)

top3_rob <- construire_top3(
  list(imp_perm_rf_rob, imp_perm_xgb_rob,
       imp_perm_svm_rob, imp_perm_ann_rob),
  c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PLOT FUNCTION
# ncol = 4 places all four models on a single row.
# panel.spacing gives enough room between panels.
# scales = "free" allows each panel to use its own axis
# range since importance magnitudes differ across models.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

plot_top3 <- function(top3_df, color, bg_color, title) {
  ggplot(top3_df,
         aes(x = Variable_Model, y = Importance)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = color, alpha = 0.85, width = 0.55) +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(Importance, 4)),
              hjust = -0.15, size = 3, color = "grey40") +
    coord_flip() +
    facet_wrap(~ Model, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = function(x) gsub("__.*", "", x)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.40))) +
    labs(title    = title,
         subtitle = "Top 3 variables by permutation importance (ΔMSE). Negative scores excluded.",
         x = NULL, y = "ΔMSE") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
      strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
      strip.background   = element_rect(fill = bg_color, color = NA),
      plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      plot.subtitle      = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40"),
      axis.text.y        = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey20"),
      axis.text.x        = element_text(size = 8, color = "grey40"),
      panel.spacing      = unit(2, "lines")
    )
}

plot_top3(top3_ara, "#8B4513", "#f5ece6",
          "Top 3 variable importance by model — Arabica futures")

plot_top3(top3_rob, "#2E8B57", "#e8f5ec",
          "Top 3 variable importance by model — Robusta futures")
```

Across the four ML models, the results for Arabica are fairly consistent. Ending stocks consistently ranks among the top three predictors across all four ML models, confirming inventory levels as a reliable short-run driver of Arabica prices. COT net MM and WTI also feature prominently, appearing in the top three for most models, which points to speculative positioning and energy costs as secondary but recurring drivers. WTI ranks third for XGBoost and ANN, while Fed Funds Rate and Sugar also feature across Random Forest and ANN. The broad agreement on Ending stocks and COT net MM across four structurally different model families is reassuring, confirming that their predictive contribution is real and not just a coincidence of one particular model's structure.

For Robusta, macroeconomic variables dominate. WTI ranks first for Random Forest, SVM and ANN, while Fed Funds Rate appears in the top three of all four models, making it the most consistently important predictor for this variety. Sugar also features in two of the four models. The ANN Robusta scores are substantially larger in magnitude than those of the other models, which is a direct consequence of its lower baseline accuracy: a less precise model is simply more sensitive to any perturbation of the input variables, amplifying the permutation importance scores relative to better-performing models.

#### Partial Dependence Plots

Partial dependence plots complement the permutation importance results by showing not just how much a variable matters to each model, but in which direction and through what kind of relationship. For a given predictor, the procedure fixes that variable at a sequence of values spanning its observed range, holds every other predictor at its actual value for each training observation, generates predictions at each step, and averages them across the training set. The resulting curve traces how the model's expected output moves as the variable changes, once the influence of the other thirteen predictors has been averaged out.

Computing this for all fourteen variables and all four ML models would produce far more panels than the main text can reasonably hold, so the comparison here is restricted to the variables that came out as consensus drivers in the permutation importance analysis for each variety: Ending stocks, COT net MM and WTI for Arabica, and Fed Funds Rate and WTI for Robusta. These are shown faceted across the four ML models so the shape of each relationship can be compared side by side. The full set of plots, covering each model's own top three variables individually, is reported in the Appendices.

*The chunk below sets up the machinery needed to compute a partial dependence curve for any combination of model and predictor, then applies it to the consensus variables identified for each coffee variety. The four ML models are not re-estimated here: they are the same objects already fitted on the full initial training window in the variable importance chunk. The grid of values tested for each variable is built over the range actually observed in the training set on the scaled axis, rather than the full [0,1] interval, so the model is never asked to predict outside the range of data it was trained on.*

```{r pdp_main_compute, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PARTIAL DEPENDENCE PLOTS — GENERIC FUNCTIONS
# A PDP measures a model's average marginal dependence on a single
# variable: for a grid of values of that variable, the value is held
# fixed across every observation in the training set, predictions are
# recomputed, and then averaged. The four ML models reuse the objects
# already fitted on the full initial training window in the
# importance_permutation_all chunk, with no re-estimation here.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# STEP 1 — Bounds in original units for each predictor and for each
# dependent variable.
# All ML models are trained on data scaled to [0,1] by minmax_scale().
# The PDP grid and the resulting predictions therefore both need to be
# converted back to original units (USD/lb, USD/tonne, %, etc.) to be
# interpretable in the plots. calculer_bornes() just pulls the min and
# max of each variable from the unscaled dataset, which serve as the
# reference points for this linear back-transformation.
calculer_bornes <- function(df, variables) {
  bornes <- lapply(variables, function(v)
    c(min = min(df[[v]], na.rm = TRUE), max = max(df[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)))
  names(bornes) <- variables
  bornes
}

# Bounds for the 14 predictors, by variety (used to convert the x-axis
# of each PDP back from the [0,1] scale)
bornes_ara <- calculer_bornes(df_ara_modele, vars_exo_ara)
bornes_rob <- calculer_bornes(df_rob_modele, vars_exo_rob)

# Bounds for the dependent variable (price), by variety (used to
# convert the y-axis, i.e. the averaged prediction, back from [0,1] to
# USD/lb or USD/tonne)
bornes_prix_ara <- c(min = min(df_ara_modele$arabica_price),
                     max = max(df_ara_modele$arabica_price))
bornes_prix_rob <- c(min = min(df_rob_modele$robusta_price),
                     max = max(df_rob_modele$robusta_price))


# STEP 2 — Predictor-only data, required by XGBoost.
# Unlike lm(), randomForest(), svm() and nnet(), which all accept a
# full data frame (the dependent variable column included, simply
# ignored by predict()), predict.xgb.Booster() requires a numeric
# matrix containing only the predictor columns. These two objects are
# built once here and reused for every PDP call involving XGBoost,
# instead of being rebuilt for each variable tested.
train_ara_xgb <- train_ara[, vars_exo_ara]
train_rob_xgb <- train_rob[, vars_exo_rob]


# STEP 3 — Named lists of the four already-fitted ML models, by variety.
# These objects (modele_rf_ara, modele_xgb_ara, etc.) were trained once
# on the full training window in the importance_permutation_all chunk
# and are reused here as-is, with no retraining. Grouping them into a
# named list allows looping over the four models with lapply() in the
# steps below, instead of duplicating the same block four times.
modeles_ara <- list("Random Forest" = modele_rf_ara, "XGBoost" = modele_xgb_ara,
                    "SVM" = modele_svm_ara, "ANN" = modele_ann_ara)
modeles_rob <- list("Random Forest" = modele_rf_rob, "XGBoost" = modele_xgb_rob,
                    "SVM" = modele_svm_rob, "ANN" = modele_ann_rob)


# STEP 4 — Select the right input dataset depending on the model.
# This function captures the only structural difference between
# XGBoost and the other three models: XGBoost needs the predictor-only
# matrix (donnees_predicteurs), while Random Forest, SVM and ANN accept
# the full data frame (donnees_full), which includes the dependent
# variable column without that causing any issue for predict().
obtenir_donnees_pdp <- function(nom_modele, donnees_full, donnees_predicteurs) {
  if (nom_modele == "XGBoost") donnees_predicteurs else donnees_full
}


# STEP 5 — Prediction wrapper, needed because XGBoost expects a matrix
# rather than a data frame.
# predict.xgb.Booster() explicitly requires a matrix or xgb.DMatrix
# object as input and fails if passed a data frame. as.matrix() is
# therefore only applied in the XGBoost branch; the other three models
# call predict() directly on the data frame, consistent with the rest
# of the document.
predire_pdp <- function(nom_modele, modele, donnees) {
  if (nom_modele == "XGBoost") {
    as.numeric(predict(modele, newdata = as.matrix(donnees)))
  } else {
    as.numeric(predict(modele, newdata = donnees))
  }
}


# STEP 6 — Compute the PDP for one model and one variable.
# What happens at each point of the grid:
#   (a) take a fresh copy of the full training set
#   (b) overwrite the column of the variable of interest with a SINGLE
#       fixed value across ALL observations (the other 13 predictors
#       stay at their real, observation-specific values)
#   (c) generate a prediction for each of these modified observations
#   (d) average these predictions across the whole training set
# The result of that average, for each grid value, is one point on the
# PDP curve. The grid itself is built over the range actually observed
# in the training set on the [0,1] scale, rather than the full [0,1]
# interval, to avoid extrapolating the model beyond values it actually
# saw during training.
calculer_pdp <- function(nom_modele, modele, donnees_train, variable,
                          bornes_var, bornes_cible, n_points = 20) {

  # (a) Grid of n_points equally spaced values, on the [0,1] scale,
  # spanning the range actually observed for this variable in the
  # training set
  grille_scaled <- seq(min(donnees_train[[variable]]),
                       max(donnees_train[[variable]]),
                       length.out = n_points)

  # (b)-(d) For each grid value: copy the data, overwrite the column of
  # the tested variable with that fixed value on every row, predict,
  # then average the predictions obtained across the training set
  predictions_moyennes <- sapply(grille_scaled, function(val) {
    donnees_modifiees <- donnees_train
    donnees_modifiees[[variable]] <- val
    mean(predire_pdp(nom_modele, modele, donnees_modifiees))
  })

  # Convert both axes, x (variable value) and y (averaged prediction),
  # back from the [0,1] scale to original units, using the bounds
  # computed in Step 1
  data.frame(
    Model = nom_modele,
    x     = bornes_var["min"] + grille_scaled * (bornes_var["max"] - bornes_var["min"]),
    y     = bornes_cible["min"] + predictions_moyennes * (bornes_cible["max"] - bornes_cible["min"])
  )
}


# STEP 7 — PDP for the consensus variables shown in the main text:
# Ending stocks, COT net MM and WTI for Arabica, Fed Funds Rate and WTI
# for Robusta, computed for all four ML models.
# generer_pdp_variable() loops over the four models of one variety
# (via lapply() on names(modeles)) and stacks (rbind) the four
# resulting curves for ONE variable, tagging each row with that
# variable's readable label.
generer_pdp_variable <- function(modeles, donnees_full, donnees_predicteurs,
                                  variable, label_variable,
                                  bornes_vars, bornes_cible) {
  resultat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(modeles), function(nom) {
    calculer_pdp(nom, modeles[[nom]],
                obtenir_donnees_pdp(nom, donnees_full, donnees_predicteurs),
                variable, bornes_vars[[variable]], bornes_cible)
  }))
  resultat$Variable <- label_variable
  resultat
}

# Arabica: three calls (one per consensus variable), stacked into a
# single data frame of 4 models x 3 variables x 20 points = 240 rows
df_pdp_ara <- rbind(
  generer_pdp_variable(modeles_ara, train_ara, train_ara_xgb,
                       "ending_stocks", "Ending stocks",
                       bornes_ara, bornes_prix_ara),
  generer_pdp_variable(modeles_ara, train_ara, train_ara_xgb,
                       "cot_net_mm", "COT net MM",
                       bornes_ara, bornes_prix_ara),
  generer_pdp_variable(modeles_ara, train_ara, train_ara_xgb,
                       "wti", "WTI",
                       bornes_ara, bornes_prix_ara)
)
# Convert to factors with a fixed level order, so facet_grid() displays
# models and variables in the intended order rather than alphabetically
df_pdp_ara$Model    <- factor(df_pdp_ara$Model,
                              levels = c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))
df_pdp_ara$Variable <- factor(df_pdp_ara$Variable,
                              levels = c("Ending stocks", "COT net MM", "WTI"))

# Robusta: same logic, with the two consensus variables specific to
# this variety
df_pdp_rob <- rbind(
  generer_pdp_variable(modeles_rob, train_rob, train_rob_xgb,
                       "fed_funds_rate", "Fed Funds Rate",
                       bornes_rob, bornes_prix_rob),
  generer_pdp_variable(modeles_rob, train_rob, train_rob_xgb,
                       "wti", "WTI",
                       bornes_rob, bornes_prix_rob)
)
df_pdp_rob$Model    <- factor(df_pdp_rob$Model,
                              levels = c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))
df_pdp_rob$Variable <- factor(df_pdp_rob$Variable,
                              levels = c("Fed Funds Rate", "WTI"))
```

*This chunk renders the main-text PDP figure for Arabica, with the three consensus variables as rows and the four ML models as columns.*

```{r pdp_main_plots_arabica, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, out.width="100%"}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PDP PLOT — ARABICA (MAIN TEXT)
# Separated into its own chunk so fig.height can be set specifically
# for this plot's 3 rows of panels (Ending stocks, COT net MM, WTI),
# rather than sharing a single height with the Robusta plot below,
# which only has 2 rows. facet_grid2() with independent = "x" frees
# the x-axis per panel rather than per column (see note in the
# pdp_main_compute chunk for why this matters given the very
# different units and ranges of the variables shown). out.width =
# "100%" caps the rendered width to the page's text width; fig.height
# is set directly here since out.width alone does not constrain the
# rendered height, which otherwise follows the fig.width:fig.height
# ratio set below.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

library(ggh4x)

ggplot(df_pdp_ara, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_grid2(Variable ~ Model, scales = "free_x", independent = "x") +
  labs(title    = "Partial dependence plots — Arabica futures",
       subtitle = "Predicted price (USD/lb), other predictors held at their observed values",
       x = NULL, y = "Predicted price (USD/lb)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f5ece6", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(size = 6)
  )
```

The Arabica results line up reasonably well across the three consensus variables, though the shape of each relationship varies a fair amount depending on the model. Ending stocks pulls prices down for all four models, which matches what inventory theory would predict, but Random Forest and XGBoost get there in a very different way than SVM and ANN. The two tree-based models show a sharp drop right at the bottom of the observed range and then go essentially flat for the rest of it, while SVM and ANN trace something closer to a straight downward slope across the whole range. This is not really a disagreement about the underlying effect so much as a difference in how each model family is built: trees split the data into a handful of regions and predict a constant value within each one, which mechanically produces these step-like jumps, whereas SVM and ANN are smooth functions and will always look smoother as a result. COT net MM is the cleanest result of the three. It rises for every single model, which fits the financialisation argument made earlier in this section about speculative positioning, and SVM in particular shows a fairly pronounced curve while ANN comes closest to a straight line. WTI follows the same step-versus-smooth split as Ending stocks, with the tree-based models again concentrating most of the increase in a narrow band before flattening out, but all four models agree on the direction: higher oil prices push the Arabica forecast up, consistent with the energy cost channel.

*The equivalent figure for Robusta follows the same structure with its two consensus variables, Fed Funds Rate and WTI.* 

```{r pdp_main_plots_robusta, fig.width=9, fig.height=4, out.width="100%"}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PDP PLOT — ROBUSTA (MAIN TEXT)
# Same logic as the Arabica chunk above, with a shorter fig.height
# since this plot only has 2 rows of panels (Fed Funds Rate, WTI)
# instead of 3.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(df_pdp_rob, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2E8B57", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_grid2(Variable ~ Model, scales = "free_x", independent = "x") +
  labs(title    = "Partial dependence plots — Robusta futures",
       subtitle = "Predicted price (USD/tonne), other predictors held at their observed values",
       x = NULL, y = "Predicted price (USD/tonne)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#e8f5ec", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(size = 6)
  )
```

*This chunk computes the mean and standard deviation of the Federal Funds Rate before and after the 2022 tightening cycle, supporting the discussion of its partial dependence shape below.*

```{r pdp_fed_funds_regimes, message=FALSE}
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# FED FUNDS RATE — TWO MONETARY REGIMES
# Quick summary statistics supporting the PDP interpretation below:
# the Federal Funds Rate behaves very differently before and after
# the 2022 tightening cycle, which is relevant context for reading
# the flat/mildly positive PDP shape observed for this variable.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

stats_pre_2022 <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  filter(date >= "2008-01" & date <= "2021-12") %>%
  summarise(moyenne = mean(fed_funds_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
            ecart_type = sd(fed_funds_rate, na.rm = TRUE))

stats_post_2022 <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  filter(date >= "2022-01") %>%
  summarise(moyenne = mean(fed_funds_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
            ecart_type = sd(fed_funds_rate, na.rm = TRUE))

cat("2008-2021 — mean:", round(stats_pre_2022$moyenne, 2),
    "| sd:", round(stats_pre_2022$ecart_type, 2), "\n")
cat("2022-2023 — mean:", round(stats_post_2022$moyenne, 2),
    "| sd:", round(stats_post_2022$ecart_type, 2), "\n")
```

Robusta tells a more mixed story. WTI is unambiguous again, rising across all four models, with the same step pattern showing up for Random Forest and XGBoost and a smoother climb for SVM and ANN. Fed Funds Rate is a messier case. Random Forest and XGBoost barely move at all across the observed range, SVM rises and then turns down slightly toward the top, and ANN rises throughout but without much curvature. None of the four models actually reproduces the negative relationship that basic monetary policy reasoning would suggest. This is worth noting because the usual culprit, multicollinearity, does not really apply here: the Federal Funds Rate carries a low VIF in the Robusta ARIMAX specification reported earlier, in contrast to CPI and DXY, whose sign reversals in the MLR results were plausibly attributed to exactly that problem. 

A more likely explanation is that the relationship between policy rates and Robusta prices is not linear over the full sample. The Federal Funds Rate averaged just 0.62% with limited variation between 2008 and 2021, save for a brief hike cycle around 2018–2019, before climbing to an average of 3.35% from 2022 onward as the Federal Reserve tightened policy sharply. A PDP averaged across the whole training period cannot really distinguish a genuinely weak effect from two very different monetary regimes blending together.

### Forecast Trajectories

*This chunk collects the actual and predicted values from all six models into a single tidy data frame, separately for Arabica and Robusta. This unified structure allows all forecast plots to be produced with a single `ggplot2` + `facet_wrap()` call rather than six separate plots. The test period dates are reconstructed from the levels datasets used during estimation, ensuring the x-axis of each plot reflects the correct calendar dates.*

```{r forecast_data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARABICA — COLLECT PREDICTIONS FROM ALL SIX MODELS
# The test period starts at observation n_train_ara_lev + 1
# in df_arabica_levels. Dates are extracted from that dataset
# to ensure the x-axis reflects actual calendar months.
# All predicted values are on the original USD/lb scale for
# ARIMAX and MLR; ML model predictions are on the [0,1]
# Min-Max scaled range and are back-transformed here using
# the min and max of the full Arabica levels series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# Actual test-set dates for Arabica
dates_test_ara <- df_arabica_levels$date[(n_train_ara_lev + 1):
                                          nrow(df_arabica_levels)]
dates_test_ara <- as.Date(paste0(dates_test_ara, "-01"))

# Actual observed prices (from ARIMAX result - identical across models)
actual_ara <- as.numeric(res_arimax_ara$actual)

# Back-transform ML predictions from [0,1] to USD/lb
# Min and Max are computed from the full levels dataset
ara_min <- min(df_arabica_levels$arabica_price, na.rm = TRUE)
ara_max <- max(df_arabica_levels$arabica_price, na.rm = TRUE)

backtransform <- function(x_scaled, x_min, x_max) {
  x_scaled * (x_max - x_min) + x_min
}

df_forecasts_ara <- data.frame(
  date   = rep(dates_test_ara, 6),
  actual = rep(actual_ara, 6),
  predicted = c(
    as.numeric(res_arimax_ara$predicted),
    as.numeric(res_mlr_ara$predicted),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_rf_ara$predicted),  ara_min, ara_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_xgb_ara$predicted), ara_min, ara_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_svm_ara$predicted), ara_min, ara_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_ann_ara$predicted), ara_min, ara_max)
  ),
  model = rep(c("ARIMAX", "MLR", "Random Forest",
                "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"),
              each = length(dates_test_ara))
) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model,
                        levels = c("ARIMAX", "MLR", "Random Forest",
                                   "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ROBUSTA — SAME STRUCTURE
# Robusta predictions are on USD/tonne for ARIMAX and MLR;
# ML predictions are back-transformed using Robusta min/max.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

dates_test_rob <- df_robusta_levels$date[(n_train_rob_lev + 1):
                                          nrow(df_robusta_levels)]
dates_test_rob <- as.Date(paste0(dates_test_rob, "-01"))

actual_rob <- as.numeric(res_arimax_rob$actual)

rob_min <- min(df_robusta_levels$robusta_price, na.rm = TRUE)
rob_max <- max(df_robusta_levels$robusta_price, na.rm = TRUE)

df_forecasts_rob <- data.frame(
  date   = rep(dates_test_rob, 6),
  actual = rep(actual_rob, 6),
  predicted = c(
    as.numeric(res_arimax_rob$predicted),
    as.numeric(res_mlr_rob$predicted),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_rf_rob$predicted),  rob_min, rob_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_xgb_rob$predicted), rob_min, rob_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_svm_rob$predicted), rob_min, rob_max),
    backtransform(as.numeric(res_ann_rob$predicted), rob_min, rob_max)
  ),
  model = rep(c("ARIMAX", "MLR", "Random Forest",
                "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"),
              each = length(dates_test_rob))
) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model,
                        levels = c("ARIMAX", "MLR", "Random Forest",
                                   "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")))


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARIMAX CONFIDENCE INTERVALS — ARABICA
# The forecast() function is re-called on the final ARIMAX
# model fitted on the full training set, using the test-set
# regressor matrix to generate h-step-ahead predictions
# with 95% confidence intervals.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

xreg_test_ara <- as.matrix(
  df_arabica_levels[(n_train_ara_lev + 1):nrow(df_arabica_levels),
                    intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df_arabica_levels))]
)

fc_ci_ara <- forecast(res_arimax_ara$model,
                      h     = nrow(xreg_test_ara),
                      xreg  = xreg_test_ara,
                      level = 95)

df_ci_ara <- data.frame(
  date  = dates_test_ara,
  lower = as.numeric(fc_ci_ara$lower[, "95%"]),
  upper = as.numeric(fc_ci_ara$upper[, "95%"])
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# ARIMAX CONFIDENCE INTERVALS — ROBUSTA
# Same procedure applied to the Robusta series.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

xreg_test_rob <- as.matrix(
  df_robusta_levels[(n_train_rob_lev + 1):nrow(df_robusta_levels),
                    intersect(vars_exo, colnames(df_robusta_levels))]
)

fc_ci_rob <- forecast(res_arimax_rob$model,
                      h     = nrow(xreg_test_rob),
                      xreg  = xreg_test_rob,
                      level = 95)

df_ci_rob <- data.frame(
  date  = dates_test_rob,
  lower = as.numeric(fc_ci_rob$lower[, "95%"]),
  upper = as.numeric(fc_ci_rob$upper[, "95%"])
)
```

#### Actual vs Predicted — Arabica

The six panels below show the actual versus predicted price trajectories for Arabica over the test period. Each model is plotted separately to make it easier to assess where forecasts diverge from the observed series and at which points in the cycle each model struggles most.

*This chunk produces the six-panel actual vs predicted plot for Arabica. Each panel corresponds to one model; the black line shows observed prices and the coloured line shows the walk-forward forecasts over the test period. A close alignment between the two lines indicates strong predictive performance; systematic gaps or phase shifts reveal structural weaknesses in the model.*

```{r forecast_plots_arabica, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}

# R² labels to display inside each panel
r2_labels_ara <- metriques_all %>%
  filter(Series == "Arabica") %>%
  mutate(R2    = as.numeric(R2),
         label = paste0("R² = ", round(R2, 3))) %>%
  select(model = Model, label) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model,
                        levels = c("ARIMAX", "MLR", "Random Forest",
                                   "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")))

ggplot(df_forecasts_ara, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = df_forecasts_ara %>%
      filter(model == "ARIMAX") %>%
      left_join(df_ci_ara, by = "date"),
    aes(x = date, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    fill        = "#8B4513",
    alpha       = 0.12,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(y = actual), color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predicted), color = "#8B4513", linewidth = 0.8,
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_label(data = r2_labels_ara,
             aes(label = label),
             x         = min(df_forecasts_ara$date) + 30,
             y         = max(df_forecasts_ara$actual) * 0.97,
             hjust     = 0, size = 2.8, fontface = "bold",
             fill      = "white", linewidth = 0, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = 3) +
  labs(title    = "Actual vs Predicted — Arabica futures (test set)",
       subtitle = "Black: observed price (USD/lb)  |  Dashed brown: model forecast  |  Shaded band: ARIMAX 95% CI",
       x = NULL, y = "USD/lb") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f5ece6", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y")
```

The plots largely confirm what the $R^2$ values already suggested. ARIMAX and XGBoost track the observed price most closely, capturing both the rise through 2021–2022 and the subsequent decline, though both tend to lag slightly at turning points, which is a typical feature of one-step-ahead walk-forward forecasts. The 95% confidence interval for ARIMAX widens as the test period progresses and the observed price stays within the band for most of it, though it should be interpreted as indicative only since it is computed from the model estimated on the full training set rather than from the walk-forward procedure. Random Forest and MLR follow the broad trend but compress the peaks and troughs relative to the actual series, producing smoother forecasts that miss the amplitude of short-term movements. SVM tracks the general direction but noticeably less closely than ARIMAX and XGBoost, with larger deviations visible around the 2022 peak. The ANN panel is cleaner than in the baseline specification: L2 regularisation has substantially reduced the instability that previously dominated the forecasts, and the model now follows the general price trajectory more consistently, which explains the improvement from 0.453 to 0.728, though it remains the weakest ML model for Arabica.

The Robusta plots tell a more varied story than Arabica. ARIMAX is clearly the strongest model, tracking the observed price closely throughout the test period including the sharp acceleration from 2023, consistent with its $R^2$ of 0.929. The 95% confidence interval widens progressively toward the end of the test period, reflecting the growing uncertainty of autoregressive forecasts over longer horizons, but the observed price stays within the band for almost the entire period. MLR fails visibly, with forecasts oscillating erratically and producing large directional errors, which explains its $R^2$ of 0.276. Among the ML models, XGBoost and Random Forest both track the upward trajectory but underestimate the pace of the acceleration from mid-2023 onward. SVM follows the general trend without any particularly notable pattern in its deviations. The ANN remains the most unstable, with visible spikes at several points, though the regularisation has reduced their severity compared to the baseline specification.

#### Forecast Residuals

The residual plots below zoom in on the forecast errors for each model, making it easier to spot any systematic bias or unusual episodes that the trajectory plots might obscure. Within each variety, the y-axis scale is fixed across all panels to allow direct comparison of residual amplitude between models.

*This chunk plots the forecast residuals (predicted minus actual) for each model over the test period. A residual series hovering around zero with no systematic pattern indicates an unbiased model; persistent positive or negative deviations reveal directional bias, while increasing variance over time suggests heteroskedasticity in the forecast errors.*

```{r residuals_plots, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}

df_residuals <- bind_rows(
  df_forecasts_ara %>%
    mutate(residual = predicted - actual,
           series   = "Arabica"),
  df_forecasts_rob %>%
    mutate(residual = predicted - actual,
           series   = "Robusta")
)

p_res_rob <- ggplot(

  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +

                  ymax = ifelse(residual > 0, residual, 0)),
```

**For Arabica** : Almost all models show a pronounced negative spike just before 2022, reflecting a common failure to anticipate the sharp price peak at that point in the cycle. MLR and ANN overestimate the most at the start of the test period, while other models also show some positive bias early on but to a lesser degree. From late 2022 onward, XGBoost and Random Forest stand out with larger positive residuals than the other models, suggesting they were slow to incorporate the price decline and continued to forecast higher prices than what was actually observed. Beyond these episodes, residuals oscillate reasonably around zero for the remaining models.

**For Robusta** : ARIMAX produces the most well-behaved residuals, oscillating around zero without any persistent directional bias. Random Forest shows two distinct negative episodes: one from mid-2021 to early 2022, and another from late 2022 through 2023. MLR follows a similar pattern but concentrated mostly in 2023, with the largest negative residuals of all models during that period. XGBoost mirrors this pattern but in a less pronounced way, with residuals that dip negative but partially recover more quickly. SVM deviates significantly at times but tends to correct itself faster than the other models when it diverges. The ANN is the most unstable, with residuals that lean predominantly negative and swing sharply in both directions throughout the test period.

# Discussion

## Interpretation of Results

### Overall Model Performance

The out-of-sample results present a consistent and interpretable picture of predictive performance across the six model families. Two broad conclusions emerge. First, models that explicitly account for the temporal dynamics of price series, whether through autoregressive components as in ARIMAX or through gradient boosting on trending levels as in XGBoost, systematically outperform static linear specifications. Second, the performance gap between the strongest and weakest models is substantially wider for Robusta than for Arabica, reflecting the more volatile and structurally demanding nature of the Robusta test period.

For Arabica, ARIMAX and XGBoost achieve near-identical $R^2$ values of 0.821 and 0.812 respectively, confirming that the autoregressive structure of price dynamics carries predictive information that neither purely cross-sectional nor purely tree-based specifications can fully replicate. The forecast trajectory plots show that both models track the broad price level and direction correctly throughout the 2021–2024 test period, including the gradual rise through 2022 and the subsequent decline, though both exhibit the typical one-step-ahead lag at turning points. Random Forest follows closely at $R^2$ = 0.811 and SVM at 0.813 following hyperparameter tuning, while MLR achieves $R^2$ = 0.784, a result that reflects the strong trending co-movement between Arabica prices and the macroeconomic variables in levels rather than genuine structural predictive power. The ANN trails at 0.728 for reasons discussed in the limitations section.

For Robusta, the performance hierarchy shifts markedly. ARIMAX delivers the strongest result under the baseline specification with $R^2$ = 0.929, driven by the strongly persistent autoregressive structure of Robusta prices over the test period, which was characterised by a near-monotonic upward trend that a high-persistence AR model naturally tracks well. XGBoost follows at $R^2$ = 0.797, while SVM and Random Forest achieve 0.761 and 0.695 respectively. The most striking result is the collapse of MLR to $R^2$ = 0.276, with forecast trajectories that oscillate erratically around the observed series and produce large directional errors. This failure reflects the well-known sensitivity of OLS to multicollinearity in short samples: with only 153 training observations and 14 highly collinear predictors, as documented in the correlation and PCA analyses, coefficient estimates become unstable and the model cannot generalise to the test period. This result underscores the importance of temporal dynamics in commodity price modelling and confirms that a static linear specification is insufficient for Robusta price prediction over the available sample.

The coefficient tables from the ARIMAX training-set estimation further illuminate the challenge of identifying interpretable linear relationships in this predictor space. For both varieties, only a small number of regressors reach conventional significance thresholds: Sugar and WTI for Arabica, CPI, WTI and COT net MM for Robusta. This outcome is not a failure of specification but a direct consequence of the severe multicollinearity documented in the correlation and PCA analyses, where Production, Consumption and Exports load almost identically on the first principal component. In the presence of such collinearity, OLS distributes explanatory power across correlated regressors in an unstable way, inflating standard errors and suppressing individual t-statistics even when the collective predictive content of the variable group is substantial. This observation provides a retrospective justification for the machine learning approach adopted in this study: Random Forest and XGBoost are specifically designed to exploit the predictive information contained in groups of correlated variables through non-linear combinations and variable selection mechanisms that are unavailable to the linear regression component of ARIMAX.

The overall level of predictive accuracy achieved, with $R^2$ values generally above 0.75 across the best-performing models for both varieties, is worth noting in context. These results are obtained on series in levels, and the co-trending of prices with macroeconomic variables may inflate $R^2$ beyond what would be achievable on stationary first-differenced series. This point is addressed explicitly in the limitations section.

### The Role of Financial and Speculative Variables

The variable importance analysis from the Random Forest model provides the clearest picture of which predictors drive out-of-sample accuracy. For Arabica, Sugar No.11 prices and the COT net Managed Money position emerge as the two dominant predictors, contributing approximately 27% and 24% increase in MSE respectively when permuted, well above all other variables. The dominance of speculative positioning reflects the progressive financialisation of the Arabica market: the Coffee C contract on ICE Futures U.S. is among the most actively traded agricultural futures contracts, and the net position of Managed Money participants captures market-wide expectations about future price direction that are not yet reflected in contemporaneous fundamentals. The strong predictive power of COT net MM at the one-month-ahead horizon suggests that this sentiment signal is not fully incorporated into current prices, creating a forecasting opportunity that the Random Forest exploits through its non-linear variable interactions.

The prominence of Sugar No.11 prices in the Arabica ranking reflects the supply-side linkage between the two commodities in Brazil, the world's largest producer of both. When sugar prices rise relative to coffee prices, the relative return to sugar cultivation increases, creating an incentive for land reallocation that is anticipated by market participants and reflected in coffee futures prices before it appears in realised production data. At monthly frequency, this anticipatory co-movement is directly exploitable by the model.

The mechanics of this signal also point to a feedback structure worth making explicit. A positive net Managed Money position reflects funds that have already taken long positions in anticipation of rising prices. If that buying pressure itself contributes to the price increase, as the positive and significant COT coefficient in both the MLR and ARIMAX specifications suggests, the resulting price rise could in principle reinforce the original bullish positioning rather than simply confirming it. This self-reinforcing dynamic would be consistent with what the permutation importance results show, namely that COT net MM contributes meaningfully to the Random Forest's one-month-ahead forecasts. However, the present analysis cannot speak to this mechanism directly: walk-forward forecasting accuracy and a positive coefficient sign are compatible with a self-reinforcing dynamic, but neither result is designed to test for one, and no claim of this kind is made here beyond noting that the observed coefficient sign and forecasting contribution do not rule it out.

For Robusta, the importance hierarchy differs markedly in its upper ranks. WTI and CPI are the two dominant predictors, contributing approximately 25% and 22% increase in MSE respectively, displacing the financial and market-specific variables that led the Arabica ranking. The stronger role of energy costs for Robusta is consistent with the production geography of this variety: Vietnam and Indonesia, which together account for approximately 45% of world Robusta production, are major energy importers whose production and export logistics are more sensitive to global oil prices than the more diversified Brazilian Arabica supply chain. The prominence of CPI reflects the fact that Robusta is primarily consumed in price-sensitive market segments, including soluble coffee and value blends, where demand responds more elastically to the general price level than in the premium Arabica segment.

Across both varieties, financial and macroeconomic variables systematically outrank supply-side fundamentals and climate variables in terms of predictive contribution at monthly frequency. This finding carries a practical implication: short-run price signals for coffee are more reliably extracted from financial positioning data and macroeconomic indicators than from production and inventory statistics, which are published at annual frequency and carry substantial measurement uncertainty.

### Climate Variables and the Lag Structure Problem

A consistent finding across both varieties is the relatively low variable importance of the climate indices compared to financial and macroeconomic predictors. For Arabica, Precipitation and Temperature rank last among all 14 predictors, each contributing approximately 3% and 6% increase in MSE respectively when permuted. For Robusta, the climate variables rank somewhat higher at approximately 6% and 8%, but remain well below the dominant financial and macro variables.

This result should not be interpreted as evidence that climate is irrelevant to coffee prices. Rather, it reflects a fundamental mismatch between the one-step-ahead monthly forecasting horizon of the models and the lag structure through which climate affects prices. Coffee cherry development, flowering and yield are influenced by temperature and precipitation conditions during the growing season, which typically spans six to twelve months before harvest. A climate shock in month $t$ affects production in month $t+6$ to $t+12$, which in turn affects prices at a further lag as supply shortfalls propagate through inventories and trade flows. A contemporaneous monthly model cannot capture this transmission channel directly, and the climate signal is therefore largely absorbed by the production and ending stocks variables that already reflect the cumulative impact of past weather conditions on realised supply.

The ONI index, which captures ENSO conditions, ranks somewhat higher than the national climate indices for both varieties, contributing approximately 17% increase in MSE for Arabica and 16% for Robusta. This relatively stronger importance likely reflects the fact that ENSO episodes affect prices not only through realised supply but also through expectation formation: market participants anticipate the supply consequences of El Niño and La Niña episodes before they materialise in production data, creating a contemporaneous price effect that a monthly model can capture. This expectational channel is absent from the national temperature and precipitation indices, which measure realised meteorological conditions rather than forward-looking anomaly signals.

The implication for future model design is clear. Incorporating lagged climate variables at horizons of three, six and twelve months would allow the model to capture the delayed transmission from weather conditions to coffee prices through the production and inventory channel.

### Arabica vs Robusta: Structural Differences

The contrast between Arabica and Robusta results across models reveals structural differences between the two markets that go beyond the shorter sample available for Robusta.

The dominance of ARIMAX on Robusta ($R^2$ = 0.929 vs 0.821 for Arabica) reflects the stronger autoregressive persistence of Robusta prices over the test period. The ARIMA(3,0,1) error structure selected for Robusta, compared to ARIMA(1,0,0) for Arabica, indicates that Robusta price dynamics involve more complex short-run autocorrelation patterns, which ARIMAX captures through its MA component in addition to the AR terms. The near-monotonic upward trend in Robusta prices during the 2021–2024 test period further amplifies the advantage of an autoregressive model, which extrapolates a persistent trend more naturally than models that rely on cross-sectional variation among predictors.

The failure of MLR on Robusta but not Arabica is partly a sample size effect, with 153 versus 211 training observations, but also reflects the more pronounced multicollinearity among Robusta predictors. Robusta production is geographically concentrated in Vietnam and Indonesia, meaning that supply shocks are more correlated with specific macroeconomic conditions in those countries, which in turn co-move with global macro variables. This amplifies the collinearity problem relative to Arabica, where production is more geographically diversified across twelve countries spanning different climatic zones and economic environments.

The relatively weaker performance of tree-based models on Robusta, with Random Forest at $R^2$ = 0.695 and XGBoost at 0.797 compared to their Arabica counterparts of 0.811 and 0.812, reflects the extrapolation limitation of ensemble methods. Random Forest and XGBoost average over training observations and cannot produce predictions that substantially exceed the range of target values seen during training. The sharp upward acceleration in Robusta prices from mid-2023 onward moves beyond the price range of the training set, causing both models to produce forecasts that flatten while the observed series continues rising. This limitation is clearly visible in the forecast trajectory and residual plots, where a persistent negative bias emerges for both tree-based models from late 2022 onward.

### Robustness of the Methodology

The four robustness checks conducted in this study provide complementary evidence on the sensitivity of the main results to key methodological choices.

The disaggregated climate robustness check provides strong validation of the production-weighted aggregation approach. Replacing the two aggregated indices with the 28 individual national series systematically deteriorates out-of-sample $R^2$ across all four ML models and both coffee varieties, with every $ΔR^2$ value negative. The degradation is moderate for Random Forest and XGBoost but severe for SVM and ANN, which produce negative $R^2$ values under the disaggregated specification. This pattern is consistent with the curse of dimensionality: with 40 regressors and approximately 170 training observations, models sensitive to input dimensionality become severely overparameterised. Beyond the dimensionality argument, the results suggest that production-weighted aggregation improves the climate signal by averaging out country-specific noise and idiosyncratic seasonal patterns that are irrelevant to global price formation. The aggregation methodology is therefore validated both statistically and economically.

The variety-specific robustness check yields asymmetric results that reveal an important structural difference between the two markets. For Robusta, restricting climate indices and fundamentals to the six actual Robusta-producing countries improves performance for four of the six models, with XGBoost reaching its strongest result across all configurations at $R^2$ = 0.849. This improvement is economically intuitive: global indices dilute the Robusta climate and supply signal by including conditions in countries that produce virtually no Robusta, and restricting to Vietnam, Indonesia, Uganda, Côte d'Ivoire, India and Brazil provides more targeted information about the supply conditions that actually drive Robusta prices. For Arabica, all six models deteriorate under the variety-specific specification. The global indices are in practice already dominated by Arabica-producing countries, as Brazil alone accounts for approximately 39% of world coffee production and approximately 47% of the Arabica-specific weight, so switching specifications changes the climate indices only marginally while simultaneously reducing the information content of the supply-demand fundamentals by excluding Robusta-producing countries whose consumption and export activity also influences global price formation.

The OECD GDP growth robustness check provides no support for including this variable as a predictor. Moving from monthly to quarterly frequency alone substantially degrades performance for most models, most severely for ANN, which collapses from $R^2$ = 0.728 to $-$0.951 for Arabica. Once frequency is held fixed, the addition of GDP growth produces no consistent improvement across models or varieties. This negative result is consistent with the information already contained in the baseline predictor set: once CPI, the Federal Funds Rate, world consumption and the dollar index are included, OECD GDP growth carries little additional demand-side information at the frequency relevant for coffee futures pricing. The result also reflects a fundamental feasibility constraint: GDP growth has no monthly equivalent, so testing its contribution necessarily means testing it jointly with a frequency change that, on its own, already degrades out-of-sample performance. A genuinely monthly test of the variable's marginal contribution is therefore not feasible with the data available.

## Limitations

### Non-Stationarity and Spurious Regression

The most significant methodological limitation of this study concerns the treatment of non-stationarity in the machine learning models. As established in the stationarity analysis, the majority of variables, including both dependent price series and most macroeconomic and fundamental predictors, are integrated of order one. The ARIMAX model handles this internally through the differencing parameter selected by `auto.arima()`, and the absence of differencing in the final specifications ($d=0$for both series) reflects the absorption of the common trend by the exogenous regressors. For the ML models, estimating on levels rather than first differences raises the spurious regression concern: two independently trending series will exhibit high $R^2$ in levels even in the absence of any genuine predictive relationship.

The decision to estimate ML models on levels was motivated by the empirical finding that first-differenced specifications produced near-zero $R^2$ values, confirming that month-to-month price changes are largely unpredictable at this frequency. While this decision is pragmatically defensible, as the models exploit genuine trending co-movement among fundamentally linked variables rather than spurious correlations between unrelated series, it implies that the reported $R^2$ values for the ML models reflect in part the shared trend component of the series rather than purely their ability to forecast price dynamics. Future work could address this through cointegration-based specifications that model the long-run equilibrium relationship between prices and fundamentals while correcting for short-run deviations.

### ANN Instability

The Artificial Neural Network implemented via the nnet package exhibits notable instability in the walk-forward forecasting setting. With only approximately 170 training observations at the early test steps and 33 connection weights to estimate for the 2-neuron Arabica architecture selected by time series cross-validation, the network is susceptible to converging to local minima that produce extreme predictions for isolated observations. A fixed random seed partially mitigates but does not eliminate this problem, as the loss landscape of a feedforward network contains multiple local optima of varying quality. The pronounced upward spikes visible in the ANN forecast trajectory plots for both varieties are a direct manifestation of this instability. More robust implementations would require ensemble averaging across multiple random initialisations, explicit regularisation such as L2 weight decay or dropout, or recurrent architectures such as Long Short-Term Memory networks that are specifically designed for sequential data and maintain a hidden state across time steps rather than reinitialising at each walk-forward step.

### Hyperparameter Sensitivity

The hyperparameter tuning procedure used for both SVM and ANN relies on a single chronological pre-loop split of the initial training window rather than a fully nested walk-forward search. This means that the selected hyperparameters minimise error on one specific validation window rather than across the full range of training window sizes encountered during the walk-forward loop. For ANN in particular, the tuning search selected a 3-neuron architecture for Robusta that performs worse out-of-sample than larger architectures would, illustrating the known sensitivity of small feedforward networks to the choice of validation window. Retaining the tuned architecture is the methodologically consistent choice, as selecting hyperparameters based on test set performance would violate the walk-forward validation protocol, but this result highlights the importance of more robust tuning procedures in future work.

### Climate Data Resolution

The national climate averages used to construct the production-weighted indices are computed as simple arithmetic means across all ADM1 regions within each country, without intra-country production weights. This implies that non-producing regions contribute equally to the national average as major producing areas. For Brazil, for example, the Amazon basin carries the same weight as the coffee-producing states of Minas Gerais and São Paulo, attenuating the climate signal in countries with large non-producing territories. Sub-national production data at the ADM1 level are not systematically available from the USDA FAS PSD database, making intra-country production weighting infeasible with the data collected for this study. Future work could address this using remote sensing-based estimates of coffee cultivation area at high spatial resolution to construct more targeted intra-country weights.

### Data Availability Constraints

Two structural data gaps restrict the estimation sample for certain model specifications. Robusta futures prices are available only from January 2008, reducing the Robusta estimation sample to 192 monthly observations compared to 288 for Arabica. The CFTC Disaggregated COT report was introduced in June 2006, so the Managed Money net position is missing for the first 77 months of the analysis period. Both gaps are handled by restricting estimation to complete-case sub-samples, but they imply that Robusta results and specifications including the COT variable are based on shorter and potentially less representative samples than the full 2000–2023 period.

### Static Model Specifications

All six models assume a static relationship between coffee prices and their predictors, with coefficients or feature importances that are fixed over time or re-estimated on an expanding window that treats all historical observations equally. This assumption is at odds with the structural changes documented in the coffee market over the analysis period, including the progressive financialisation of commodity markets from the mid-2000s onward, the post-2008 shift in monetary policy regimes, and the supply chain disruptions of the COVID-19 period. Time-varying parameter models, such as rolling-window ML specifications with a fixed rather than expanding training window, would allow predictor relationships to evolve over time and may improve performance in structurally shifting environments.

### ARIMAX Residual Autocorrelation

The ACF and PACF diagnostics of the ARIMAX residuals reveal an asymmetry between the two series. For Robusta, the ARIMA(3,0,1) error structure has fully absorbed the short-run autocorrelation, with no significant spike across all 24 lags. For Arabica, significant spikes remain at lags 1, 2, 5, 6, 16 and 24 in the ACF, and at lags 1, 5, 8 and 10 in the PACF, indicating that the ARIMA(1,0,0) error structure does not fully capture the medium-range autocorrelation dynamics of the Arabica residuals. A higher-order specification incorporating additional AR terms at lags 5 or 6 would likely reduce this residual dependence, though the walk-forward computational constraints imposed a maximum order of $p=3$in the `auto.arima()` search. This limitation does not invalidate the out-of-sample results given the $R^2$ of 0.821 achieved for Arabica, but it represents a direction for future refinement.

# Conclusion

This study estimated six forecasting models, two econometric benchmarks in the form of ARIMAX and Multiple Linear Regression and four machine learning algorithms comprising Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine and Artificial Neural Network, applied to monthly Arabica and Robusta coffee futures prices over the 2000–2023 period. Using a walk-forward expanding window validation protocol with an 80/20 train/test split, all models were evaluated on three out-of-sample metrics across a rich predictor set spanning macroeconomic, fundamental, climatic and speculative variables.

The principal empirical finding is that ARIMAX and XGBoost emerge as the strongest models for both coffee varieties under the baseline specification, achieving out-of-sample $R^2$ values of 0.821 and 0.812 for Arabica and 0.929 and 0.797 for Robusta respectively. The strong performance of ARIMAX confirms that the persistence of prices around their own past values is a primary source of short-run predictability in coffee futures markets. The competitive performance of XGBoost demonstrates that gradient boosting can identify non-linear relationships among predictors that the linear regression component of ARIMAX cannot accommodate. The Multiple Linear Regression benchmark performs reasonably well for Arabica but collapses for Robusta at $R^2$ = 0.276, confirming that a static linear model without temporal dynamics is insufficient when the estimation sample is short and predictors are highly correlated.

The variable importance analysis reveals that financial and speculative variables dominate the predictor rankings for both varieties. For Arabica, Sugar No.11 prices and the COT net Managed Money position are the two most influential predictors, reflecting the financialisation of the coffee futures market and the supply-side linkage between coffee and sugar in Brazil. For Robusta, WTI crude oil and CPI rank first, consistent with the energy-intensive production logistics of Vietnam and Indonesia and the price-elastic demand structure of the soluble coffee segment. Climate variables contribute relatively little predictive power at the one-month-ahead forecasting horizon, a finding explained by the long lag, typically six to twelve months, between climate shocks and their effect on prices through the production and inventory channel. This is not evidence that climate is irrelevant to coffee prices, but rather that a contemporaneous monthly model is not designed to capture this delayed transmission.

The three robustness checks yield several findings of independent interest. The disaggregated climate check confirms that the production-weighted aggregation of climate indices is the appropriate specification: replacing the two global indices with the 28 individual national series systematically worsens performance across all ML models, validating the aggregation approach both statistically and economically. The variety-specific check reveals an important asymmetry: restricting climate and supply variables to Robusta-producing countries improves performance for four of the six models, with XGBoost reaching its strongest result at $R^2$= 0.849, while the same restriction uniformly deteriorates Arabica performance because the global indices are already dominated by Arabica-producing countries. The GDP growth check provides no support for including this variable as a predictor, with its marginal contribution found to be small, inconsistently signed across models and series, and confounded by the cost of moving to quarterly frequency that the absence of a monthly equivalent necessitates.

Several limitations constrain the interpretation of these results. Estimating ML models on non-stationary price levels raises the risk of spurious correlations driven by common trends. The ANN exhibits instability under walk-forward re-estimation with small training samples. The hyperparameter tuning procedure relies on a single pre-loop validation split rather than a fully nested walk-forward search. The national climate averages do not account for the distribution of coffee cultivation within each country. And all six models assume static predictor relationships over a 24-year period that witnessed substantial structural change in the coffee market.

These limitations point to several directions for future work. Cointegration-based error correction specifications would better handle the non-stationarity of the series while preserving the long-run equilibrium relationships among prices and fundamentals. Incorporating lagged climate variables at three, six and twelve months would allow the model to capture the delayed weather-to-price transmission channel that contemporaneous specifications cannot exploit. Recurrent neural network architectures, in particular Long Short-Term Memory networks, would address the ANN instability by maintaining a hidden state across time steps rather than reinitialising at each walk-forward step. Finally, rolling-window or regime-switching specifications would allow predictor relationships to evolve over time, better reflecting the structural shifts the coffee market has undergone over the analysis period.

From a practical standpoint, the results suggest that market participants seeking short-run price signals for coffee would benefit most from monitoring speculative positioning in the futures market and energy prices rather than focusing on supply fundamentals or climate conditions at monthly frequency. The variety-specific results further suggest that Robusta-focused analysts should track supply conditions in Vietnam and Indonesia specifically, as global aggregates dilute the variety-relevant signal. The consistent performance of multiple model families across both series and multiple specifications strengthens the reliability of these conclusions and suggests that the predictor set constructed in this study captures genuine and robust information about the drivers of coffee futures prices.

```{r importance_detailed_appendix, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
options(scipen = 999)  # Force decimal notation, avoid scientific notation

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# DETAILED PERMUTATION IMPORTANCE PLOTS — APPENDICES

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — PLOT FUNCTION

plot_importance_appendix <- function(imp_df, color, bg_color,
                                      title, subtitle = NULL) {

  # Format labels: round to 4 decimal places for ML models,
  # round to 0 for ARIMAX which has very large values
  imp_df <- imp_df %>%
    mutate(label = ifelse(abs(Importance) > 100,
                          format(round(Importance, 0), big.mark = ","),
                          as.character(round(Importance, 4))))

  ggplot(imp_df, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Importance),
                     y = Importance)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity",
             fill = ifelse(imp_df$Importance >= 0, color, "grey70"),
             alpha = 0.85, width = 0.65) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey40",
               linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_text(aes(label = label),
              hjust = ifelse(imp_df$Importance >= 0, -0.15, 1.15),
              size = 3, color = "grey30") +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.2, 0.3))) +
    labs(title    = title,
         subtitle = subtitle,
         x = NULL, y = "ΔMSE") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
      panel.background   = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA),
      strip.background   = element_rect(fill = bg_color, color = NA),
      plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      plot.subtitle      = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey50"),
      axis.text.y        = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey20"),
      axis.text.x        = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40"),
      plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(10, 20, 10, 10)
    )
}
```
