## Partial Dependence Plots — Per-Model Detail

```{r pdp_appendix, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PARTIAL DEPENDENCE PLOTS — APPENDIX (PER-MODEL DETAIL)
# Unlike the main text, which is restricted to a few consensus
# variables, this section produces the PDP for the three variables
# specific to EACH individual model, as already identified by top3_ara
# and top3_rob in the Variable Importance section. One figure is
# produced per model and per variety (4 + 4 = 8 figures), each showing
# that model's three variables as separate panels.
# Unlike the main-text figures, no facet_grid2()/independent = "x"
# workaround is needed here: facet_wrap() with scales = "free_x"
# already frees the x-axis per panel rather than per row or column,
# since each panel in a facet_wrap() grid is independent by
# construction. out.width = "100%" caps the rendered width to the
# page's text width, consistent with the main-text PDP chunks.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# STEP 1 — Reverse mapping from label to internal variable name.
# labels_mlr already maps each internal name (e.g. "ending_stocks") to
# its readable label (e.g. "Ending stocks"). labels_inverse builds the
# opposite mapping, needed here because top3_ara$Variable stores the
# readable labels, while calculer_pdp() needs the internal name to
# pull the right column from the training set.
labels_inverse <- setNames(names(labels_mlr), labels_mlr)


# STEP 2 — Compute the PDP for the 3 variables of ONE given model.
# For nom_modele, first filter top3_df down to its 3 most important
# variables (top3_df$Model == nom_modele), convert their labels to
# internal names via labels_inverse, then compute the PDP for each one
# using the same calculer_pdp() function as in the main text, stacking
# the 3 results with rbind().
generer_pdp_appendice <- function(nom_modele, modele, top3_df,
                                  donnees_full, donnees_predicteurs,
                                  bornes_vars, bornes_cible) {

  # Internal names of this model's 3 most important variables
  vars_internes <- labels_inverse[
    as.character(top3_df$Variable[top3_df$Model == nom_modele])
  ]

  # Appropriate input dataset (matrix for XGBoost, full data frame
  # otherwise), resolved once here and reused for all 3 variables of
  # this model
  donnees_pdp <- obtenir_donnees_pdp(nom_modele, donnees_full,
                                      donnees_predicteurs)

  # Loop over the 3 variables: compute the PDP, then attach the
  # readable label (rather than the internal name) for display in the
  # plot
  do.call(rbind, lapply(vars_internes, function(var_int) {
    res <- calculer_pdp(nom_modele, modele, donnees_pdp, var_int,
                        bornes_vars[[var_int]], bornes_cible)
    res$Variable <- labels_mlr[var_int]
    res
  }))
}


# STEP 3 — Generic plotting function, reused for all 8 figures (4
# models x 2 varieties). facet_wrap() lays out a model's 3 variables
# side by side, each panel with its own free x-axis since the 3
# variables don't share the same unit.
plot_pdp_appendice <- function(df_pdp, couleur, bg_couleur, titre, unite_y) {
  ggplot(df_pdp, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    geom_line(color = couleur, linewidth = 0.9) +
    facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
    labs(title = titre, x = NULL, y = unite_y) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9),
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = bg_couleur, color = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fafafa", color = NA)
    )
}


# STEP 4 — Generate the 4 Arabica figures (one per ML model).
# Using a for() loop here rather than lapply(), since each iteration
# needs to display a plot immediately via print() — this is required
# for ggplot2 to actually render a plot inside an R Markdown / Quarto
# chunk when called from within a loop rather than at the chunk's top
# level.
for (nom in names(modeles_ara)) {
  df_pdp_modele <- generer_pdp_appendice(nom, modeles_ara[[nom]], top3_ara,
                                         train_ara, train_ara_xgb,
                                         bornes_ara, bornes_prix_ara)
  print(plot_pdp_appendice(df_pdp_modele, "#8B4513", "#f5ece6",
                           paste0("Partial dependence — ", nom, " (Arabica)"),
                           "Predicted price (USD/lb)"))
}

# STEP 5 — Generate the 4 Robusta figures, same logic as Step 4 above
for (nom in names(modeles_rob)) {
  df_pdp_modele <- generer_pdp_appendice(nom, modeles_rob[[nom]], top3_rob,
                                         train_rob, train_rob_xgb,
                                         bornes_rob, bornes_prix_rob)
  print(plot_pdp_appendice(df_pdp_modele, "#2E8B57", "#e8f5ec",
                           paste0("Partial dependence — ", nom, " (Robusta)"),
                           "Predicted price (USD/tonne)"))
}
```

# Robustness Checks

## Disaggregated Climate Variables

The main model specifications rely on two production-weighted climate indices that aggregate temperature and precipitation conditions across 14 producer countries into single monthly series. While this aggregation is methodologically motivated, as it avoids endogeneity, reduces dimensionality, and is consistent with the fixed-weight approach documented in the data section, it raises the question of whether relevant country-specific climate information is lost in the process.

To assess this, the four ML models are re-estimated under an alternative specification in which the two aggregated indices are replaced by the 28 individual national series (14 countries × 2 climate variables), holding all other predictors constant. A comparison of out-of-sample $R^2$ between the two configurations provides direct evidence on whether disaggregation improves predictive accuracy. ARIMAX and MLR are excluded from this comparison: ARIMAX is computationally prohibitive with 40 regressors in a walk-forward loop, and MLR is ill-conditioned with 40 predictors on approximately 170 training observations.

*The chunk below re-estimates the four ML models using the disaggregated variable list and stores the results for comparison with the baseline specification. The model functions are identical in structure to those used in the main results, with a `vars_exo_vec` argument replacing the global `vars_exo` list.*

```{r robustness_disaggregated, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — LOAD THE DISAGGREGATED CLIMATE SERIES AND BUILD
# THE DISAGGREGATED DATASET
# The two production-weighted indices (indice_precip,
# indice_temp) are dropped from the monthly dataset and
# replaced by the 28 individual national series, 14 for
# precipitation and 14 for temperature.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_precip_dis <- read_csv(
  file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "precip_disaggregated_2000_2023.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE)

df_temp_dis <- read_csv(
  file.path(PATH_OUTPUT, "temp_disaggregated_2000_2023.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE)

dataset_disagg <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  select(-indice_precip, -indice_temp) %>%
  left_join(df_precip_dis, by = "date") %>%
  left_join(df_temp_dis,   by = "date")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — DEFINE THE DISAGGREGATED EXOGENOUS VARIABLE LIST
# vars_climate_dis lists the 28 national climate columns
# (precip_bresil, precip_vietnam, ..., temp_bresil, ...).
# vars_exo_dis replaces indice_precip and indice_temp in the
# baseline vars_exo list with these 28 columns, keeping the
# other 12 baseline predictors unchanged.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_climate_dis <- c(
  paste0("precip_", names(POIDS_PRODUCTION)),
  paste0("temp_",   names(POIDS_PRODUCTION))
)

vars_exo_dis <- c(
  "sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
  "dxy", "production", "consumption", "exports",
  "ending_stocks", "oni", "cot_net_mm",
  vars_climate_dis
)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — PREPARE THE DISAGGREGATED DATASETS
# Same logic as preparer_niveaux() in the preprocessing chunk:
# keep the dependent variable and the 40 exogenous predictors,
# drop rows with any missing value, and sort by date.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

preparer_niveaux_dis <- function(df, var_dep) {
  colonnes_a_garder <- c("date", var_dep, vars_exo_dis)
  df_modele         <- df[, colonnes_a_garder]
  df_modele         <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele[order(df_modele$date), ]
}

df_arabica_dis <- preparer_niveaux_dis(dataset_disagg, "arabica_price")
df_robusta_dis <- preparer_niveaux_dis(
  dataset_disagg[!is.na(dataset_disagg$robusta_price), ], "robusta_price")

n_train_ara_dis <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_dis) * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_dis <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_dis) * split_ratio)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — GENERIC MODEL FUNCTIONS
# Identical in structure to the main model functions, with
# an added vars_exo_vec argument so the same function can
# be reused with different predictor lists without copying
# the function body.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_rf_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    foret <- randomForest(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                          ntree = 500, importance = TRUE)
    predictions[i] <- predict(foret, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}

fit_xgb_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  colonnes_predicteurs <- setdiff(colnames(df_modele_scaled), var_dep)
  X       <- as.matrix(df_modele_scaled[, colonnes_predicteurs])
  y       <- df_modele_scaled[[var_dep]]
  n_total <- length(y)
  n_test  <- n_total - n_train

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    indices_fenetre  <- 1:(n_train + i - 1)
    indice_a_predire <- n_train + i
    modele_xgb <- xgboost(data      = X[indices_fenetre, ],
                          label     = y[indices_fenetre],
                          nrounds   = 100, max_depth = 4,
                          eta       = 0.1, subsample = 0.8,
                          verbose   = 0,
                          objective = "reg:squarederror")
    ligne_a_predire <- matrix(X[indice_a_predire, ], nrow = 1)
    predictions[i]  <- predict(modele_xgb, newdata = ligne_a_predire)
  }

  list(actual = y[(n_train + 1):n_total], predicted = predictions)
}

fit_svm_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    modele_svm <- svm(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                      kernel = "radial", cost = 1, gamma = 0.1)
    predictions[i] <- predict(modele_svm, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}

fit_ann_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {
  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele_scaled     <- as.data.frame(sapply(df_modele, minmax_scale))

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele_scaled)
  donnees_train <- df_modele_scaled[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele_scaled[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  set.seed(42)
  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    modele_ann <- nnet(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement,
                       size = 5, linout = TRUE, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE)
    predictions[i] <- predict(modele_ann, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 5 — RUN ALL FOUR MODELS ON BOTH SERIES
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("Running disaggregated RF - Arabica...\n")
res_rf_dis_ara  <- fit_rf_generique(df_arabica_dis, "arabica_price",
                                    vars_exo_dis, n_train_ara_dis)
cat("Running disaggregated RF - Robusta...\n")
res_rf_dis_rob  <- fit_rf_generique(df_robusta_dis, "robusta_price",
                                    vars_exo_dis, n_train_rob_dis)

cat("Running disaggregated XGBoost - Arabica...\n")
res_xgb_dis_ara <- fit_xgb_generique(df_arabica_dis, "arabica_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_ara_dis)
cat("Running disaggregated XGBoost - Robusta...\n")
res_xgb_dis_rob <- fit_xgb_generique(df_robusta_dis, "robusta_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_rob_dis)

cat("Running disaggregated SVM - Arabica...\n")
res_svm_dis_ara <- fit_svm_generique(df_arabica_dis, "arabica_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_ara_dis)
cat("Running disaggregated SVM - Robusta...\n")
res_svm_dis_rob <- fit_svm_generique(df_robusta_dis, "robusta_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_rob_dis)

cat("Running disaggregated ANN - Arabica...\n")
res_ann_dis_ara <- fit_ann_generique(df_arabica_dis, "arabica_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_ara_dis)
cat("Running disaggregated ANN - Robusta...\n")
res_ann_dis_rob <- fit_ann_generique(df_robusta_dis, "robusta_price",
                                     vars_exo_dis, n_train_rob_dis)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 6 — COMPILE RESULTS INTO A COMPARISON TABLE
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_robustness <- data.frame(
  Model  = rep(c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"), each = 2),
  Series = rep(c("Arabica", "Robusta"), 4),
  R2_baseline = as.numeric(c(
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "Random Forest", Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "Random Forest", Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "XGBoost",       Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "XGBoost",       Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "SVM",           Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "SVM",           Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "ANN",           Series == "Arabica") %>% pull(R2),
    metriques_all %>% filter(Model == "ANN",           Series == "Robusta") %>% pull(R2)
  )),
  R2_disaggregated = c(
    calculer_metriques(res_rf_dis_ara$actual,  res_rf_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_rf_dis_rob$actual,  res_rf_dis_rob$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_xgb_dis_ara$actual, res_xgb_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_xgb_dis_rob$actual, res_xgb_dis_rob$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_svm_dis_ara$actual, res_svm_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_svm_dis_rob$actual, res_svm_dis_rob$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_ann_dis_ara$actual, res_ann_dis_ara$predicted)$R2,
    calculer_metriques(res_ann_dis_rob$actual, res_ann_dis_rob$predicted)$R2
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    Delta_R2         = round(R2_disaggregated - R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_baseline      = round(R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_disaggregated = round(R2_disaggregated, 4)
  )
```

*The table below compares the out-of-sample $R^2$ of each model under the baseline aggregated specification and the disaggregated specification. A positive $ΔR^2$ indicates that disaggregation improves predictive accuracy; a negative value indicates deterioration.*

```{r robustness_table}

df_robustness %>%
  arrange(Series, factor(Model, levels = c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))) %>%
  select(Model, R2_baseline, R2_disaggregated, Delta_R2) %>%
  kable(caption   = "Robustness check — aggregated vs disaggregated climate indices (out-of-sample R²)",
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        col.names = c("Model", "R² (aggregated)",
                      "R² (disaggregated)", "ΔR²")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(4, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 4,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 5, 8,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec") %>%
  column_spec(4, color = ifelse(
    df_robustness %>%
      arrange(Series, factor(Model, levels = c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))) %>%
      pull(Delta_R2) > 0,
    "darkgreen", "red"))
```

The robustness check confirms that the production-weighted aggregation of climate indices is the appropriate specification. Disaggregation systematically deteriorates out-of-sample $R^2$ across all four ML models and both coffee varieties, with every $ΔR^2$ value negative. The deterioration is moderate for Random Forest ($ΔR^2$ of −0.042 for Arabica, −0.115 for Robusta) and XGBoost (−0.014 and −0.059), but severe for SVM and ANN, which produce negative $R^2$ values under the disaggregated specification, indicating performance worse than a naive mean forecast.

This pattern is consistent with the curse of dimensionality: with 40 regressors and approximately 170 training observations, models sensitive to input dimensionality become severely overparameterised and fail to generalise to the test period. The ensemble methods Random Forest and XGBoost are more robust to this problem through their built-in variable selection mechanisms, but still suffer a meaningful performance loss. These results suggest that the production-weighted aggregation improves the climate signal by filtering out country-specific noise, and that the information gain from disaggregation is outweighed by the dimensionality cost at the sample sizes available in this study.

## Variety-Specific Model Specification

The robustness check conducted in the preceding section validated the production-weighted aggregation methodology by showing that disaggregated climate indices systematically deteriorate out-of-sample performance. A second robustness check is now conducted by re-estimating all six models under a variety-specific specification. Rather than using global climate indices and world supply-and-demand fundamentals, this specification assigns each model its own set of variety-relevant predictors: the Arabica models use climate indices and fundamentals aggregated across the ten Arabica-producing countries, while the Robusta models use the equivalent aggregates for the six Robusta-producing countries. This specification is motivated by the structural concentration of Robusta production in Vietnam and Indonesia (approximately 67% combined) and the broader geographic diversification of Arabica production. Using global indices for Robusta in particular dilutes the climate and supply signal by including conditions in countries that produce virtually no Robusta.

*This chunk defines the variety-specific exogenous variable lists and prepares the two datasets used in the re-estimation below. Sample sizes are printed to the console for verification.*

```{r preprocessing_vs, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# VARIETY-SPECIFIC EXOGENOUS VARIABLE LISTS
# Two separate lists replace the global vars_exo: one for
# Arabica models (climate indices and fundamentals aggregated
# across the 10 Arabica-producing countries) and one for
# Robusta models (aggregated across the 6 Robusta-producing
# countries). All other predictors (sugar, cocoa, macro
# variables, ONI, COT) are unchanged from the baseline.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_exo_ara_vs <- c(
  "sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
  "dxy", "production_ara", "consommation_ara", "exportations_ara",
  "ending_stocks_ara", "indice_precip_arabica", "indice_temp_arabica",
  "oni", "cot_net_mm"
)

vars_exo_rob_vs <- c(
  "sugar_price", "cocoa_price", "cpi", "wti", "fed_funds_rate",
  "dxy", "production_rob", "consommation_rob", "exportations_rob",
  "ending_stocks_rob", "indice_precip_robusta", "indice_temp_robusta",
  "oni", "cot_net_mm"
)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# PREPARE THE VARIETY-SPECIFIC DATASETS
# Same logic as preparer_niveaux() used throughout the
# document: keep the dependent variable and the relevant
# exogenous predictors, drop rows with any missing value,
# and sort by date.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

preparer_niveaux_vs <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec) {
  colonnes_a_garder <- c("date", var_dep, vars_exo_vec)
  df_modele         <- df[, colonnes_a_garder]
  df_modele         <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]
  df_modele[order(df_modele$date), ]
}

df_arabica_vs <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_arabica_vs, "arabica_price", vars_exo_ara_vs)

df_robusta_vs <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_robusta_vs[!is.na(dataset_robusta_vs$robusta_price), ],
  "robusta_price", vars_exo_rob_vs)

# 80/20 split, using the same split_ratio as every other model
n_train_ara_vs <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_vs) * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_vs <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_vs) * split_ratio)

cat("Arabica VS - Train:", n_train_ara_vs,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_arabica_vs) - n_train_ara_vs, "\n")
cat("Robusta VS - Train:", n_train_rob_vs,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_robusta_vs) - n_train_rob_vs, "\n")
```

Sample sizes for the variety-specific datasets mirror those of the baseline specification, 168 training and 43 test observations for Arabica, and 153 training and 39 test observations for Robusta, confirming that the variety-specific variable substitution does not alter the temporal coverage of either dataset.

All six models are re-estimated under this specification using the same walk-forward protocol as the baseline. The Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM and ANN models reuse the generic functions already defined in the disaggregated robustness check above, called here with the variety-specific variable lists. ARIMAX and MLR are generalised below by adding a `vars_exo_vec` argument following the same pattern.

*The chunk below defines the generic ARIMAX and MLR functions and re-estimates all six models under the variety-specific specification.*

```{r modeles_vs, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — GENERIC ARIMAX FUNCTION
# Identical to fit_arimax() defined earlier, except that the
# predictor list is passed in as vars_exo_vec rather than
# always using the global vars_exo. This allows the function
# to be called with any predictor list without modification.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_arimax_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {

  serie_dependante    <- df[[var_dep]]
  matrice_regresseurs <- as.matrix(df[, vars_exo_vec])

  colonnes_valides    <- apply(matrice_regresseurs, 2,
                               function(col) !all(is.na(col)))
  matrice_regresseurs <- matrice_regresseurs[, colonnes_valides, drop = FALSE]

  n_total    <- length(serie_dependante)
  y_train    <- serie_dependante[1:n_train]
  y_test     <- serie_dependante[(n_train + 1):n_total]
  xreg_train <- matrice_regresseurs[1:n_train, ]
  xreg_test  <- matrice_regresseurs[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test     <- length(y_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_observations_vues <- i - 1
    indices_vus          <- seq_len(nb_observations_vues)
    y_vu                 <- y_test[indices_vus]
    xreg_vu              <- xreg_test[indices_vus, , drop = FALSE]
    y_fenetre            <- c(y_train, y_vu)
    xreg_fenetre         <- rbind(xreg_train, xreg_vu)

    modele_arima <- tryCatch(
      auto.arima(y_fenetre, xreg = xreg_fenetre,
                 stepwise = TRUE, approximation = TRUE,
                 max.p = 3, max.q = 3, max.d = 1),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )

    if (is.null(modele_arima)) { predictions[i] <- NA; next }

    ligne_regresseurs_futurs <- matrix(xreg_test[i, ], nrow = 1)
    prevision <- forecast(modele_arima, h = 1,
                          xreg = ligne_regresseurs_futurs)
    predictions[i] <- prevision$mean[1]
  }

  list(actual = y_test, predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — GENERIC MLR FUNCTION
# Identical to fit_mlr() defined earlier, except that the
# predictor list is passed in as vars_exo_vec. intersect()
# ensures only columns present in df are used, guarding
# against any name mismatch between the variable list and
# the dataset columns.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

fit_mlr_generique <- function(df, var_dep, vars_exo_vec, n_train) {

  vars_exo_disponibles <- intersect(vars_exo_vec, colnames(df))
  df_modele            <- df[, c(var_dep, vars_exo_disponibles)]
  df_modele            <- df_modele[complete.cases(df_modele), ]

  n_total       <- nrow(df_modele)
  donnees_train <- df_modele[1:n_train, ]
  donnees_test  <- df_modele[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]
  n_test        <- nrow(donnees_test)

  predictions <- numeric(n_test)
  formule     <- as.formula(paste(var_dep, "~ ."))

  for (i in 1:n_test) {
    nb_lignes_test_vues  <- i - 1
    lignes_test_vues     <- donnees_test[seq_len(nb_lignes_test_vues), ]
    fenetre_entrainement <- rbind(donnees_train, lignes_test_vues)
    modele_ols           <- lm(formule, data = fenetre_entrainement)
    predictions[i]       <- predict(modele_ols, newdata = donnees_test[i, ])
  }

  list(actual = donnees_test[[var_dep]], predicted = predictions)
}


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — RUN ALL SIX MODELS ON BOTH SERIES
# Each model is called twice: once for Arabica using
# df_arabica_vs and vars_exo_ara_vs, and once for Robusta
# using df_robusta_vs and vars_exo_rob_vs. The four ML
# generic functions were defined in the disaggregated
# robustness check chunk and are reused here unchanged.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("Running variety-specific ARIMAX - Arabica...\n")
res_arimax_ara_vs <- fit_arimax_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                          vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific ARIMAX - Robusta...\n")
res_arimax_rob_vs <- fit_arimax_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                          vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific MLR - Arabica...\n")
res_mlr_ara_vs <- fit_mlr_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                    vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific MLR - Robusta...\n")
res_mlr_rob_vs <- fit_mlr_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                    vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific RF - Arabica...\n")
res_rf_ara_vs <- fit_rf_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                  vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific RF - Robusta...\n")
res_rf_rob_vs <- fit_rf_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                  vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific XGBoost - Arabica...\n")
res_xgb_ara_vs <- fit_xgb_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                     vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific XGBoost - Robusta...\n")
res_xgb_rob_vs <- fit_xgb_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                     vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific SVM - Arabica...\n")
res_svm_ara_vs <- fit_svm_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                    vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific SVM - Robusta...\n")
res_svm_rob_vs <- fit_svm_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                    vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)

cat("Running variety-specific ANN - Arabica...\n")
res_ann_ara_vs <- fit_ann_generique(df_arabica_vs, "arabica_price",
                                    vars_exo_ara_vs, n_train_ara_vs)
cat("Running variety-specific ANN - Robusta...\n")
res_ann_rob_vs <- fit_ann_generique(df_robusta_vs, "robusta_price",
                                    vars_exo_rob_vs, n_train_rob_vs)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — STACK PERFORMANCE METRICS
# calculer_metriques() is applied to each model's actual and
# predicted vectors. Results are stacked into a single 12-row
# data frame (6 models × 2 series) and numeric columns are
# coerced from character to numeric as in metriques_all.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_vs_all <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_ara_vs$actual, res_arimax_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ARIMAX", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_arimax_rob_vs$actual, res_arimax_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_ara_vs$actual, res_mlr_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "MLR", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_mlr_rob_vs$actual, res_mlr_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_ara_vs$actual, res_rf_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_rob_vs$actual, res_rf_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_ara_vs$actual, res_xgb_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_rob_vs$actual, res_xgb_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_ara_vs$actual, res_svm_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_rob_vs$actual, res_svm_rob_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_ara_vs$actual, res_ann_ara_vs$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_rob_vs$actual, res_ann_rob_vs$predicted))
) %>%
  mutate(across(c(R2, MSE, MAE), as.numeric))
```

*The table and chart below compare the out-of-sample $R^2$ of each model under the baseline and variety-specific specifications. A positive $ΔR^2$ indicates improvement under the variety-specific specification; a negative value indicates deterioration.*

```{r comparative_vs, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(ggh4x)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — BUILD THE COMPARISON DATA FRAME
# The baseline R² from metriques_all is joined to the
# variety-specific R² from metriques_vs_all. Delta_R2 is
# the difference between the two, positive values indicating
# improvement under the variety-specific specification.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_comparison_vs <- metriques_all %>%
  select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
  mutate(R2 = as.numeric(R2)) %>%
  rename(R2_baseline = R2) %>%
  left_join(
    metriques_vs_all %>%
      select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
      rename(R2_vs = R2),
    by = c("Model", "Series")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Delta_R2    = round(R2_vs - R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_baseline = round(R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_vs       = round(R2_vs, 4)
  )

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — DISPLAY THE COMPARISON TABLE
# Models are sorted by decreasing baseline R² within each
# series. pack_rows() adds colour-coded group headers for
# Arabica and Robusta. The Delta_R2 column is coloured green
# for positive values and red for negative values.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_comparison_vs %>%
  arrange(Series, factor(Model, levels = c("MLR", "ARIMAX", "Random Forest",
                                            "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))) %>%
  select(Model, R2_baseline, R2_vs, Delta_R2) %>%
  kable(caption   = "Baseline vs variety-specific specification — out-of-sample R²",
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        col.names = c("Model", "R² (baseline)",
                      "R² (variety-specific)", "ΔR²")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(6, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 6,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 7, 12,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec") %>%
  column_spec(4, color = ifelse(
    df_comparison_vs %>%
      arrange(Series, factor(Model, levels = c("MLR", "ARIMAX", "Random Forest",
                                                "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))) %>%
      pull(Delta_R2) > 0,
    "darkgreen", "red"))

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — BAR CHART
# Models are ordered by decreasing baseline R² to match the
# table ordering. The two specifications are shown side by
# side within each model, faceted by coffee variety.
# facet_wrap2() from ggh4x allows different strip background
# colours per panel, using Arabica brown and Robusta green
# consistent with the palette used throughout the document.
# geom_text() adds R² labels above each bar for readability.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_vs_all %>%
  mutate(Specification = "Variety-specific") %>%
  bind_rows(
    metriques_all %>%
      mutate(across(c(R2, MSE, MAE), as.numeric),
             Specification = "Baseline")
  ) %>%
  mutate(Model = factor(Model,
                        levels = c("MLR", "ARIMAX", "Random Forest",
                                   "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Model, y = R2, fill = Specification)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge",
           alpha = 0.85, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(R2, 3)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 2.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Baseline"         = "#95A5A6",
                               "Variety-specific" = "#2E5090")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.05),
                     breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  facet_wrap2(~ Series, ncol = 2,
              strip = strip_themed(
                background_x = list(
                  element_rect(fill = "#f5ece6"),
                  element_rect(fill = "#e8f5ec")
                ),
                text_x = list(
                  element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, color = "#8B4513"),
                  element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, color = "#2E8B57")
                )
              )) +
  labs(title = "Baseline vs variety-specific specification — out-of-sample R²",
       x = NULL, y = expression(R^2), fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x      = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
    legend.position  = "top"
  )
```

The variety-specific specification yields asymmetric results across the two coffee varieties, revealing an important structural difference in how variety-relevant climate and supply information contributes to predictive accuracy.

**For Robusta**, the variety-specific specification improves out-of-sample performance for four of the six models. ARIMAX gains marginally (+0.008, $R^2$ = 0.937), while Random Forest (+0.026) and XGBoost (+0.052) show more meaningful improvements, with XGBoost in particular reaching $R^2$ = 0.849 under the variety-specific specification, its strongest result across all configurations tested in this study. This confirms the central hypothesis motivating this robustness check: using climate indices and fundamentals restricted to the six Robusta-producing countries provides more relevant supply-side information than the global aggregates, which dilute the Robusta signal by including conditions in countries that produce virtually none. The improvement is most pronounced for the gradient boosting models, which are best placed to exploit the more targeted non-linear relationships between Robusta-specific supply conditions and price dynamics.

**For Arabica**, the picture is reversed. All six models deteriorate under the variety-specific specification, with ARIMAX losing 0.177 $R^2$ points and ANN producing a negative $R^2$ of −0.413. The reasons for this deterioration are discussed in the limitations section.

Taken together, these results suggest that variety-specific predictors are a genuine improvement for Robusta but not for Arabica, where the global specification already captures the relevant producing-country conditions. The XGBoost model under the Robusta variety-specific specification ($R^2$= 0.849) represents the strongest result for that variety across all configurations and specifications estimated in this study.

## OECD GDP Growth (Quarterly Specification)

This robustness check addresses a variable suggested during supervision: OECD real GDP growth, a demand-side macroeconomic indicator published only at quarterly frequency, with no monthly equivalent available. Incorporating it therefore requires moving estimation to quarterly frequency rather than approximating it within the monthly pipeline. Because changing frequency and adding a predictor are two distinct changes, three configurations are compared rather than two: the monthly baseline already reported in the comparative performance section, a quarterly configuration that aggregates the same 14 baseline predictors without GDP growth, and a quarterly configuration that adds GDP growth as a fifteenth predictor. Comparing the second and third configurations isolates the marginal contribution of GDP growth at a fixed quarterly frequency. All six models are re-estimated using the generic functions already defined for the preceding robustness checks.

*The chunk below reads the OECD quarterly GDP series, aggregates the monthly dataset to quarterly frequency, and builds the two quarterly dataset variants used in the re-estimation below.*

```{r robustness_pib_data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — READ THE OECD QUARTERLY GDP SERIES
# Quarter labels are in row 5, growth rates in row 8, both
# starting at column 3 of the raw OECD export file. The
# "trimestre" label is renamed to "date" so that the existing
# preparer_niveaux_vs() function can be reused unchanged in
# the next chunk — it only requires a column called "date"
# to sort on, regardless of its granularity.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_pib_raw <- read_excel(FICHIER_PIB, col_names = FALSE)

trimestres <- as.character(df_pib_raw[5, 3:ncol(df_pib_raw)])
pib_vals   <- as.numeric(df_pib_raw[8, 3:ncol(df_pib_raw)])

df_pib <- data.frame(date       = trimestres,
                     pib_growth = pib_vals,
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE) %>%
  filter(!is.na(date), !is.na(pib_growth), grepl("Q", date)) %>%
  filter(date >= "2000-Q1" & date <= "2023-Q4") %>%
  arrange(date)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — AGGREGATE THE MONTHLY DATASET TO QUARTERLY
# Every numeric column of dataset_mensuel is averaged within
# each quarter. na.rm = TRUE means a quarter with only one or
# two valid months (e.g. June 2006 for cot_net_mm, the first
# month the COT report exists) still produces a non-missing
# average from the months available. Quarters with zero valid
# months (e.g. cot_net_mm before mid-2006, robusta_price
# before 2008) correctly produce NaN, which is.na() treats
# as missing.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

dataset_trimestriel_base <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  mutate(date = paste0(
    substr(date, 1, 4), "-Q",
    ceiling(as.integer(substr(date, 6, 7)) / 3)
  )) %>%
  select(-date_fmt) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(date >= "2000-Q1" & date <= "2023-Q4") %>%
  arrange(date)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — BUILD THE TWO QUARTERLY DATASET VARIANTS
# dataset_trimestriel_nogdp: the 14 baseline predictors at
# quarterly frequency, no GDP — isolates the frequency effect.
# dataset_trimestriel_gdp: the same base, plus GDP growth —
# the variant of primary interest in this robustness check.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

dataset_trimestriel_nogdp <- dataset_trimestriel_base

dataset_trimestriel_gdp <- dataset_trimestriel_base %>%
  left_join(df_pib, by = "date")

cat("Quarterly base - rows:", nrow(dataset_trimestriel_base), "\n")
cat("Quarters with available GDP growth:",
    sum(!is.na(dataset_trimestriel_gdp$pib_growth)), "\n")
```

The quarterly base dataset contains 96 rows, matching the expected 288 months divided into 96 quarters with full coverage from 2000-Q1 to 2023-Q4. All 96 quarters have an available GDP growth observation, confirming that the OECD series introduces no additional missing-data constraint beyond those already present in the baseline predictors.

*The chunk below defines the variable lists for the two quarterly variants, prepares the four datasets (two series × two specifications), and computes the 80/20 train/test split indices used in the re-estimation below.*

```{r robustness_pib_split, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — VARIABLE LISTS FOR THE TWO VARIANTS
# The "no GDP" variant reuses the global vars_exo list (14
# predictors) already defined in the preprocessing chunk.
# The "with GDP" variant adds pib_growth as a 15th predictor.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_exo_pib <- c(vars_exo, "pib_growth")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 5 — PREPARE THE FOUR QUARTERLY DATASETS
# preparer_niveaux_vs() is reused unchanged from the
# variety-specific robustness check — it only requires a
# "date" column to sort on and a vars_exo_vec argument,
# both satisfied here.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_arabica_trim_nogdp <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_trimestriel_nogdp, "arabica_price", vars_exo)

df_robusta_trim_nogdp <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_trimestriel_nogdp %>% filter(!is.na(robusta_price)),
  "robusta_price", vars_exo)

df_arabica_trim_gdp <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_trimestriel_gdp, "arabica_price", vars_exo_pib)

df_robusta_trim_gdp <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_trimestriel_gdp %>% filter(!is.na(robusta_price)),
  "robusta_price", vars_exo_pib)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 6 — 80/20 SPLIT, SAME split_ratio AS EVERY OTHER MODEL
# ----------------------------------------------------------

n_train_ara_trim_nogdp <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_trim_nogdp) * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_trim_nogdp <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_trim_nogdp) * split_ratio)
n_train_ara_trim_gdp   <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_trim_gdp)   * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_trim_gdp   <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_trim_gdp)   * split_ratio)

cat("Arabica quarterly, no GDP   - Train:", n_train_ara_trim_nogdp,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_arabica_trim_nogdp) - n_train_ara_trim_nogdp, "\n")
cat("Robusta quarterly, no GDP   - Train:", n_train_rob_trim_nogdp,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_robusta_trim_nogdp) - n_train_rob_trim_nogdp, "\n")
cat("Arabica quarterly, with GDP - Train:", n_train_ara_trim_gdp,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_arabica_trim_gdp) - n_train_ara_trim_gdp, "\n")
cat("Robusta quarterly, with GDP - Train:", n_train_rob_trim_gdp,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_robusta_trim_gdp) - n_train_rob_trim_gdp, "\n")
```

The resulting training and test sizes are 56 and 15 quarters for Arabica and 51 and 13 quarters for Robusta, identical across the two variants since GDP growth does not remove any additional observation. The Arabica sample is constrained by the COT report, available only from June 2006, while the Robusta sample is constrained by its own data availability from 2008 onward, the same binding constraints as in the monthly specification, simply expressed in quarters rather than months. All six models are re-estimated using the generic functions already defined in the preceding robustness checks (`fit_arimax_generique`, `fit_mlr_generique`, `fit_rf_generique`, `fit_xgb_generique`, `fit_svm_generique`, `fit_ann_generique`), called here with the quarterly datasets and either the baseline `vars_exo` list or the extended `vars_exo_pib` list.

*The chunk below re-estimates all six models under both quarterly variants and stacks the performance metrics into two data frames for comparison in the table chunk that follows.*

cat("Running quarterly SVM (with GDP) - Arabica...\n")
res_svm_ara_trim_gdp <- fit_svm_generique(

cat("Running quarterly SVM (with GDP) - Robusta...\n")
res_svm_rob_trim_gdp <- fit_svm_generique(

*The chunk below builds the three-way comparison table and bar chart. The baseline $R^2$ is pulled directly from `metriques_all` rather than hard-coded, so the table always reflects the value produced by the most recent run.*

```{r robustness_pib_table, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 9 — COMPARISON TABLE: MONTHLY VS QUARTERLY (NO GDP / GDP)
# Baseline R² is pulled directly from metriques_all, never
# hard-coded, so the table always reflects the value actually
# produced by the most recent run. Delta_GDP isolates the
# marginal contribution of GDP growth at quarterly frequency.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_robustness_pib <- metriques_all %>%
  select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
  mutate(R2 = as.numeric(R2)) %>%
  rename(R2_mensuel = R2) %>%
  left_join(
    metriques_trim_nogdp_all %>%
      select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
      rename(R2_trim_nogdp = R2),
    by = c("Model", "Series")
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    metriques_trim_gdp_all %>%
      select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
      rename(R2_trim_gdp = R2),
    by = c("Model", "Series")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Delta_GDP     = round(R2_trim_gdp - R2_trim_nogdp, 4),
    R2_mensuel    = round(R2_mensuel, 4),
    R2_trim_nogdp = round(R2_trim_nogdp, 4),
    R2_trim_gdp   = round(R2_trim_gdp, 4)
  )

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 10 — SINGLE COMPARISON TABLE WITH pack_rows()
# Models are sorted by decreasing monthly baseline R² within
# each series. pack_rows() adds colour-coded group headers
# for Arabica and Robusta, consistent with the rest of the
# document. The Delta_GDP column is coloured green for
# positive values and red for negative values.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_robustness_pib %>%
  arrange(Series, factor(Model, levels = c("MLR", "ARIMAX", "Random Forest",
                                            "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))) %>%
  select(-Series) %>%
  kable(caption   = "Monthly baseline vs quarterly specifications, without and with GDP growth (out-of-sample R²)",
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        col.names = c("Model", "R² (monthly)", "R² (quarterly, no GDP)",
                      "R² (quarterly, with GDP)", "ΔR² (GDP effect)")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(6, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 6,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 7, 12,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec") %>%
  column_spec(5, color = ifelse(
    df_robustness_pib %>%
      arrange(Series, factor(Model, levels = c("MLR", "ARIMAX", "Random Forest",
                                                "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))) %>%
      pull(Delta_GDP) > 0,
    "darkgreen", "red"))
```

The comparison across the three configurations isolates two distinct effects: moving from monthly to quarterly frequency, and adding GDP growth as a predictor once frequency is held fixed. The frequency effect dominates. For Arabica, the two econometric benchmarks tolerate the change reasonably well, with ARIMAX falling only marginally from 0.821 to 0.815 and MLR even improving slightly to 0.820, while the four machine learning models deteriorate substantially, most severely ANN, which collapses from 0.728 to −0.951. For Robusta, the deterioration is broader and affects every model: ARIMAX drops to 0.552 at quarterly frequency, and MLR turns negative at −0.054. The most plausible explanation is sample size. The quarterly training window covers only 56 observations for Arabica and 51 for Robusta, against 168 and 153 at monthly frequency, a reduction that disproportionately penalises the more data-hungry machine learning models, in particular ANN and SVM.

Once frequency is held fixed, the addition of GDP growth produces no consistent improvement. For Arabica, five of the six models deteriorate further, in two cases substantially: SVM loses 0.123 of $R^2$ and ANN, already negative, falls another 0.800 to −1.751. For Robusta, the picture is mixed but the gains are small relative to the losses. ARIMAX, MLR and XGBoost improve marginally, by between 0.002 and 0.009 points, Random Forest deteriorates marginally, and SVM loses more than a fifth of its $R^2$ at −0.224. The one substantial gain, ANN at +0.201, starts from a negative baseline and still leaves the model only modestly above zero.

Taken together, these results provide no support for including GDP growth as a predictor. Its marginal contribution is small, inconsistently signed across models and series, and dwarfed by the cost of moving to quarterly frequency in the first place.

## Lagged COT Net Managed Money Position

The discussion of the variable importance results above raised the possibility that the COT net Managed Money position is involved in a self-reinforcing dynamic with prices, where positioning and price changes feed into each other over time rather than COT simply acting as a contemporaneous signal. If that is genuinely happening, then past values of COT net MM, not just the current month's value, should carry some additional predictive content. This robustness check tests that directly by adding the COT position lagged by one, two and three months to the baseline predictor set, alongside the contemporaneous COT variable already used throughout the study. The comparison is not between COT and no COT, but between the baseline 14-predictor specification and an extended 17-predictor specification, which isolates the marginal contribution of the lagged values specifically. All four ML models are re-estimated for both Arabica and Robusta under the extended specification, following the same walk-forward protocol used in the main results.

*This chunk constructs the lagged COT predictors and prepares the extended dataset used in the robustness check below. Three lagged versions of the net Managed Money position, one, two and three months back, are added to the baseline 14-predictor list alongside the contemporaneous COT variable already used throughout the study, yielding a 17-predictor extended specification.*

```{r robustness_cot_lag_data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — BUILD THE LAGGED COT VARIABLES
# dplyr::lag() shifts the cot_net_mm column down by n rows.
# dataset_mensuel is already sorted ascending by date (built
# that way in the assemblage chunk), so lag(cot_net_mm, 1)
# at row t returns the value from row t-1, i.e. one month
# earlier. Each additional lag introduces one more leading
# NA on top of the 77 already present at the start of the
# COT series (no Disaggregated report before June 2006).
# ----------------------------------------------------------

dataset_cot_lag <- dataset_mensuel %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(
    cot_net_mm_lag1 = dplyr::lag(cot_net_mm, 1),
    cot_net_mm_lag2 = dplyr::lag(cot_net_mm, 2),
    cot_net_mm_lag3 = dplyr::lag(cot_net_mm, 3)
  )


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — EXTENDED EXOGENOUS VARIABLE LIST
# The three lagged COT variables are added to the baseline
# 14-predictor list, alongside the contemporaneous cot_net_mm
# already included in vars_exo. This isolates the marginal
# contribution of the lagged values rather than replacing the
# contemporaneous signal.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

vars_exo_cot_lag <- c(vars_exo, "cot_net_mm_lag1", "cot_net_mm_lag2", "cot_net_mm_lag3")


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 3 — PREPARE THE TWO DATASETS (ARABICA AND ROBUSTA)
# preparer_niveaux_vs() is reused unchanged from the
# variety-specific robustness check — it only requires a
# "date" column to sort on and a vars_exo_vec argument.
# Dropping rows with any missing value here removes the
# additional 3 leading months introduced by cot_net_mm_lag3,
# on top of the 77-month COT gap already present.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_arabica_cot_lag <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_cot_lag, "arabica_price", vars_exo_cot_lag)

df_robusta_cot_lag <- preparer_niveaux_vs(
  dataset_cot_lag %>% filter(!is.na(robusta_price)),
  "robusta_price", vars_exo_cot_lag)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 4 — 80/20 SPLIT, SAME split_ratio AS EVERY OTHER MODEL
# ----------------------------------------------------------

n_train_ara_cot_lag <- floor(nrow(df_arabica_cot_lag) * split_ratio)
n_train_rob_cot_lag <- floor(nrow(df_robusta_cot_lag) * split_ratio)

cat("Arabica with lagged COT - Train:", n_train_ara_cot_lag,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_arabica_cot_lag) - n_train_ara_cot_lag, "\n")
cat("Robusta with lagged COT - Train:", n_train_rob_cot_lag,
    "| Test:", nrow(df_robusta_cot_lag) - n_train_rob_cot_lag, "\n")
cat("(Baseline for comparison - Arabica:", n_train_ara_lev,
    "train | Robusta:", n_train_rob_lev, "train)\n")
```

*The chunk below re-estimates the four ML models under the extended 17-predictor specification, reusing the generic functions already defined for the preceding robustness checks.*

```{r robustness_cot_lag_models, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# RUN THE FOUR ML MODELS, BOTH SERIES, EXTENDED SPECIFICATION
# fit_rf_generique(), fit_xgb_generique(), fit_svm_generique()
# and fit_ann_generique() were defined in the disaggregated
# robustness check and are reused unchanged here.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

cat("Running lagged-COT RF - Arabica...\n")
res_rf_ara_cotlag <- fit_rf_generique(df_arabica_cot_lag, "arabica_price",
                                      vars_exo_cot_lag, n_train_ara_cot_lag)
cat("Running lagged-COT RF - Robusta...\n")
res_rf_rob_cotlag <- fit_rf_generique(df_robusta_cot_lag, "robusta_price",
                                      vars_exo_cot_lag, n_train_rob_cot_lag)

cat("Running lagged-COT XGBoost - Arabica...\n")
res_xgb_ara_cotlag <- fit_xgb_generique(df_arabica_cot_lag, "arabica_price",
                                        vars_exo_cot_lag, n_train_ara_cot_lag)
cat("Running lagged-COT XGBoost - Robusta...\n")
res_xgb_rob_cotlag <- fit_xgb_generique(df_robusta_cot_lag, "robusta_price",
                                        vars_exo_cot_lag, n_train_rob_cot_lag)

cat("Running lagged-COT SVM - Arabica...\n")
res_svm_ara_cotlag <- fit_svm_generique(df_arabica_cot_lag, "arabica_price",
                                        vars_exo_cot_lag, n_train_ara_cot_lag)
cat("Running lagged-COT SVM - Robusta...\n")
res_svm_rob_cotlag <- fit_svm_generique(df_robusta_cot_lag, "robusta_price",
                                        vars_exo_cot_lag, n_train_rob_cot_lag)

cat("Running lagged-COT ANN - Arabica...\n")
res_ann_ara_cotlag <- fit_ann_generique(df_arabica_cot_lag, "arabica_price",
                                        vars_exo_cot_lag, n_train_ara_cot_lag)
cat("Running lagged-COT ANN - Robusta...\n")
res_ann_rob_cotlag <- fit_ann_generique(df_robusta_cot_lag, "robusta_price",
                                        vars_exo_cot_lag, n_train_rob_cot_lag)


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STACK PERFORMANCE METRICS
# Same pattern as every other robustness check: each model's
# actual and predicted vectors are passed to
# calculer_metriques(), and the eight resulting rows (4 models
# x 2 series) are stacked into a single comparison-ready frame.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

metriques_cot_lag_all <- rbind(
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_ara_cotlag$actual, res_rf_ara_cotlag$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "Random Forest", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_rf_rob_cotlag$actual, res_rf_rob_cotlag$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_ara_cotlag$actual, res_xgb_ara_cotlag$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "XGBoost", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_xgb_rob_cotlag$actual, res_xgb_rob_cotlag$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_ara_cotlag$actual, res_svm_ara_cotlag$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "SVM", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_svm_rob_cotlag$actual, res_svm_rob_cotlag$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Arabica",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_ara_cotlag$actual, res_ann_ara_cotlag$predicted)),
  cbind(Model = "ANN", Series = "Robusta",
        calculer_metriques(res_ann_rob_cotlag$actual, res_ann_rob_cotlag$predicted))
) %>%
  mutate(across(c(R2, MSE, MAE), as.numeric))
```

*The table below compares the out-of-sample $R^2$ of each ML model under the baseline 14-predictor specification and the extended 17-predictor specification that adds COT lagged by one, two and three months. A positive $ΔR^2$ indicates that the lagged COT values improve predictive accuracy beyond what the contemporaneous COT position already provides.*

```{r robustness_cot_lag_table, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1 — BUILD THE COMPARISON DATA FRAME
# The baseline R² is pulled from metriques_all (the main
# results table), filtered down to the four ML models since
# MLR and ARIMAX are not part of this comparison. It is
# joined to the lagged-COT R² computed above, and Delta_R2
# is the difference between the two: positive values mean
# the lagged COT predictors improve accuracy beyond the
# contemporaneous COT signal already in the baseline.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_robustness_cot_lag <- metriques_all %>%
  filter(Model %in% c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN")) %>%
  select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
  mutate(R2 = as.numeric(R2)) %>%
  rename(R2_baseline = R2) %>%
  left_join(
    metriques_cot_lag_all %>%
      select(Model, Series, R2) %>%
      rename(R2_cot_lag = R2),
    by = c("Model", "Series")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Delta_R2    = round(R2_cot_lag - R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_baseline = round(R2_baseline, 4),
    R2_cot_lag  = round(R2_cot_lag, 4)
  )


# ----------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 2 — DISPLAY THE COMPARISON TABLE
# Same pack_rows() / column_spec() pattern as every other
# robustness check table in this document: models sorted by
# variety, colour-coded group headers, and the Delta_R2
# column coloured green for improvement, red for deterioration.
# ----------------------------------------------------------

df_robustness_cot_lag %>%
  arrange(Series, factor(Model, levels = c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))) %>%
  select(Model, R2_baseline, R2_cot_lag, Delta_R2) %>%
  kable(caption   = "Robustness check — baseline vs lagged COT specification (out-of-sample R²)",
        booktabs  = TRUE,
        col.names = c("Model", "R² (baseline)", "R² (with COT lags)", "ΔR²")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"),
                font_size = 11, full_width = FALSE) %>%
  row_spec(4, extra_css = "border-bottom: 2px solid #333;") %>%
  pack_rows("Arabica", 1, 4,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#8B4513",
            background = "#f5ece6") %>%
  pack_rows("Robusta", 5, 8,
            bold       = TRUE,
            color      = "#2E8B57",
            background = "#e8f5ec") %>%
  column_spec(4, color = ifelse(
    df_robustness_cot_lag %>%
      arrange(Series, factor(Model, levels = c("Random Forest", "XGBoost", "SVM", "ANN"))) %>%
      pull(Delta_R2) > 0,
    "darkgreen", "red"))
```

The results provide little support for the hypothesis that lagged COT positioning carries additional predictive information beyond the contemporaneous signal already used throughout this study. Of the eight model-variety combinations tested, only two show improvement under the extended specification: XGBoost for Arabica gains a marginal 0.008 points of $R^2$, and ANN for Robusta gains a more visible 0.071 points, though this still leaves it as the weakest model for that variety. The remaining six combinations deteriorate, in some cases substantially. SVM loses 0.092 points for Arabica and 0.095 for Robusta, Random Forest loses 0.043 for Robusta, and XGBoost loses 0.054 for Robusta. The most striking result is ANN for Arabica, which collapses from an $R^2$ of 0.728 under the baseline specification to 0.184 once the three lagged COT variables are added, a deterioration of 0.545 points.

This pattern is consistent with the curse of dimensionality already documented in the disaggregated climate robustness check earlier in this section. Lagged values of the same series are by construction highly autocorrelated with each other and with the contemporaneous COT variable, so adding three additional, closely related predictors increases the dimensionality of the input space without adding much genuinely new information for the model to exploit, while shrinking the effective degrees of freedom available given the already limited training samples. The collapse of the Arabica ANN is particularly consistent with this explanation: the ANN was already flagged as the most unstable of the four ML models under walk-forward re-estimation with small samples, and three additional, highly correlated inputs are exactly the kind of change that would be expected to aggravate that instability rather than improve it.

It is worth being precise about what this result does and does not say. It does not contradict the possibility of a self-reinforcing dynamic between COT positioning and prices raised earlier in this section, since that discussion was deliberately framed as compatible with, rather than demonstrated by, the available evidence. What this check does show is that, at least for the lag structure and model specifications tested here, giving the models explicit access to COT values from one, two and three months back does not translate into better one-month-ahead forecasts. A plausible reading is that whatever information lagged COT carries is already implicitly absorbed by the contemporaneous COT variable and the other trending predictors in the baseline specification, leaving little marginal signal for the additional lags to contribute.
